articles.title: Russia receives over 8,000 North Korean troops, including hundreds of drone operators who could attack Ukraine
articles.body:
Russia receives over 8,000 North Korean troops, including hundreds of drone operators who could attack Ukraine
Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, Deputy Head of Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, has said that Russia has deployed 8,500 North Korean troops in Kursk Oblast, including 400 drone operators who are likely to use UAVs to carry out attacks on Ukraine.
Source: CNN, citing Skibitskyi
Quote: "A new wave of North Korean troops, already numbering 8,500 in Russia, contains a drone unit that could attack targets inside Ukraine, according to a senior Ukrainian intelligence official."
Details: According to Skibitskyi, thousands of North Korean engineers and bomb disposal experts are mostly dispersed across Kursk Oblast. The North Korean forces deployed in Russia also include 400 UAV operators, many of whom already have experience, and whose drones are likely to be used both for reconnaissance and attacks on Ukraine.
Around 25,000 North Koreans have so far either been part of the forces deployed in Russia or passed through the Russian armed forces, Skibitskyi said. He said that Russia could request up to 50,000 more troops during a meeting between Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un in September.
As CNN writes, such a move would represent a significant expansion of military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang and would be another sign of Russia's limited resources, as it is prepared to accept assistance despite public claims about its economic resilience and military-industrial capabilities.
Ukrainian intelligence believes that the North Koreans sent to Russia will not fight on Ukrainian territory, but will reinforce Russia's rear positions, freeing up Russian troops for offensives in Ukraine.
According to Skibitskyi, in exchange for supplying Russia with personnel and ammunition, North Korea requested S-400 air defence systems and has already received a Pantsir-S1 surface-to-air missile system.
Background:
- On 25 July, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for the arrival of another 30,000 troops from North Korea, along with new launchers for ballistic missiles. Later, in early August, he reported that Russia had received additional ballistic missiles from North Korea and planned to deploy between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans on its territory.
- Also in early August, Defence Intelligence representative Andrii Cherniak said that a North Korean missile unit had begun deploying in Russia's Voronezh Oblast. It could reportedly be equipped with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine. At the time, Pyongyang had already supplied Russia with a batch of 40 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles and sent personnel.
- On 30 July, Russia used a North Korean missile to strike a village near Kryvyi Rih, killing six members of the same family. Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the president's sanctions policy commissioner, said later that another crater from a North Korean KN-23 ballistic missile had been found, indicating that the Russians had launched at least two such missiles on Ukraine.
	
Your support on Patreon helps us keep the news free and accessible.

articles.title: Is Israel trying to start a proxy war in Syria?
articles.body:
Is Israel trying to start a proxy war in Syria?
Israeli airstrikes on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur airbase on August 18 unexpectedly turned what might otherwise have looked like another familiar episode of Israeli military activity inside a neighboring country into something far more dangerous.
This time, the real recipient of Israel’s warning was neither Iran nor Hezbollah, but Türkiye, which has emerged as one of the principal political and military partners of Syria’s new leadership since the fall of Bashar Assad. Eight strikes hit the airbase, located roughly 70 kilometers from the Turkish border, damaging runways and military infrastructure.
Israel said the operation was intended to prevent Syria from allowing Turkish forces to establish a presence there, while US and Israeli officials indicated that one of the objectives was also to disrupt the delivery of advanced Turkish weapons systems to the facility. Shortly before the attack, Mossad chief Roman Gofman had reportedly discussed with Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Shaibani the expansion of Türkiye’s military footprint, arms sales to Damascus and the possible transfer of drones to the Syrian armed forces.
Turkish-Syrian military cooperation itself is hardly a secret. As early as August 2025, Ankara formally agreed to assist the reconstruction of Syria’s armed forces through weapons, military equipment, logistics, training and advisory support, and over the past year, the two governments have steadily deepened that relationship. What remains unconfirmed, however, is whether a new shipment of Turkish weaponry was physically delivered to Syria on August 20. Yet the issue goes beyond that particular shipment.
Israel increasingly views the transformation of Turkish assistance from a reconstruction program into a permanent military infrastructure as a strategic shift in the regional balance. It is especially concerned about drones, electronic warfare systems, radar networks and, above all, the eventual deployment of modern air-defense systems that could restrict Israel’s long-standing freedom of action in Syrian airspace.
The escalation between Türkiye and Israel is advancing at a remarkable speed. For the moment, the confrontation remains largely rhetorical, diplomatic and indirect, but Syria has created the very real possibility of a proxy conflict between two states that both possess modern armed forces, sophisticated defense industries and competing visions of the regional order. Syria could become the arena in which those visions collide via the arming of allies, the destruction of military infrastructure and attempts to enforce rival red lines. Such a scenario could become the point of no return.
Syria is no longer just a buffer zone
The most important change is that post-Assad Syria is no longer merely a battleground for Israel’s campaign against Iranian influence. For years, Israel operated within a relatively predictable framework. Airstrikes targeted assets linked to the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, weapons depots and supply routes serving Hezbollah, Syrian air-defense systems and other infrastructure capable of restricting Israeli operational freedom. Türkiye was not directly a part of that equation.
Now, Ankara has acquired the opportunity to rely not only on its long-standing military presence in northern Syria and on armed groups historically aligned with it, but increasingly on the central government in Damascus itself. Syria’s new authorities need investment, reconstruction, military training, infrastructure and international political backing, all of which Türkiye is well placed to provide. For Ankara, this represents an unusually favorable strategic opening, allowing it to convert years of costly involvement in the Syrian conflict into lasting influence over the political and military architecture of the neighboring state.
Israel sees the Turkish presence as a threat. If the Syrian army remains weak, fragmented and technologically backward, Israel can preserve near-unrestricted operational freedom across large parts of Syrian territory. But if Türkiye helps Damascus rebuild a centralized army, restore airfields and radar networks, acquire drones and eventually field modern defensive systems, Israel could face a fundamentally different Syria within several years. More importantly, that Syria would no longer be backed by a sanctions-battered Iran, but by a NATO member with a rapidly expanding defense-industrial base.
The attack on Abu al-Duhur is an attempt to establish a preventive red line. Netanyahu said after the strike that Israel would not tolerate a Turkish military presence in Syria that threatened Israeli security, adding that an earlier message had apparently not been understood clearly enough. Türkiye replied by accusing the Israeli prime minister of pursuing an “expansionist and destabilizing policy,” while Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz warned Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan against testing Israel’s determination.
Even Israel’s allies in Washington are concerned. US envoy Tom Barrack described the strike as an unnecessary escalation, while the US has accelerated efforts to create a deconfliction mechanism between Israel, Türkiye and Syria. The very fact that such a mechanism is now considered necessary shows that Washington is increasingly treating an accidental or deliberate confrontation between two of its most important regional partners as a scenario that requires technical safeguards rather than as an abstract possibility.
Netanyahu needs an enemy before October
Yet it would be a mistake to think that Israel is solely pursuing military goals. Parliamentary elections are scheduled for October 27, and the campaign has already transformed Israel’s foreign policy into one of the central arenas of domestic political competition.
For Benjamin Netanyahu, this may be one of the most difficult election campaigns of his career. For decades, he built his political brand around two propositions – that he alone could guarantee Israel’s security and that he possessed a unique ability to manage relations with Washington and other world powers. Both claims are now under scrutiny. The October 7 attack shattered much of Netanyahu’s long-cultivated image as Israel’s ultimate guarantor of security. Years of war and mobilization have not produced an uncontested political outcome; relations with allies have grown more complicated, and domestic tensions have been intensified by disputes over ultra-Orthodox military service, the confrontation over the judiciary and Netanyahu’s continuing criminal trial on charges of bribery, fraud and breach of trust, all of which he denies.
His problem is compounded by shifts within the electorate itself. Netanyahu must simultaneously recover more moderate right-wing voters and prevent the radical wing of the nationalist camp from drifting toward politicians such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and other parties positioned to the right of Netanyahu’s Likud party. That creates almost ideal conditions for a return to one of Netanyahu’s most effective political instruments – the politics of the besieged fortress.
The more threatening the external danger appears, the easier it becomes to move the election away from questions about Netanyahu’s personal responsibility, his court cases, the social cost of prolonged mobilization and economic pressures, and instead turn it into a referendum on who can be trusted to lead Israel against a growing circle of enemies.
That strategy has become explicit in Likud’s campaign messaging. Billboards have placed Erdoğan alongside Iran’s supreme leader, Hezbollah Secretary-General Naim Qassem and New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, beneath the slogan that they all want Netanyahu to lose. Erdoğan is no longer a difficult foreign leader or an unreliable partner, he now stands among Israel’s traditional adversaries and is being used as part of domestic electoral mobilization.
Netanyahu’s critics are attacking him from opposite directions. Naftali Bennett, himself hardly a dove, argues that Israel’s international position has deteriorated dramatically under Netanyahu and has proposed the creation of a special public-diplomacy body to fight for Israel’s image abroad. Bennett’s criticism carries weight: There is no fundamental disagreement between him and much of the Israeli right over the need to confront hostile regional forces. The disagreement is over method and results. According to Bennett, Israel possesses enormous military power but has failed to efficiently convert it into diplomatic clout.
Ehud Barak, by contrast, has attacked Netanyahu for moving too far in the opposite direction. He described the strike on Abu al-Duhur as “reckless and foolish” and argued that it carried a strong political flavor of manufacturing security fears before the election. Barak’s position is that Türkiye is not Iran and not Assad’s Syria, and that the tensions with Ankara can still be managed through discreet channels coordinated with Washington.
Netanyahu now finds himself squeezed between those that demand he prove that Israel can still impose its will on the region, and those accusing him of turning foreign policy into an extension of his election campaign. In this tight spot, backing down before Ankara may carry almost as much domestic political risk as escalating further.
Erdoğan has reasons of his own
The situation in Türkiye’s domestic politics is similar in some aspects, but different in others. The next scheduled presidential and parliamentary elections are formally due in 2028, yet the possibility of an early vote remains a recurring subject in Turkish politics. The issue is especially relevant for Erdoğan because constitutional limits complicate another presidential run unless the legal and electoral framework changes or early elections are triggered under specific conditions. At the same time, the government continues to promote the idea of a new constitution, a project that the opposition views partly through the lens of Erdoğan’s political future.
Türkiye is also approaching the next electoral cycle from a position of persistent economic and political strain. Inflation remains high, purchasing power has been severely eroded, and the cost of housing and food continues to shape everyday voter sentiment. Even as Ankara has adopted more orthodox economic policies and rebuilt parts of its financial credibility, the social consequences of years of inflation remain politically toxic.
The political environment is also tense. Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu, Erdoğan’s most formidable long-term rival, has been imprisoned, while the main opposition party CHP has endured a severe internal crisis and leadership struggle. Turkish authorities reject accusations that legal proceedings against opposition figures are politically motivated, but the struggle over the country’s post-Erdoğan future, or perhaps Erdoğan’s continued political dominance, has already begun well before the formal campaign.
Confrontation with Israel offers Erdoğan several political advantages. It appeals simultaneously to religious-conservative and nationalist constituencies, allows Türkiye to present itself as a state capable of shaping the Middle East, and turns foreign policy activism into proof that Ankara remains an autonomous center of power despite its economic problems.
By backing the government in Damascus, Türkiye can embed itself in Syria’s future security and political architecture, weaken Kurdish armed formations, expand markets for its defense industry and deepen its political presence all the way to the Mediterranean. Erdoğan has already argued that Israeli military activity in Syria and Lebanon has reached a stage where it threatens Türkiye’s own security.
This creates a problem similar to Netanyahu’s. Once Ankara publicly presents itself as a state capable of protecting its partners and influencing the regional balance, retreating after a direct Israeli strike on an object associated with Turkish-Syrian cooperation becomes politically costly. The more Türkiye’s regional strategy depends on the perception that it can defend its interests, the harder it becomes to ignore Israeli attempts to define the limits of Turkish involvement by force.
The Mecca pact and the fear of a new Sunni axis
On August 7, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a defense agreement in Mecca. The pact reportedly includes principles of mutual protection, political and military coordination, joint exercises and cooperation in defense production, including drone manufacturing, electronic warfare and emerging technologies. Riyadh has emphasized that the arrangement should not be understood as a sectarian bloc or as an alliance directed against any particular state.
The agreement brings together Türkiye, which possesses one of NATO’s largest militaries and a rapidly growing defense industry, Saudi Arabia, which features enormous financial resources and ambitions to shape the Arab political order, and Pakistan, a nuclear-armed state with one of the largest militaries in the Muslim world.
From an Israeli perspective, this is the kind of development that feeds concern over the emergence of a new Sunni axis. What matters is not whether the three countries have formally created an anti-Israel alliance. They have not. Their interests differ, their relationships with Washington are distinct, and Saudi Arabia in particular has reasons to avoid being locked into an overtly anti-Israeli structure. But Israeli strategists are increasingly focused on the possibility that Turkish military power, Saudi financial weight and Pakistani strategic capabilities could gradually become parts of a broader political-security architecture capable of limiting Israel’s freedom of maneuver.
This concern is not limited to Netanyahu’s camp, either. Bennett has previously warned of the danger of Türkiye becoming a kind of “new Iran” and of a hostile Sunni strategic framework emerging with the involvement of nuclear-armed Pakistan. Once Saudi Arabia is added to that picture, the implications become even more uncomfortable for Israel, especially because normalization with Riyadh was for years regarded as one of the top strategic objectives of Israeli diplomacy. After decades of confronting what Israeli strategists described as an Iranian-led “Shiite crescent,” Israel may now be facing the early outlines of a very different regional center of gravity – one that conflicts with the idea of Israel as the uncontested dominant power of the region, and potentially with the nationalist expansionist vision of ‘Greater Israel’ itself.
For Ankara, on the other hand, the Mecca pact is another opportunity to evolve from an autonomous regional player into one of the architects of a new Middle Eastern security order. It allows Erdoğan to deepen strategic ties with the largest Arab economy, reinforce relations with a nuclear power, consolidate influence in Syria and demonstrate to Turkish voters that, despite domestic economic difficulties and political tensions, Türkiye is capable of shaping events far beyond its borders.
The current Turkish-Israeli confrontation is about more than Erdoğan and Netanyahu, or even about Syria itself. It is the product of two processes occurring simultaneously. At home, both leaders have powerful incentives to demonstrate strength amid electoral pressure, economic problems and social polarization. Abroad, competition for regional leadership and military-political influence is intensifying rapidly in a Middle East where the old post-Assad balance has already begun to disappear.
Neither Ankara nor West Jerusalem appears to want a direct war – yet if Türkiye continues to arm and train the Syrian military while Israel systematically destroys the infrastructure created with Turkish assistance, a de facto proxy conflict will already exist. But if Turkish servicemen are killed in a future strike, or if Israel deliberately destroys a major Turkish military asset inside Syria, the domestic political cost of restraint for Erdoğan would rise dramatically. Conversely, if Syrian forces using Turkish-supplied systems were to shoot down an Israeli aircraft, Netanyahu would face exactly the same political dilemma, particularly only weeks before the October election.
When foreign confrontation starts to define a leader’s domestic political legitimacy, the space for compromise contracts much faster than the space for military action.

articles.title: The dragon spreads its wings: China is balancing between rival powers to expand its influence
articles.body:
While the U.S. and Russia remain bogged down in their wars of choice, China's formal. neutrality has allowed it to benefit from the situation, hosting Trump, Putin, and various European leaders in Beijing. Balancing between the opposing sides in Ukraine and the Middle East, China is doing everything it can to avoid direct involvement while continuing to provide measured support to its authoritarian partners. While presenting itself as a peacemaker, China is in fact not particularly interested in establishing any peace that would deprive it of its leverage.
As early as 2017, Chinese leader Xi Jinping described the state of affairs in the world as a period of “changes unseen in a century.” Since then, the international order has faced a series of serious challenges, from the war in Ukraine to the protracted conflict in the Middle East and the military confrontation between Iran and the U.S. All of these upheavals have one thing in common: Chinese involvement — not as a direct participant, but as an interested party nevertheless.
The forms of this involvement can vary, from indirect support for one side to mediation efforts in disputes between countries friendly to Beijing. In Western analytical circles, such behavior is often described as opportunistic – aimed at capitalizing on chaos.
Yet viewing all of Beijing’s moves through this lens would be an oversimplification. China’s responses do indeed vary depending on how strongly its key interests are affected, the level of risk involved, and the opportunities that arise. Protecting national interests while maintaining relations with all sides is not a neutral position; it is a deliberate strategy in which the long-term strengthening of China’s position always takes precedence over short-term gains.
What drives Beijing
Until the mid-2010s, China and its position on international conflicts were noticeably more restrained. Before Xi Jinping came to power, the foreign policy of the People’s Republic of China was cautious and even reactive. This approach is often described using the well-known dictum of Deng Xiaoping: “Hide your capabilities and bide your time.” For nearly three decades, Beijing deliberately prioritized economic development over geopolitical ambitions, avoided unnecessary friction with the West, and avoided taking on the role of arbiter in other countries’ disputes.
The shift began after Xi took the helm of the country in 2012–2013. Within the Chinese leadership, there was growing discussion that Beijing's international status no longer corresponded to its dramatically increased economic power.
Foreign policy therefore became more assertive. China launched global initiatives, above all the Belt and Road Initiative, established its first overseas military base in Djibouti, and, most importantly, became more willing to defend its own interests. This meant not only greater involvement in global affairs but also an attempt to gradually reshape the international order.
China’s behavior in international conflicts is determined above all by a hierarchy of interests. These can broadly be divided into two groups. The first consists of core interests. When a conflict touches on them, compromises are effectively off the table, and Beijing’s actions become significantly more assertive. These absolute priorities include the country’s territorial integrity (including the Taiwan issue), economic development, and the stability of the political system.
When secondary interests are at stake, China’s approach can become more pragmatic. If a crisis does not threaten the country’s vital interests, Beijing can use it to strengthen its image as a responsible international player and expand its influence. Moreover, participation in such processes allows China to promote its own vision of international relations and present an alternative to Western approaches to conflict resolution.
When a crisis does not threaten the country’s vital interests, Beijing uses it to strengthen its image as a responsible international player
According to political scientist Rush Doshi, China pursues a long-term strategy in international politics aimed at displacing the United States from the regional and global. Ultimately, Beijing seeks to become the power that shapes the world’s destiny. Similarly, international relations scholar Oriana Skylar Mastro argues that China uses its “agents of chaos” – Iran, Russia, and North Korea – to create problems for the U.S. and its allies. In her view, these actions weaken Washington's power by diverting its attention and resources.
However, China rarely opts for direct confrontation with the West. The logic behind its foreign policy is best described by the Chinese concept of relationality, which contrasts with the emphasis that the Western school of international relations places on the rational calculations of individual states and their national interests. According to relationality proponent Qin Yaqing, China views the world not through the prism of individual countries’ interests but through the relationships that are constantly evolving among the participants in global politics. From the Chinese perspective, relations between states should be maintained despite disagreements. When conflicts arise, they should be contained in order to minimize the damage to those relationships.
Closely linked to relationality is another important concept in Chinese foreign policy: the principle of peaceful coexistence. Formulated by Chinese Premier Zhou Enlai as early as 1954, this principle includes mutual respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, mutual non-aggression, noninterference in internal affairs, equality and mutual benefit, and peaceful coexistence.
Beijing invokes these principles when commenting on international conflicts as well. In doing so, China demonstrates its willingness not to intervene directly in other countries’ disputes while at the same time demanding the same treatment for itself. This approach allows it to maintain relations with all sides even in tense situations.
Yet it would be inaccurate to portray Chinese foreign policy exclusively in pacifist terms. Since the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, there have been numerous instances when the principles of respect for sovereignty, territorial integrity, and non-aggression gave way to military force. This was the case, for example, during the invasion of Vietnam in 1979 and the armed clashes with India along the disputed border in 1962. During the Maoist period, Beijing also actively interfered in the internal affairs of other countries, supporting communist insurgencies in the so-called Third World.
After the launch of the reform and opening-up policy in the late 1970s, the Chinese authorities no longer took such overtly adventurous steps, instead favoring gray-zone tactics, economic pressure, and diplomacy. Strategically, if China were to behave the way it alleges the U.S. does, Beijing would lose an important advantage: its image as a restrained and “constructive” player. For this reason, China generally adheres to the fundamental principles of its foreign policy, but it is nevertheless prepared to selectively depart from them when its core interests are threatened.
This combination of factors – the primacy of interests, a focus on relationships, and a desire to play a greater role in global affairs – allows China to take a flexible approach to conflicts. Chinese diplomatic strategy is thus aimed at building the desired type of relations with other countries while strengthening China’s image as a defender of peace. Beijing does not always succeed in this, however, and calls for peace are sometimes replaced by shows of force.
What kind of China are you today?
In responding to different crises, China actively adjusts its role and chooses the strategy it considers most appropriate. These roles can broadly be divided into four types: the coexisting titan, the uncompromising master, the wise judge, and the advocate of “everything good.”
Chinese diplomacy adopts the first role in its relations with the U.S. Although Washington and Beijing are not engaged in an armed conflict, their strategic rivalry is one of the major potential conflicts of the 21st century.
Even under the Biden administration, the U.S. National Security Strategy described China as its main long-term competitor. China, for its part, also acknowledges that its relationship with the United States is the most important in the world and that it needs to be managed carefully to avoid a crisis.
The contentious nature of the relationship stems from the fact that China poses a threat to the U.S. in virtually every key sphere. The rivalry between the two powers encompasses semiconductors, trade, the military sphere, technological development, as well as the struggle for influence around the world.
As a rising great power, China has its own vision of the future world order. In Beijing’s view, the existing international system should not be dismantled but reformed along multipolar lines. In the model of the world order that China openly advocates, it does not seek the emergence of a single hegemon but instead says it wants to create an order based on dialogue. Within this framework, the U.S. still has an important role, but in the long term Beijing hopes to secure Washington’s recognition of a multipolar world, respect for its “red lines,” and fairer competition.
China’s strategy is aimed at preventing open conflict, which is why Xi has consistently advocated building a “new type of great-power relations.” The idea is to acknowledge the differences between the two countries and continue competing while maintaining direct, high-level dialogue in the political and military spheres.
When conflict cannot be avoided, China responds to pressure with symmetrical measures. For example, during the latest tariff war of Donald Trump’s second presidential term, Beijing not only responded to U.S. tariffs with tariffs of its own, but also restricted exports of rare earth minerals. Even amid intense rivalry, the PRC seeks less to gain a decisive advantage than to preserve the status quo by keeping the competition within reasonable limits.
However, when disputes directly affect China’s core interests — territorial integrity, sovereignty, and national security — Beijing’s pragmatism takes a back seat. Geographically, most of these interests are concentrated in East Asia, a region where China expects to become the dominant power.
When it comes to territorial disputes, rhetoric about mutual benefit gives way to assertive and forceful action, as is most clearly evidenced in the case of Taiwan (and the debate over a possible Chinese attempt to forcibly annex the island by 2027). China insists that it does not want an escalation of the conflict over the island, but it is also unwilling to tolerate manifestations of political support for the democratic authorities in Taipei. Rather than openly seeking to alter the status quo in the Taiwan Strait, Beijing actively uses “gray-zone” tactics that include expanding the area of its naval exercises, conducting regular flights by military aircraft, and patrolling the waters around the island. This allows China to deter Taiwan’s allies from becoming involved lest they cross the threshold into direct armed confrontation.
When it comes to territorial disputes, rhetoric about mutual benefit gives way to assertive and forceful action
China responds similarly to other challenges of this kind. For example, Beijing often answers with forceful measures to what it considers unfriendly moves by Japan. In November 2025, when Tokyo's newly appointed Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi described a possible attack on Taiwan as an existential threat to Japan itself, China’s reaction was swift. Japan was hit by a barrage of restrictive measures, including the suspension of imports of Japanese seafood and the cancellation of flights. In this way, China demonstrates that any actions it considers to be an infringement on its sovereign interests will be met with the strongest possible response.
China also participates in conflicts as a mediator. This usually occurs in situations where Beijing has significant economic interests, the U.S. has a relatively weak presence, and the risk of being drawn into armed confrontation is minimal. In such circumstances, Beijing seeks to maintain an equidistant position from the conflicting parties while preserving working relations with each side until an agreement is reached.
One notable success of Chinese diplomacy was the normalization of relations between Saudi Arabia and Iran in 2023. Thanks to Chinese mediation, on March 10 of that year the two sides signed a joint statement in which they pledged, among other things, to restore diplomatic relations.
It was not by chance that China achieved this success. The PRC buys substantial volumes of oil from both countries and is a particularly important oil export market for Iran. Second, Beijing maintains good relations with both Riyadh and Tehran, whereas the U.S. could not credibly claim the role of a neutral mediator because of its decades-long confrontation with Iran. The combination of these factors enabled China to mediate in a distant conflict while simultaneously strengthening its image as a peace-loving power.
However, the latest escalation of the Middle East conflict – between Iran on one side and the U.S. and Israel on the other – demonstrated the limitations of China’s peacemaking capacity. After the armed conflict in Iran entered a hot phase in late February, China’s Foreign Ministry condemned the actions of the U.S. and Israel and expressed concern over the developments. At the same time, Zhai Jun, the Chinese government’s special envoy for Middle Eastern affairs, engaged in shuttle diplomacy, visiting regional capitals in an attempt to maintain contact with all its partners.
As the conflict dragged on, Beijing again called on the sides to resolve their differences as soon as possible and return to dialogue. The results of China’s 2023 efforts did not go to waste: Iran and Saudi Arabia maintained diplomatic relations despite U.S. strikes against Iran launched from Saudi territory.
In practice, however, this was the extent of China’s role in the conflict. Beijing’s actions demonstrated that Chinese diplomacy can help improve relations only when the parties themselves are willing to do so. In a hot conflict where Beijing lacks coercive tools comparable to those available to Washington, China’s peacemaking efforts prove ineffective.
There is, however, a fourth role China plays in international conflicts, one that has been most clearly manifested in its position on the war in Ukraine. After February 24, 2022, Beijing found itself in a difficult position. On the one hand, its key economic partners in the West expected China to pressure the Kremlin and work to stop the war. On the other hand, there is Russia, which Beijing needs as a counterweight in its strategic confrontation with the West.
To preserve its image as a constructive player, China had to adopt a position that many researchers describe as pro-Russian neutrality. Beijing continued to develop economic ties with Moscow, providing Moscow with dual-use goods and assistance in circumventing some sanctions. Formally, China does not supply Russia with lethal weapons, and in its official statements it continues to emphasize the importance of the principle of respect for territorial integrity – a message aimed at Western audiences. In reality, however, military cooperation with Russia is far broader than officially acknowledged.
At the same time, the war in Ukraine remains fairly remote from China’s vital interests. Although both Russia and Ukraine are important partners for China, it has little reason to intervene directly in the conflict. That is why Beijing’s policy on the issue remains highly abstract. In a peace plan published in February 2023, China called for a ceasefire and the start of negotiations, but offered no concrete measures for ending the war.
This once again shows that Beijing has no desire to act as the world’s policeman, certainly not when it comes to faraway conflicts that have little bearing on its interests. Instead, in such conflicts, China balances between the interests of the various parties, makes peace proposals largely for the sake of appearances, and waits for an opportunity to normalize relations and further develop ties.
China’s involvement in the war between Iran and the U.S. has taken on features broadly similar to its position on the conflict in Ukraine. According to media reports, Beijing is supplying Iran with dual-use goods, intelligence and satellite imagery, and, according to some reports, is also making commercial arms shipments. The Chinese side, however, denies all allegations of any involvement in military operations.
As in the case of Russia, Beijing has no interest in the fall of Iran’s regime – an important oil supplier – and is therefore prepared to support the combat capability of Iranian forces to some extent. However, this assistance is provided in ways that preserve as much room as possible for plausible deniability.
More than just calculation
In practice, Beijing’s involvement in conflicts does not always lead to success. By trying to balance between the opposing sides in the war in Ukraine, China’s close ties with Russia have in one way or another undermined the trust of Western countries. Although China’s peacemaking efforts have produced some successes, they are typically undertaken reluctantly. Meanwhile, attempts to impose its preferred order in the Taiwan Strait or the South China Sea encourage its rivals to strengthen their own military and political coordination with the U.S.
Importantly, China’s strategy in different conflicts is not driven by material gain alone. Whenever fighting breaks out anywhere in the world today, the international community inevitably asks: what will China gain from it? The answer is most often sought in economic or geopolitical terms. However, if Beijing’s main objective truly were to maximize the benefits it derives from other countries’ conflicts, its actions would be far more aggressive.
For example, it would use crises to resolve disputes along its borders by force, or else impose more favorable terms of cooperation on Russia and Iran, both of which are already dependent on China to some extent. Yet this does not happen.
For Beijing, involvement in international conflicts is neither an end in itself nor a means of scoring political points. Moreover, when it comes to conflicts that are distant and have little bearing on its interests, China’s leadership seeks to distance itself by limiting its actions to calls for peace. By playing different roles depending on the situation, China is pursuing broader goals: strengthening its power, pushing for changes to the international order, and turning itself into a recognized center of influence.
China has ambitious goals: to strengthen its power, reshape the international order, and turn itself into a recognized center of power
In the view of China’s ruling elite, the desired global order has several distinctive features. First, there should be no single hegemon in the world, and international relations should be “democratized.” Second, great powers must respect each other’s sovereignty and “red lines,” recognize the legitimacy of different political systems (rather than just liberal democracy), and build relations on the basis of managed competition rather than direct confrontation. Third, in the future world order envisioned by Beijing, greater weight should be given not only to international organizations but also to countries of the Global South.
Judging by the statements and actions of the Chinese leadership, the transition to such an order should take place gradually and relatively smoothly, without immediately undermining the existing system. That is why maximizing the benefits of each individual conflict is not a priority. Instead, China’s strategy continues to put long-term relationships and the protection of its interests first – a foundation whose returns will become evident in the future.

articles.title: Kyiv is asking Musk to let it strike inside Russia. Its best line to Musk is gone
articles.body:
Ukraine is asking Elon Musk to let it arm deep-strike drones with his Starlink network and turn them on Russian ballistic-missile launchers far inside Russia, the Financial Times reported. The plan needs Musk's approval — and US President Donald Trump was cool to the idea when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy raised it at the White House on 28 July, with people present expecting Musk to refuse.
Kyiv is chasing the workaround because its air defenses are stretched: Russia keeps escalating its missile and drone strikes, and Ukraine is running low on the Patriot interceptors that are its only dependable answer to Russian ballistic missiles. As Russia builds more missiles and drones, Ukraine's interceptor needs run into the hundreds before the year is out.
At the meeting, FT reported, Zelenskyy pressed Trump to lobby Musk for permission to fly Starlink-linked drones across the Russian border. He capped the pitch at 200 km into Russia — far enough to reach launch sites, command posts, and other targets — on the calculation that a shallower limit might make Musk likelier to agree.
Starlink could extend Ukrainian drone strikes
Riding SpaceX's satellites, Starlink drones hold a steadier link to their pilots at long range than ordinary radio allows, and they shrug off the jamming that grounds other drones. The drones have already shown their worth in the fighting at home, and Vienna-based military analyst Franz-Stefan Gady said that across the border they "could be very useful in hunting" Russian launchers, FT wrote.
Kyiv's best channel to Musk has also just closed: Zelenskyy recently fired his defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov, who had a direct line to the billionaire.
Speaking to a Ukrainian podcast on 6 August, Fedorov said that even with a channel to Musk still open after his firing, he had made no progress on cross-border Starlink use—"a difficult task right now."
The Fedorov protesters lost. But they backed a man for what he built, not what he promised—and that may be new in Ukraine.
Musk’s Starlink decisions have affected both sides in the Russo-Ukrainian war
Musk has backed Ukraine's heavy dependence on Starlink for military command and comms. In 2022, Musk declined to extend Starlink coverage for Ukrainian troops mid-operation near occupied Crimea, citing his fear of triggering a nuclear escalation.
He has also acted against Moscow: in February, at Fedorov's direct request, Musk shut down the Starlink terminals that Russian forces had been operating illicitly against Ukraine.
Now, Musk answered Fedorov's Monday post with a line about "trying to do the right thing" and wanting peace — and said nothing about the Starlink ask.

articles.title: Ukraine finally hit three Russian Kalibr ships on 12 August. On the 19th, an untouched one hit Kyiv
articles.body:
- After months of trying, Ukrainian forces may have finally hit some of the Russian Black Sea Fleet's Kalibr missile-armed warships
- The 2,500-km Kalibr is often in the mix when Russian forces bombard Ukrainian cities
- Hitting any Kalibr shooter is a win for Ukraine, but Russia still has at least five intact Kalibr-compatible ships on the Black Sea
The Russian navy still has enough missile-armed warships in its battered Black Sea Fleet to sustain Kalibr cruise missile attacks on Ukrainian cities, if recent launches are any indication.
Overnight on 19 August, an unscathed Russian corvette lobbed eight Kalibrs at Ukraine. Seven were intercepted. The eighth struck the Antonov Aircraft Plant in Kyiv, according to the open-source monitor OSINT Warfare. Ukrainian commanders had hoped that wouldn't be possible. A week earlier, they thought they had knocked the Kalibr shooters out of the fight.
Overnight on 12 August, Ukrainian drones and missiles targeted the Black Sea Fleet's main anchorage in Novorossiysk in southern Russia. Russians on the ground recorded fireballs billowing into the night sky, seemingly indicating significant damage to the port or its moored warships, potentially including the Black Sea Fleet's seven or eight surviving frigates, corvettes, and submarines that are compatible with the 2,500-km Kalibr.
The Ukrainian general staff in Kyiv claimed its forces had struck three Kalibr carriers—the frigates Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen and a Buyan-M corvette—as well as a lightly armed guard ship. But the uncertainty was, and still is, high. Even the general staff stressed its munitions had inflicted "varying degrees" of damage "according to preliminary information."
"Information is being clarified," the general staff stressed.
When the sun rose over the following days, commercial satellites snapped high-resolution photos of Novorossiysk, helping analysts assess damage from the 12 August strikes. The photos were hard to interpret. Yes, there were dark patches on the hulls of the two frigates and single corvette, but the discoloration didn't necessarily indicate drone or missile damage—to say nothing of confirming serious damage.
The pro-Ukraine Conflict Intelligence Team concluded Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen "sustained damage in the area of their launchers," potentially impacting the ships' ability to fire Kalibrs. But even CIT conceded that "the extent of the damage remains unclear."
Uncertainty
Caution was prudent. In the first three years of Russia's wider war on Ukraine, Ukrainian forces succeeded in destroying or damaging around two dozen of the roughly 85 large ships in the Black Sea Fleet. Perhaps most notably, a pair of Ukrainian Neptune cruise missiles holed and sank the Russian missile cruiser Moskva in April 2022.
But the strikes mostly missed the Kalibr carriers. Yes, the Ukrainians took out a Kalibr-armed Improved Kilo-class submarine in September 2023 and a Karakurt-class corvette, also armed with Kalibrs, in November 2023. But that left at least seven Kalibr shooters in the Black Sea Fleet. Eight if the Russians have managed to repair the Improved Kilo that apparently suffered some damage from a Ukrainian one-way unmanned attack submarine back in December.
It wasn't for a lack of trying that Ukrainian forces failed to eliminate, or even seriously dent, the Black Sea Fleet's Kalibr capacity prior to the 12 August raid on Novorossiysk. On 22 May, Fire Point FP-1 drones operated by the Ukrainian 414th Separate Unmanned Strike Aviation System Brigade motored the roughly 430 km to Novorossiysk and spotted a warship moored to a pier.
Putin’s Mach-10 wonder weapon misses by 30 meters. Russia stopped building it in April.
Trending Now
The 414th Brigade believed it was Admiral Essen—and also believed it may have hit the ship. "The frigate Admiral Essen … entered the strike zone," the brigade crowed. "Damage level unknown."
In fact, it seems the ship the propeller-driven FP-1 barreled toward, and potentially struck with its warhead, wasn't Admiral Essen. The vessel in the FP-1's video feed, relayed via satellite or a mesh radio network, appeared to be a derelict Krivak-class frigate. Not Admiral Essen.
It was yet another near miss. Earlier, on 6 April, FP-1s dove down on Admiral Makarov. The Ukrainian Unmanned Systems Forces posted footage from the FP-1s' forward-facing thermal cameras that indicated the drones got close to Admiral Makarov. But the footage didn't point to an obvious hit.
Overhead satellite imagery from later on 6 April seemingly told a more complete story. The drones may have left a scorch mark on the frigate's bow, but there was no sign of structural damage. If the 12 August raid really did inflict meaningful damage on Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen and a Buyan-M, it represented a profound reversal for Ukrainian forces. After trying and trying again for months, they'd finally hit some of the ships that really mattered among the survivors of the Black Sea Fleet.
The problem for the Ukrainians is that, even if three Kalibr shooters are temporarily out of the fight, there are still five Kalibr shooters left. And that's enough to sustain frequent attacks on Ukrainian cities. A single Buyan-M corvette can fire eight Kalibrs at a time. And eight, as it turns out, is a typical number of Kalibrs in the mix when Russian air, sea, and ground forces launch their combined drone and missile barrages.
The Black Sea Fleet reminded everyone of that uncomfortable fact overnight on 19 August. A Buyan-M corvette at Novorossiysk fired eight Kalibrs—exactly one magazine—into a barrage that also carried Onyx and Zircon missiles, Iskander-M and KN-23 ballistic missiles, three dozen air-launched cruise missiles, and 168 drones. Ukrainian air defenses stopped seven of the eight Kalibrs. They could not stop the ballistic missiles, and the eighth Kalibr got through to the Antonov plant, which had already been hit that night by Iskanders and Zircons.
If the attack on 12 August actually did eliminate or even just temporarily sideline three Kalibr carriers, it still represents a partial victory for Ukraine. It's likely no fewer than five shooters remain. And given how long it took Ukrainian deep strike forces to maybe damage Admiral Makarov and Admiral Essen and that Buyan-M, the Black Sea Fleet may be able to continue blasting away at Ukrainian cities for many months to come.

articles.title: The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) stated that North Korea has sent a new military contingent to Russia, including 400 drone operators
articles.body:
The Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) stated that North Korea has sent a new military contingent to Russia, including 400 drone operators
Kyiv • UNN
The new wave of North Korean troops in Russia includes 400 drone operators capable of conducting reconnaissance and attacking targets in Ukraine. Pyongyang may be asked to send up to 50,000 more troops.
The new wave of North Korean troops, whose number in Russia has already reached 8,500, includes a drone unit that may attack targets in Ukraine. This was reported by a high-ranking Ukrainian intelligence official, UNN reports, citing CNN.
Details
North Korea, which signed a NATO-style mutual defense pact with Russia two years ago, has been sending troops since late 2024 to assist Moscow’s military operations. According to Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, deputy head of the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine, it may be asked to provide up to 50,000 more servicemen during President Vladimir Putin’s meeting with his counterpart Kim Jong Un in September.
The outlet notes that such a move would mark a significant expansion of military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang, taking place amid an acute shortage of air defense systems in Ukraine. This is another sign that Russia’s resources are limited and that it is ready to accept assistance despite public statements about its economic resilience and military-industrial capacity.
Skibitskyi said that the North Korean troops already deployed are spread mostly across Russia’s Kursk region and include 1,000 engineers and sappers. They also include 400 drone operators, many of whom gained experience either during or as a result of previous North Korean deployments, and whose drones will likely be used both for reconnaissance and to attack targets in Ukraine.
The media outlet notes that North Korea’s deepening ties with Russia concern many NATO alliance members, especially after President Donald Trump announced on Sunday that military exercises with South Korea would be scaled back so as not to provoke hostility from Kim Jong Un — the reclusive North Korean leader whom Trump seeks to meet again.
Earlier, Kim’s influential sister, Kim Yo Jong, denied claims that tens of thousands of North Koreans would soon join Russia’s efforts, calling them a "groundless self-invented scenario."
In addition
Ukrainian intelligence believes that the North Korean troops sent to Russia will not fight on Ukrainian territory, Skibitskyi said, but will reinforce Russia’s rear positions, freeing Russian troops for attacks inside Ukraine.
Although Ukraine first warned that North Korean troops were using attack drones on its territory last October, this is the first indication that the new wave of troops will have this capability. In addition to Putin’s likely request for more troops, approximately 25,000 North Koreans have already been deployed or rotated through Russia’s armed forces, Skibitskyi added.
Context
The first North Korean deployment began in the Kursk region in October 2024 to repel Ukraine’s incursion, the first on Russian soil since the Nazis. North Korea remained silent for months about its initial deployment of troops to assist Russia’s war machine and confirmed that its soldiers were fighting against Ukraine only in April 2025. An estimated 10,000 North Koreans were deployed and suffered significant losses, using suicidal tactics to conduct mass assaults on Ukrainian positions.
The media outlet notes that North Korea’s willingness to sustain such losses reflects the scale of Russia’s global alliances and Moscow’s need for additional manpower. The wounded returned to North Korea, where they were able to teach their colleagues how to use drones and about the new reality of technologically dominated front lines.
Underscoring the strength of ties between the two countries, Russian state media over the past year showed photographs of North Korean troops training in Russia, while Kim Jong Un opened a memorial to North Koreans killed in Ukraine in April.

articles.title: Iran modernizing defense industry in response to US-Israeli aggression: Defense Ministry
articles.body:
Iran modernizing defense industry in response to US-Israeli aggression: Defense Ministry
TEHRAN — Iran's Defense Ministry has announced that the country is comprehensively modernizing its defense industry in the wake of the recent wars launched by the US and Israel. In an official statement issued on Thursday, the ministry declared that these conflict periods “were an opportunity to gain a more precise understanding of capabilities, reveal new needs, and chart the path for the future. We have learned never to stop.”
The statement, released on the occasion of Iran’s National Defense Industry Day on August 22, added: “Accordingly, we consider the recent imposed war a war of the past; without pride or apprehension, we continuously modernize, reinvent, and update the defense industry in line with these findings and lessons.” The ministry emphasized that Iran’s defense capabilities—developed over decades by Iranian experts, alongside the high operational readiness of the country's armed forces and the steadfast resilience of the Iranian nation—“thwarted a significant part of the enemy's calculations and goals and left them astonished.”
Furthermore, the ministry noted that recent military aggression has proved that national unity remains the fundamental pillar of national security, underpinning the Islamic Republic's ongoing strength and progress. “The experience of recent wars has shown that the stronger the bond between the nation and the armed forces, the greater the country's ability to confront threats and overcome crises,” the statement read. It stressed that decades of illegal Western sanctions and aggressive threats have only hardened Iran’s resolve to rely on its domestic capabilities. The ministry also paid solemn tribute to the martyrs of the Defense Ministry who made the ultimate sacrifice “in defense of the country and the Iranian nation” during the June 2025 war and the 39-day war launched by the US and Israel in late February.
Outlining its core mandate, the ministry asserted that its overarching mission is “to transform battlefield experience into knowledge, knowledge into technology, and technology into the defense capability of the future.” “This path will continue with reliance on God Almighty, under the strategic command of His Eminence Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, and with the unwavering support of the Iranian people alongside the dedicated efforts of a new generation of scientists, specialists, and youth of this land.”
Unprovoked aggression
The US and Israel initiated another round of unprovoked aggression against Iran on February 28, coming approximately eight months after their previous unlawful attacks on Iranian territory in June 2025. Exercising its inherent right to self-defense under Article 51 of the UN Charter, Iran swiftly responded by launching devastating barrages of advanced, domestically produced precision ballistic missiles and long-range attack drones. These retaliatory strikes systematically targeted critical military infrastructure within the Israeli-occupied territories as well as key US command facilities across the region. After 39 days of intense operational exchanges, a ceasefire officially took effect on April 8.
Demonstrating its goodwill and commitment to regional tranquility from a position of undeniable military strength, Iran subsequently engaged in negotiations. On June 17, a memorandum of understanding (MoU) was signed between the Iranian and US presidents, intended to establish a durable framework to end hostilities and launch a 60-day diplomatic process to resolve underlying disputes.
However, Washington's persistent bad faith and reliance on coercive diplomacy were laid bare once again when renewed US strikes flagrantly violated the MoU framework, forcing Iran to deploy its decisive counter-strike capabilities once more.
The doctrines of deterrence
The Defense Ministry’s statement on the eve of National Defense Industry Day is more than a routine commemoration; it is a clear declaration of a paradigm shift in West Asian strategic dynamics. The recent military confrontations have shattered long-held Western military assumptions regarding the vulnerability of sovereign nations under total blockade.
For decades, military planners in Washington and Tel Aviv relied on the doctrine of absolute aerial superiority and sophisticated missile defense umbrellas. However, the operational reality of recent conflicts demonstrated that Iran’s asymmetrical warfare doctrine—driven by hypersonic maneuverability, decentralized drone swarms, and hardened underground launch complexes—has rendered conventional Western defense doctrines obsolete. By converting real-time tactical intelligence into industrial modifications within weeks, Iranian defense engineers successfully bypassed enemy air defenses, establishing a strategic equilibrium that foreign aggressors cannot break.
The breach of the June 17 MoU by the United States highlights a chronic structural flaw in Western strategy: the inability to honor international commitments when military coercion fails. Much like previous illegal treaty breaches, Washington’s failure to abide by the diplomatic framework underscores that US foreign policy remains held hostage by regional warmongers and Israeli expansionism. Iran’s swift counter-retaliation served notice that the era of "hit-and-run" aggression without consequence has permanently ended.
The Defense Ministry’s explicit emphasis on transforming "battlefield experience into technology" highlights the maturity of Iran’s defense-industrial complex. Unlike regional US client states that depend entirely on imported military hardware, maintenance contractors, and foreign operational approval, Iran’s defense infrastructure is entirely indigenous. Decades of unilateral sanctions—intended to cripple the nation's scientific sector—have instead forced the emergence of a self-sustaining defense ecosystem led by young Iranian scientists, technical universities, and strategic research centers.
The underlying calculation of Western strategists during foreign aggressions was that external military pressure would create internal societal fractures within the Islamic Republic. Once again, foreign intelligence agencies fundamentally misread the Iranian psyche. External threats have historically served to solidify national cohesion, uniting diverse socio-economic strata behind the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic. The public's steadfast endurance under aggression proved that popular support remains Iran's most potent defense asset.
As Iran enters a new era of defense development under the strategic guidance of Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei, the message from Tehran is clear: Iran seeks neither war nor escalation, but its response to external aggression will remain swift, proportionate, and technologically superior.  By treating recent military encounters not as crises, but as industrial laboratories for technical refinement, Iran’s Defense Ministry is laying the groundwork for a deterrence architecture capable of neutralizing next-generation threats. Washington and its regional surrogates must realize that continued aggression will only accelerate the expansion of Iran's defensive radius, solidifying the Islamic Republic's position as an immovable wall against imperial hegemony in West Asia.

articles.title: Fire Point’s Denmark missile-fuel plant delayed to 2027 as costs potentially triple
articles.body:
Ukrainian defense manufacturer Fire Point has delayed its Danish missile-fuel plant until late 2027 after the original building failed to meet safety requirements, pushing the estimated cost above €150 million, Euractiv reported on 19 August.
The plant will produce solid rocket propellant for Fire Point’s Flamingo cruise missiles. Denmark was the first NATO country to permit Ukrainian military production on its territory, the German outlet BILD reported. The site is intended to move some production away from Russian attacks in Ukraine, but the delay postpones that capacity by a year.
Fire Point is building the plant in Vojens, near Skrydstrup Air Base in southern Denmark, Euromaidan Press reported.
Fire Point CEO Iryna Terekh announced the revised plan at DALO Industry Days, a defense-industry conference in Herning. She said Fire Point had originally expected the project to cost €50 million and called the new estimate “very rough.”
Denmark had already removed more than 20 legal barriers to speed up the project, Euractiv reported. Terekh said other European countries also remained interested in hosting Fire Point production.
What is Fire Point
Fire Point currently makes missiles and drones at 90 locations across Ukraine, Terekh told Euractiv in July.
The company supplies more than half of Ukraine’s deep-strike weapons—arms used to hit targets far behind the front line—and says it produces 300 drones daily, in a July 2026 interview with Liga.
In August 2025, Fire Point was producing 100 FP-1 long-range attack drones each day, according to the Associated Press. Its later figure includes FP-1 and FP-2 drones.
Denmark directly funds Ukrainian arms makers
Denmark has created the “Danish model” of aid, which uses allied money to buy weapons directly from Ukrainian manufacturers instead of taking equipment from donor stockpiles.
About $200 million of the €590 million military aid package announced in June was directed through the mechanism, Euromaidan Press reported. Denmark has committed about $11.7 billion in military support to Ukraine from 2022 through 2028, according to its Defense Ministry.

articles.title: Russian strike kills at least 6 at shopping center in central Ukrainian city
articles.body:
Russian drones kill 15 people at a shopping mall in a central Ukrainian city, officials say
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian drones struck a shopping center in the city of Kryvyi Rih in central Ukraine on Friday, killing at least 15 people and wounding scores more, authorities said.
The shopping mall strikes, plus two other separate Russian attacks in the Mykolaiv and Kharkiv regions, left a total of 21 people dead across Ukraine on Friday, authorities said.
Kryvyi Rih is the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who described the attack as a double-tap strike, in which an initial wave of drones hit the area, followed by a second wave as rescue workers responded.
“Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media. In a video address several hours later, he said Ukraine would respond to the shopping mall attack.
Oleksandr Hanzha, who heads the Dnipropetrovsk regional military administration, said Friday evening that the attack on the mall killed at least 15 people and injured 130, including 23 children.
Kryvyi Rih has been hit multiple times during the more than 4-year-old war, with one of the deadliest occurring in April 2025, when 20 people, including nine children, were killed.
Russia exploits Ukraine’s shortage of defensive systems
Earlier on Friday, a Russian drone attack on Ukraine’s Kharkiv region killed two women, aged 73 and 66, and wounded two others, said regional head Oleh Syniehubov.
Another Russian attack on Friday evening killed four people, including three children, in Ukraine’s southern Mykolaiv region, emergency services said.
Ukraine shot down or suppressed 107 out of 135 drones launched by Russia overnight, according to a statement from Ukraine’s air force on Telegram.
Friday’s attacks came just 24 hours after Russia pounded the capital of Kyiv with scores of missiles and drones in a nighttime aerial attack that killed 16 people.
Large-scale Russian strikes have become a regular occurrence this summer. Just over two weeks ago, a Russian attack on Kyiv and its surrounding region killed 17 people, and nine were killed in the city two days before that. The United Nations said last week that Kyiv was one of the hardest hit cities in July, with at least 54 civilians killed and 202 injured.
Moscow’s forces have recently intensified their ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv, exploiting Ukraine’s chronic shortage of U.S.-made Patriot air defense interceptors, the sole weapon in its arsenal able to shoot down the missiles.
Ukrainian drones hit Russian oil refinery
A Ukrainian drone attack killed one person and wounded four others when a car was struck Friday in Russia’s Belgorod region near the village of Razumnoye, local officials said, adding that two of the injured were in serious condition.
Earlier, Zelenskyy said a separate Ukrainian drone attack hit an oil refinery in Perm, more than 1,600 kilometers (about 995 miles) from his country’s border. Also struck was the Marinovka military airfield in Russia’s Volgograd region, he said.
The Russian online news outlet Astra reported that the Ukrainian drone had set ablaze a Lukoil-operated oil refinery in Perm. Local officials said damage was recorded at an unidentified “industrial facility.”
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses overnight intercepted 325 Ukrainian drones over 15 Russian regions, as well as Crimea. The peninsula was illegally annexed by Moscow in 2014.
Later Friday, it said its defenses shot down another 211 drones.
Long-range strikes between Russia and Ukraine have escalated as troops continually fail to make significant battlefield progress, analysts say. Troop movements along the roughly 1,250-kilometer (780-mile) front line in eastern and southern Ukraine are severely restricted by large numbers of drones and ground robots that threaten infantry and vehicles.
In the past year, Ukraine has devised and deployed domestically produced long-range drones for strikes deep inside Russia, capturing the attention of governments and defense manufacturers around the world.
Officials in Kyiv aim to make the Russian public feel the war’s consequences and pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiating a peace settlement. Putin has so far shown no sign he intends to stop the invasion.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the war in Ukraine at https://apnews.com/hub/russia-ukraine

Troop movements along the roughly 780-mile front line in eastern and southern Ukraine are severely restricted by large numbers of drones and ground robots that threaten infantry and vehicles.
In the past year, Ukraine has devised and deployed domestically produced long-range drones for strikes deep inside Russia, capturing the attention of governments and defense manufacturers around the world.
Officials in Kyiv aim to make the Russian public feel the war's consequences and pressure Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiating a peace settlement. Putin has so far shown no sign he intends to stop the invasion.

articles.title: Italy’s largest arms maker had no plans for a Ukraine factory—a year later, it has a Kyiv subsidiary
articles.body:
Italian defense giant Leonardo has quietly registered a research subsidiary in Kyiv, planting a direct corporate flag in Ukraine's wartime defense ecosystem, Euractiv reported. The move reverses the company's previous public stance against opening operations in Ukraine.
European defense firms are quickly embedding inside Ukraine's defense industry, as Ukraine's wartime manufacturing base has become a draw rather than a risk for Western capital.
Kyiv-based R&D company
Leonardo Ukraine appeared in Ukraine's business register on 20 May, but the company disclosed the step only in its H1 2026 financial report at the end of July. The subsidiary's share capital stands at about $125,000. Leonardo International wholly owns it.
"We have completed the legal process to begin operations. The new company will be used to work in this region," a Leonardo spokesperson said.
The subsidiary will focus on R&D covering communications and navigation systems, software, IT services, and electronic and optical technologies. The step brings Leonardo closer to Ukraine's drone and missile industry, which has expanded rapidly during the war.
Italy wants continental defense alliance, including Ukraine. Kyiv already out-produces all of NATO on drones
From no factory to a Kyiv office
Just over a year ago, then-CEO Roberto Cingolani said that Leonardo had no plans to open a factory in Ukraine, as Reuters reported. At the same time, Cingolani pledged to test Leonardo's Michelangelo Dome air defense system in Ukraine. The Italian government did not reappoint him in April 2026. Lorenzo Mariani took over as CEO in May.
The subsidiary is not a factory. But it gives Mariani a registered legal presence inside Ukraine's defense innovation ecosystem, positioned near the drone and electronic warfare sectors Leonardo wants to tap.
Leonardo is not the first major European defense firm to set up inside Ukraine. Germany's Quantum Systems established three joint ventures and made the country its second-largest international base. Rheinmetall is building an ammunition plant there. Ukrainian defense companies, in turn, have opened production facilities across Europe.

articles.title: Russia Deploys North Korean Ballistic Missiles Within Reach of 7 Ukrainian Regions
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to expand its use of North Korean ballistic missiles, with six launchers deployed in Voronezh Oblast that could put seven Ukrainian regions within range, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) reported on Friday, Aug. 21.
The Ukrainian military’s Main Intelligence Directorate (HUR) confirmed on Aug. 20 that North Korea had transferred around 50 KN-23, KN-24 and KN-30 ballistic missiles to Russia as of July 2026, according to ISW.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian launchers in Voronezh could reportedly strike targets in Sumy, Kharkiv, Chernihiv, Poltava, Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhzhia oblasts, ISW said.
The KN-30, also known as the Hwasong-11C, is an upgraded version of the KN-23 ballistic missile and can reportedly carry a warhead weighing up to 2,500 kilograms (2.75 tons).
ISW said it has not observed evidence that Russian forces have used the KN-30 against Ukraine.
Russia expands North Korean missile capability
According to Ukraine’s military intelligence, Russia has begun deploying six launchers for North Korean missiles in Voronezh Oblast. The launchers could collectively fire up to 120 missiles, ISW reported.
The deployment would give Russia another ballistic missile capability for striking Ukrainian targets from Russian territory.
Ukrainian military expert Anatoly Khrapchinsky cautioned that Russia does not necessarily use every available launcher as part of a strike package during a single mission.
How Energy-Exporting Russia Is Turning Into a Fuel Importer – Thanks to Ukraine
Russia has around 160 Iskander launchers capable of carrying two missiles each, but Russian forces launch an average of 16 to 26 missiles per strike package, Khrapchinsky said.
North Korean missiles also differ from Russia’s Iskander-M missiles in accuracy and warhead size.
Khrapchinsky said Iskander-M missiles can strike within approximately 5 to 20 meters of their intended target, while North Korean KN-23 missiles have reportedly missed their targets by hundreds of meters or even kilometers.
However, the North Korean missiles can carry substantially heavier warheads.
KN-23-series missiles can reportedly carry warheads weighing up to 1ton (970 kilograms), compared with the standard 480-kilogram warhead on Russia’s Iskander-M, resulting in larger craters and stronger shock waves.
The reported deployment indicates that Russia continues to develop ways to incorporate North Korean missiles into its assaults against Ukraine.
