articles.title: Russia open to new ideas; peace will come with rules
articles.body:
Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergei Ryabkov said Moscow is open to new proposals to end the war in Ukraine, but any offers must reflect reality, Reuters reported.
In an interview published by News.ru on the 21st of August, Ryabkov said the United States was demonstrating its readiness for constructive dialogue and understanding of Russia’s position. He said the key issue now was how much the United States could influence the decisions of “the Kiev regime and its sponsors in Europe, who still dream of Russia’s strategic defeat.” Talks between Russia and the United States on peace in Ukraine have virtually ground to a halt after U.S. and Israeli strikes triggered a war in Iran.
The Kremlin said on the 20th of August that it had no information on when the next visit to Moscow by US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner might take place. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in July after meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov that Washington was committed to helping end the war, but warned that a solution would not be quick and that Moscow was trying to find a compromise.
Ryabkov said that Russia was ready to listen to Rubio’s ideas and was open to constructive talks.
After almost four and a half years of hostilities, Russia has occupied about a fifth of Ukraine’s territory. Moscow regularly says it is ready for talks, but that they must reflect reality.
The deputy foreign minister also said in an interview that Russia wants to hold discussions with the USSR on nuclear weapons. The previous nuclear treaty expired in February, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear powers without any agreement on the use of their strategic arsenals for the first time in more than 50 years.
Moscow has said it will continue to abide by the terms of the treaty and the number of warheads allowed, as long as Washington does the same.
Read also: British drones used in strikes on Russia; Moscow threatens retaliation

articles.title: New Ukrainian sanctions target multiple levels of Russia's war machine – sanctions commissioner
articles.body:
New Ukrainian sanctions target multiple levels of Russia's war machine – sanctions commissioner
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the President's Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"The four new sanctions packages target several levels of the Russian system supporting the war against Ukraine. They include representatives of occupation administrations, people involved in the economic exploitation of temporarily occupied territories and the material supply of the Russian military," he said.
According to Vlasiuk, the sanctions demonstrate a consistent effort to dismantle the occupation hierarchy at every level.
"The cases of Yury Turulyov and Sanal Adyayev in the Kherson region show that pressure is being brought both on those organizing the administrative and legal integration of the seized territories and on individuals involved in their economic exploitation, including the illegal removal of Ukrainian grain. At the same time, sanctions against Russian lawmaker Viktor Kushnir disrupt the covert supply of drones and equipment to the Russian military through private and political networks," Vlasiuk said.
The list also includes Sergei Baburin, deputy speaker of Russia's State Duma, who publicly promotes claims about the "legality" of the occupation of Ukrainian territories, denies Ukrainian identity and seeks to discredit Ukraine.
Vlasiuk stressed that a strategic core of the package is the sanctions imposed on companies belonging to the Rusal group, including the Sayanogorsk, Krasnoyarsk, Bratsk and Ural aluminum plants, as well as Russian Aluminium Management, the group's management company. He noted that "aluminum is a critical raw material for the enemy's aircraft, missiles and artillery." The company's management has also been sanctioned.
Vlasiuk stressed the importance of disrupting the entire production chain, noting that alumina, for example, is supplied by Aughinish Alumina, which is owned by Rusal.
"We are working to ensure that the EU and/or the Irish government makes a decision to restrict the supply of alumina to the enterprises that have now been sanctioned," he said.
According to Vlasiuk, a preventive strike against the infrastructure supporting Russian drone technologies is equally important.
"Sanctions against the so-called Crimean Research Institute of Unmanned Technologies, initiated by sanctioned official Sergei Aksyonov, are aimed at suppressing enemy capabilities at the development stage. Since this structure is involved not only in the development of FPV drones, electronic warfare systems and artificial intelligence, but also in training operators and engineers, the restrictions cover the entire ecosystem," he said.
The sanctions also target companies without which Russia's defense industry cannot operate normally. For example, Metall Industry supplies metalworking equipment and software to Russian defense-industry enterprises. Its counterparties include the sanctioned Kalashnikov, Istok and Design Bureau of Chemical Automation. Another example is the Engineering and Industrial Company research and production enterprise, which manufactures specialized equipment, including TDA-3 smoke generators used to conceal troops and facilities from reconnaissance and precision weapons.
In other words, Vlasiuk said, the sanctions target specific production links that supply the Russian military and its defense industry.
"Finally, the inclusion of animation content producers such as Masha and the Bear LLC, Animaccord studio and Studio MiM shows that sanctions pressure is expanding into the humanitarian sphere," he said.
According to the commissioner, imposing restrictions on specific legal entities in Russia blocks the use of children's media products as an instrument of propaganda and influence over Ukrainian children.
"Ukraine now has legal grounds to approach global platforms, including Netflix and YouTube, to request that they cease cooperation with sanctioned entities and block the monetization and distribution of their content to Ukrainian audiences," Vlasiuk said.
As reported, President Volodymyr Zelensky recently signed four decrees enacting National Security and Defense Council decisions to impose sanctions on Russian defense-industry enterprises, companies belonging to the Rusal group, collaborators, senior officials, and the creators and distributors of the animated series "Masha and the Bear."

articles.title: Ukrainian drone unit seriously wounded Colonel Dmitry Shabaev, commander of Russia’s 64th brigade, tied to 2022 Bucha atrocities that killed 637 civilians
articles.body:
Ukraine has hit the commander of a Russian brigade notorious for one of the war's worst atrocities. The 423rd Separate Unmanned Systems Regiment "Scythian Griffons" struck the car of Dmitry Shabaev, commander of Russia's 64th brigade, seriously wounding him, the regiment reported.
The target commands the unit most associated with the killing of civilians in Bucha in spring 2022. During the Russian occupation, 637 civilians were killed in the small town of Bucha alone. 460 infrastructure facilities were damaged or destroyed, according to the Ukrainian Prosecutor General's Office.
The strike hit the commander 80 km behind the front
According to military intelligence, the Russian colonel's movements had been tracked for a long time, and the drone crew hit his service vehicle roughly 80 kilometers from the line of contact.
Both men aboard were badly hurt. Shabaev and his driver received serious injuries, and both were evacuated to a Russian military hospital, the regiment said.
The brigade is tied to Bucha
After the atrocities in Bucha, the brigade remains in the fight. It now forms part of Russia's southern grouping in Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk oblasts and continues to commit crimes.
The unit is targeting Russian command posts
The strike reflects a deliberate focus on Russian command. Regiment commander Colonel Vitalii Hersak said that after becoming a separate regiment with strengthened capabilities, the unit set a strategic task of concentrating on the command posts of enemy brigades and battalions.
"After we became a separate regiment and our combat capabilities strengthened, I set the guys a strategic task to focus especially on working the command posts of enemy brigades and battalions. This is only the beginning. To be continued," Hersak said.
Targeting commanders and command posts aims to degrade Russian units by removing the officers who direct them, a higher-value target than the front-line troops they command.

articles.title: Kuchma names three fatal mistakes in Ukraine's years of independence
articles.body:
Kuchma names three fatal mistakes in Ukraine's years of independence
Kuchma, Ukraine's second president, expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
"Among the unquestionable mistakes, I would definitely name the catastrophic decision not to sign the Association Agreement with the European Union in Vilnius. But, emotionally, the hardest thing for me personally to accept is the de facto surrender of Crimea in February-March 2014. There was no response to the actions of the 'little green men,' who calmly and brazenly took control of the Ukrainian peninsula. Let me remind you: formally, they were not even identified as Russians. They were unknown terrorists, and they should have been dealt with accordingly. A decisive response in Crimea could have stopped the attempted annexation at its very beginning," Kuchma said.
He also separately mentioned the loss of Ukraine's nuclear weapons. According to the former president, agreeing to the removal of Ukraine's tactical nuclear weapons in 1992 was a fatal mistake. He said that by 1994, when the Budapest Memorandum was concluded, there was essentially nothing left to decide regarding Ukraine's strategic security – everything had already been settled two years earlier.
"The point is that the Budapest Memorandum deprived Ukraine of strategic weapons whose condition and characteristics would not have allowed them to provide nuclear deterrence anyway. But at the beginning of our independence, we did have the weapons needed for that. We had about 3,000 tactical nuclear warheads. In principle, we could have used them to defend ourselves against Russia at that time. They had an optimal range of operation and included nuclear aviation bombs, artillery shells and naval torpedoes – in other words, the entire range of tactical nuclear weapons. And unlike the strategic arsenal, Ukraine could control and deploy them itself," Kuchma said.
As reported, the removal of all tactical nuclear weapons from Ukrainian territory to Russia was completed on May 7, 1992. About 2,500 tactical warheads were transferred under pressure from international partners and because Ukraine lacked the technical and financial resources to maintain them.
At a Cabinet meeting on November 21, 2013, the Ukrainian government adopted a resolution titled "Issues Concerning the Conclusion of the Association Agreement between Ukraine, on the one hand, and the European Union, the European Atomic Energy Community and their Member States, on the other," suspending preparations for the signing of the Association Agreement between Ukraine and the EU. The decision triggered mass protests that eventually grew into the Revolution of Dignity.
On February 20, 2014, Russian troops without identifying insignia began landing in Crimea. On March 16, 2014, a so-called referendum on Crimea's status was held in the temporarily Russian-occupied Crimea and the city of Sevastopol, in violation of Ukrainian and Crimean legislation. It took place under pressure from Russian troops and paramilitary "self-defense" groups and with the support of Russian propaganda media.
Photo: Maksymilian Ilchenko

articles.title: Trump Rejects Push to Give Ukraine Starlink for Long-Range Strikes on Russia – FT
articles.body:
US President Donald Trump has rejected Ukraine’s request to use Starlink to guide drone strikes against Russian military targets inside Russia, the Financial Times reported Friday, citing people familiar with the matter.
The appeal came during a late-July meeting at the White House, when President Volodymyr Zelensky reportedly asked Trump to intervene with Musk, the owner of SpaceX, which operates Starlink.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Kyiv wants to hit Russian missile launchers
Zelensky wants Ukrainian long-range drones to use the satellite network to more accurately target Russian military sites, particularly mobile ballistic missile launchers and related infrastructure located up to 200 kilometers (124 miles) from Ukraine’s border.
The request is aimed in part at reducing Russia’s ability to launch ballistic missiles at Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, while easing pressure on Ukraine’s increasingly limited stock of Patriot air-defense interceptors.
Trump reportedly said he would consider the request but made no commitment to support it. The FT now reports that he did not back the proposal.
Musk has already blocked Starlink strikes
Musk is also refusing to grant Ukraine permission to use Starlink inside Russian territory, The Atlantic previously reported.
SpaceX currently allows Ukraine to use Starlink on Ukrainian-controlled territory, including Russian-occupied areas such as Crimea, but blocks the network inside Russia. Ukrainian long-range drones therefore rely on alternative navigation systems, including AI-based technology, when operating across the border.
Ukraine Calls for Urgent Global Response After Russia’s 9-Hour Assault
Zelensky reportedly argued that improved targeting is needed to destroy Russia’s mobile ballistic missile launchers before winter, when Moscow is expected to intensify attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
Kyiv had hoped that limiting strikes to targets within 200 kilometers of the Ukrainian border could persuade Musk to reconsider. The billionaire, however, has previously restricted Starlink’s use for attacks deep inside Russia over concerns about nuclear escalation.
Zelensky also sought a meeting with Musk during his US visit, but the billionaire reportedly declined.
Earlier this year, former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov reportedly reached an agreement with Musk to restrict Starlink access for the Russian military.
However, efforts to secure expanded access for Ukrainian strikes inside Russia have produced no positive decision, The Atlantic reported.
Musk has argued that the war can only end through a peace agreement between Kyiv and Moscow and has said Russia is unlikely to withdraw its troops without concessions from Ukraine.

articles.title: Trump’s threat to Oman signals more than the end of US diplomacy
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Trump’s threat to Oman signals more than the end of US diplomacy
Trump has threatened to “bomb the s**” out of Oman for the second time this year. A shocking repeat threat against a country that has served as a friend and mediator for the US for years.
What’s new about US power in the Middle East under Trump is not its destructive capacity, its blatant disregard for the lives of ordinary people, or its desire to keep oil and petrodollars flowing its way. No, all of this is simply how America operates. Trump is no aberration.
What is new is the absence of any diplomatic speak that paints over its violence and gags its belligerent confidence. Trump’s particularly fickle form of verbal vomit sees him adulate dictators in the same week he threatens his partners. The volatility of American discourse under his leadership compounds the anxiety and instability resulting from his behaviour.
Threats and more threats
Fox News reporter Trey Yingst said he had asked the president about parallel talks taking place between Iran and Oman about the control of the Strait of Hormuz, to which Trump replied: “If Oman gets in the way, we’ll bomb the s*** out of them.” In May, also speaking about opening the Strait, Trump made a similar threat: “Oman will behave like everybody else, or we’ll have to blow them up.”
The day after the latest threat, the White House shared Donald Trump’s Truth Social post on their official X account, with an image identifying the Strait of Hormuz as “New U.S. Territory,” echoing the president’s comment that “pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz Strait a territory of the United States.”
Encompassed within the identifying circle in the image of the Strait are not only Iranian territory but also Omani and Emirati territory. Crossing this key waterway requires ships to pass through the territorial waters of Iran and Oman, making Iran’s ability to close it and threaten international shipment a key thorn in the side of the president’s flesh.
Trump’s threats sound alarming in the world of diplomacy, even if no one expects him to actually bomb the Sultanate.
Why target a longstanding ally?
Today, Oman is appreciated as a country that has carefully cultivated its neutrality, allowing it to serve as a trusted mediator. It is credited with playing a key role behind the Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), and Muscat has served as a vital backchannel between Washington and Tehran for years.
The Gulf country has also played an important role in the release of various American hostages in Iran and Yemen over the years.
This relationship emerges from a long history of friendship between the countries, with ties sitting among the longest of any Arab nation. These extend from the 1833 treaty of friendship and commerce between the two nations to the signing of the US-Oman Free Trade Agreement in 2006 (in effect since 2009) – one of the US’s only 20 bilateral FTAs worldwide.
This rich diplomatic history includes Oman being credited with dispatching the first Arab emissary to the United States in 1840 when Ahmad bin Na̔aman, special envoy of Sayyid Sa̔id bin Sultan (the Sultan of Oman and Zanzibar), visited New York. Not only this, but the first Arab head of state to make an official visit to Washington was Omani Sultan Sa̔id bin Taimur who met with US President Franklin Roosevelt in 1938.
Within this context, Trump’s threats to Oman appear puzzling. Both instances emerge as reactions to Oman’s role negotiating with Iran over access and navigation through the Strait. It’s not only Oman’s record of diplomacy and its proven status as a mediator with Iran, but also the geographic position that makes it both logical and necessary for the Gulf country to be involved.
Even more peculiarly, the June 17th 14-point Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding Between the United States of America and the Islamic Republic of Iran specified in point 5 that: “Iran will conduct dialogue with the Sultanate of Oman to define the future administration and maritime services in the Strait of Hormuz”. Observers had hoped the current dialogue would be a precursor to a renewal as the 60-day MOU was about to expire.
The agreement had already frayed by the beginning of July as Iran launched strikes on a number of ships and the US renewed its strikes on Iran for nearly two weeks. It was after this that Iran blatantly refused direct talks with the US, accusing it of first violating the terms of the MOU, and began talks with Oman.
Mediators Pakistan and Qatar were reportedly exchanging messages, but Iran has denied any negotiations. In the end, the deal expired.
Undermining peace
Oman’s independent policy toward Iran means it does not always align with US foreign policy, but this characteristic is what enables the country to facilitate dialogue and negotiations. Oman was in fact hosting nuclear talks between the US and Iran just before Trump and Netanyahu launched the war in February. Oman’s foreign minister Badr Al Busaidi tried to pre-empt this by publicly declaring that “a peace deal is within our reach” just the night before bombs started falling.
He later expressed his dismay that “active and serious negotiations [had] yet again been undermined,” referring to the launch of the 12-day war the previous year, which Israel started just two days before the sixth round of US-Iran nuclear talks were set to begin in Oman.
Trump is indeed upending the niceties of American diplomacy and rupturing long-standing relationships. He has recently given a cold shoulder to South Korea as he rekindles his love affair with Kim Jong-Un, has sided with Russia in UN resolutions on Ukraine, and has repeatedly made obnoxious, expansionist threats to make Canada the fifty-first state and seize control of Greenland. In that vein, Trump has already unilaterally renamed the Gulf of Mexico the Gulf of America and violated international law by abducting Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
It’s muzzle off, open bullying.
No force of good
We might consider it a collapse of American diplomacy and its cover of democracy promotion around the world.
But let’s not kid ourselves. People who mourn the US’ role in the world are mourning an illusion. Authors have challenged this virtuous self-delusion for decades, trying to explain to Americans just why people hate America.
Indeed, the US in the Middle East was no force for good. Ask the Palestinians bearing the brunt of American support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza under Biden, Yemeni wedding attendees murdered by Obama’s drones, or the hundreds of thousands of children who died of starvation under Clinton-supported sanctions (infamously deemed “worth it” by then US ambassador to the UN, Madeleine Albright). The list can go on at length and extend well beyond the confines of the Middle East.
The US’ ongoing support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza and its war on Iran are only the latest episodes in what Marc Lynch has dubbed America’s “ruination of a region.”
Trump’s only stable regional pursuit may be expanding the number of Gulf signatories to the Abraham Accords, a desire that Kayhan Valadbaygi calls “low-cost US hegemony,” which positions Israel as its central military-security node.
The Accords are consistent with around four decades of USFP in the region, built on several goals. One includes fostering or forcing Middle East allies into relations with Israel – exemplified by the 1996 Qualifying Industrial Zones initiative, which gives goods produced in Jordan and Egypt duty-free access to US markets on the condition that they include Israeli inputs. The other goal is containing (previously Iraq and) Iran and its proxies. The war has exposed the failure of the latter.
Iran has not been contained, and this policy has had deleterious effects on people, communities, and regional security.
Oman’s foreign minister recently wrote that containment is a “myth” and “an error of nearly half a century” and has called for replacing containment with a new security logic to govern the region - one based on inclusion. This will require, in his assessment, “Gulf conversations for Gulf states” to reassess their ties with powerful allies like the US – “not to discard these…but perhaps to reset them” to match the realities revealed during the war. This avoidable war has forced an “essential” question for Oman and its GCC partners: which partnerships genuinely delivery security, and which "bring unwanted vulnerabilities.”
The unsettling difference in current US foreign policy is Trump’s unpredictability. Sandwiched between the US and Iran, Oman remains the only adult in the room – a stable mediator not retaliating in words but sufficiently confident to condemn poor behaviour and violations of international law.
Indeed, the region, middle powers worldwide, and the wider international community would benefit from considering Oman’s words. In fact, the region is overdue for a new security arrangement that takes into account the lives and aspirations of its people.
Crystal A. Ennis is a scholar of global political economy and international relations based at Leiden University, the Netherlands. She is author of Millennial Dreams in Oil Economies (Cambridge University Press, 2025).
Follow Crystal on Bluesky: @crystalennis.bsky.social or X: @Crystal_Ennis
Have questions or comments? Email us at: editorial-english@alaraby.co.uk

articles.title: Gun stash in German forest believed to be linked to Russia, say reports
articles.body:
Germany is seeking to extradite a suspect from Romania over the discovery of an underground stash of weapons in a forest near Berlin that German media reports have linked to Russian intelligence.
Two weeks after German authorities found a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, the interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, confirmed federal prosecutors had opened an investigation related to the secret cache of guns “on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence that threatens national security”.
“This case demonstrates that we are operating under a high threat level,” he told reporters. As with the Leipzig incident, Dobrindt said he could not rule out the involvement of “foreign powers”.
Earlier, local media had reported that German authorities had unearthed two handguns and ammunition about a year ago in a wooded area outside the German capital after agents of the domestic intelligence service received a tip.
The find has been the focus of covert investigations by state security and counterespionage services on suspicion Russian intelligence was plotting assassinations on German soil, according to separate reports by Der Spiegel magazine and an investigative team led by Süddeutsche Zeitung.
Rather than removing the arms, German authorities left them on site after rendering them unusable in the hope they would lead to clues during a months-long electronic surveillance operation, Dobrindt said.
No one was observed trying to collect the weapons, leading investigators to believe the agent or agents had learned of the cache’s discovery and it was now “dead”.
Dobrindt described the suspect in Romania, whose nationality was not disclosed, as a “low-level agent” and noted several other such operatives had been detained so far this year.
Although the investigation into the Berlin stash has been long-running, the revelations apparently led Dobrindt to hastily call the news conference on Friday.
Sinan Selen, the head of the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency, has warned for months of more aggressive tactics by Russian secret services, including plans for targeted attacks on German soil.
Moscow’s potential hit list is believed to include weapons contractor executives, opposition figures in exile and other prominent Ukraine supporters, according to the report by Süddeutsche and the public broadcasters NDR and WDR.
The federal prosecutor’s office and the Russian embassy declined to comment. A BfV spokesperson said: “As a matter of principle, we don’t comment on matters relating to any specific intelligence activities.”
Spiegel said German authorities were looking into possible links between the arms cache – a familiar Soviet tactic during the cold war – and a sabotage campaign against Ukrainian logistics routes blamed on Russia.
Last year Polish security officials arrested several people allegedly planning to mail parcels containing incendiary devices or detonators, some of them reportedly posted from Romania.
Investigators believe the packages could have been remotely ignited or set off using timers during transit to do serious damage to vehicles, cargo planes or logistics centres and spread fear in the EU.
In 2024, a firebomb in a parcel posted via DHL exploded in a freight container on the tarmac at Leipzig airport. Only a delayed flight kept it from going off in the air.
Ukraine has been using the facility in Leipzig as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records.
This month the German newspaper Die Zeit reported that Russian secret services were plotting an attack against Stefan Thumann, the head of German drone manufacturer Donaustahl.
The report said German investigators were tipped off by a foreign intelligence service at the end of last year and arrested a Ukrainian man and a Romanian woman this spring.
Thumann is said to be under police protection. The case recalled reports in 2024 that US intelligence services had foiled a Russian plot to assassinate the chief executive of Germany’s leading arms manufacturer, in an apparent attempt to retaliate over the company’s role in providing armaments for Ukraine.
The plan to murder Armin Papperger, the chief executive of Rheinmetall, was reportedly one of several Russian government schemes to kill defence industry executives in several countries in Europe that have been supporting Ukraine’s war effort. The plot against Papperger was believed to be the most advanced.
Russia has repeatedly denied any involvement in sabotage, disruption or intimidation against EU member states.

articles.title: Ukraine eyes anti-ballistic systems with EU’s €90 billion loan
articles.body:
Officials in Kyiv have floated the idea of using the next parcel of funds from the European Union’s €90 billion loan to purchase anti-ballistic missile capabilities, an official close to the discussions told Euronews. Questions loom over where they could come from.
A European Commission official close to discussions over the EU's €90 billion loan for Ukraine has told Euronews that Kyiv has suggested that the next defence funding envelope could be used to acquire anti-ballistic missile systems, among other capabilities.
The official could not specify whether these would be the American-made Patriot air defence missile system or its European equivalent — the Franco-Italian SAMP/T NG ground-to-air missile system — as the discussions were ongoing and no formal product schedule had been placed.
The upcoming order is expected to be made before September, with missiles and drones expected to also be requested.
The comments come as European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen condemned a deadly Russian attack in Ukraine overnight on Wednesday, which killed at least 16 and wounded 33. She hinted that anti-ballistic support was on the way.
“Russia is losing the war it started. And it is retaliating by targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure,” she said in a statement posted on social media platform X.
“We are working with Member States and our partners to support Ukraine’s anti-ballistic capabilities. So that Ukraine has the means to prevent the loss of lives.”
The origin of potentially upcoming anti-ballistic missile systems could ruffle feathers as many EU member states, such as France, argue that financial support from the bloc should be used to buy European arms and support Europe’s defence industry.
While others believe that Ukraine must be given full flexibility to buy whatever it needs to immediately defend against Russia's full-scale invasion.
"Ukraine's urgent needs should be front and centre," defence ministers from Finland, Sweden, Lithuania, Denmark, Poland, Estonia and Latvia wrote in a letter published in July arguing for greater flexibility regarding the financial assistance.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy recently reiterated calls for Washington to release more Patriot interceptors so that Ukraine's armed forces can repel Russian missiles, get through the winter and “save people’s lives".
However, he also announced in July that Ukraine would become the first "combat user" of the Franco-Italian SAMP/T NG missile systems.
According to a public statement, Kyiv intends to order the systems through the 2026 and 2027 tranches of the Ukraine support loan, which should be delivered "as soon as possible" from next year.
'Made in Europe'
Some €60 billion from the total €90 billion of the loan will be provided to bolster the country’s defences during wartime, with the remainder propping up Ukraine's national budget.
A total of €28.3 billion will be provided to Ukraine in 2026 to support Ukraine's defence industrial capacities, with some already paid out.
The 'Made in Europe' provision of the defence envelope aims to ensure as much funding as possible goes to European rather than foreign producers of military capabilities.
Priority is given to producers in Ukraine, the EU and EEA-EFTA defence industries, with certain third-country access also possible.
Brussels can grant a defence derogation if the Ukrainians want to proceed with acquiring any weapons, such as the Patriot air defence missile system, not made in Europe. Exemptions have been granted previously for the acquisition of drone equipment.

articles.title: Ukraine’s biggest weakness against Russia isn’t interceptor shortage, analyst argues. It’s what happens before missiles even launch
articles.body:
Ukraine’s failure to anticipate and prepare for Russian threats is a bigger problem than the shortage of air defenses, says Oleksandr Kovalenko of the Information Resistance group. Russia, meanwhile, has demonstrated its ability to develop and execute medium-term plans for terror operations that can take years to prepare, according to Obozrevatel.
Russian forces adapt almost every month to new challenges and opportunities, scaling up their attacks. The use of jet-powered Banderol drone missiles is one example.
Russia is now employing a “tactical adaptive distribution” approach, flexibly redirecting missiles and strike drones toward different regions and rear cities depending on Ukrainian air-defense capabilities.
The main difference
The key change in Russia’s 2026 campaign against Ukraine’s rear areas has been the growing use of jet-powered drones based on the Iranian Shahed-238 and Karrar, which Russia has localized as Geran-3/4/5.
Russia first used a jet-powered kamikaze drone against Ukraine in January 2024. These weapons have been continuously upgraded over the past two years.
Ukraine, however, failed to adequately anticipate the threat and now lacks an effective, low-cost way to intercept Geran-3/4/5 drones, Kovalenko says. Russian forces used more than 1,400 jet-powered drones in the first half of 2026 alone, compared with 180 throughout all of 2025.
“It is possible that the facility in Alabuga, Tatarstan, could eventually be fully converted to producing jet-powered kamikaze drones as part of this strategy,” the analyst said.
What comes next: strikes on Kyiv to exert psychological pressure
A significant share of Russia’s new hard-to-intercept weapon variants appears to be concentrated for strikes on Kyiv.
Russian forces are seeking to exploit Ukraine’s acute shortage of Patriot and SAMP/T interceptors, using the opportunity to intensify their campaign of terror. Russia has previously used similar tactics to exert psychological pressure on civilians and disrupt economic activity in regions including Kharkiv and Odesa.
The same approach could increasingly be directed at the capital, particularly ahead of and during Ukraine’s Independence Day.

articles.title: Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ will turn into ‘dud day’
articles.body:
Trump’s ‘economic D-Day’ will turn into ‘dud day’
China rejects Trump’s economic pressure on Iran, while Russia warns the US has chosen the wrong way
TEHRAN — As the unprovoked war launched by the United States and Israel against Iran approaches its six-month mark, Washington is confronting diminishing weapon stockpiles, a stalled aggression campaign, and growing domestic political distress ahead of crucial US midterm elections that will decide control of Congress.
In a transparent effort to conceal these strategic miscalculations, US President Donald Trump has turned to bombastic rhetoric, touting a crushing financial campaign against Tehran and promising an “economic D-Day” against a nation that has steadfastly resisted nearly five decades of punishing American blockades. With sparse details, Trump announced that Washington would impose an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on Iran. The coercive action aims to force Tehran into caving to illegal demands regarding its peaceful civilian nuclear program and demanding the complete opening of the strategic Strait of Hormuz to oil and natural gas tankers.
This escalation reflects the dire political reality facing Trump, who finds himself entangled in an increasingly unpopular war that he cannot end. Refusing to learn from the failures of past administrations, the US president is attempting to refocus American power on forcing Iranian submission through an accelerated sanctions push against one of the most economically penalized countries in the world. Laying out the mechanics of this next phase of hostility during a Thursday interview on CNBC, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened secondary sanctions against sovereign nations and foreign companies that maintain lawful commercial ties with Tehran.
Under the framework of "Operation Economic Fury"—which previously targeted entities purchasing Iranian energy or conducting banking transactions with Tehran—Bessent issued an explicit ultimatum to global trading partners, including major buyers such as China and India. “If you insist on doing business with them, then the US Treasury and US government will put its full might and force against you,” Bessent declared arrogantly. “It’s time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision.”
Iranian officials quickly dismantled Washington's posture, exposing the domestic crises propelling Trump's theatrical announcements.
In a statement published on his official X account, Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi exposed the true motives behind the American claims. “The so-called ‘Economic D-Day’ is a diversion from America's own crisis: unprecedented debt & surging interest costs,” Araqchi wrote, emphasizing that “doubling down on failed policies will only bring further defeat—and enmity of Iranians. US economic terrorism threatens global economy and sovereignty worldwide.”
Iran’s Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi mocked the glaring contradiction between Washington’s claims of strength and its real-world dependence on foreign support. “They claim Iran is on the brink of collapse and hanging by a thread, yet they beg all their allies to help them! The problem is the wrong calculations that, each time to cover them up, they’re forced to create a bigger failure for themselves,” Gharibabadi posted Thursday on social media. Highlighting the military stalemate after six months of direct fighting, Gharibabadi added: “The military war didn’t yield results, so now they’ve named the next failure ‘economic war’.”
Washington’s demand for international compliance with its illegal economic blockade was met with immediate, explicit rejection from key world powers. In Beijing, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian told reporters on Thursday that sanctions cannot resolve the crisis. “Sanctions and pressure tactics are not the solution. China calls on parties to act responsibly and stick to the political and diplomatic approach,” Lin stated, reiterating that “China opposes illicit unilateral sanctions that lack basis in international law and UN Security Council mandate. We call on parties to act responsibly and stick to the political and diplomatic approach.”
Russia’s Permanent Representative to International Organizations in Vienna, Mikhail Ulyanov, similarly described Trump’s strategy as a doomed endeavor. "Iran has remained under US sanctions for decades. Tehran demonstrated its ability to withstand 'maximum pressure' during Trump's first tenure," Ulyanov noted on X, emphasizing that Washington has consistently pursued "the wrong way" in the region. "Positive results are possible only through honest diplomacy. The sooner the US understands that, the better," Ulyanov concluded.
Further details on American sanctions designations can be monitored via the US Department of the Treasury. This latest economic siege is merely the continuation of a long history of US-Zionist military, covert, and economic aggression against the Iranian nation. Ever since the Islamic Revolution ended Western domination, the United States and Israel have waged a persistent war against Iranian sovereignty. This aggressive campaign has included military invasions, state-sponsored terrorism, extrajudicial assassinations of Iranian nuclear scientists, cyber attacks on civilian infrastructure, and joint airstrikes targeting sovereign defense facilities. Despite decades of relentless pressure, Washington and Tel Aviv have repeatedly failed to destabilize the Islamic Republic or curb its regional influence.
Washington's persistent reliance on economic terrorism reveals a fundamental inability to comprehend that coercive pressure without genuine diplomacy is an exercise in futility. Rather than forcing capitulation, American sanctions have historically backfired, accelerating Iran's industrial self-sufficiency, strengthening national unity, and deepening strategic integration with non-Western powers across Eurasia. As the United States struggles under severe fiscal deficits, depleted arms inventories, and international isolation following the unprovoked war launched by the US and Israel on February 28, Tehran’s strategic fortitude guarantees that Washington's proclaimed "economic D-Day" will ultimately join a long line of failed American military and economic ventures in West Asia.

articles.title: Russian drones set fire to the biggest shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, a steel city in central Ukraine. Half an hour later, they came back for the rescue crews.
articles.body:
Russian drones set fire to the biggest shopping mall in Kryvyi Rih, a steel city in central Ukraine. Half an hour later, they came back for the rescue crews.
The Russian military attacked Kryvyi Rih’s largest shopping mall, said Oleksandr Vilkul, head of the city’s defense council. Videos posted on social media indicate the target was Sonyachna Halereya (“Sunny Gallery”), where a major fire broke out after the strike.
The Russian attack has killed 15 people and wounded 130. These are the most recent figures from Ukrainian authorities, though they may not be final while the search-and-rescue operation continues. Of the wounded, 29 — including five children — are in serious condition. In all, 23 of the injured are children.
We updated the casualty figures after receiving new information.
“Strikes like this are simply acts of terrorism,” said Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. Drones struck the mall in two waves, he said: “Half an hour after the first hit and the fire, a second strike hit the rescue crews.”
Russia is deliberately targeting places where civilians gather, added Ukrainian human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets: “People came to the mall to shop, to work, or to spend time with loved ones. That means nothing to Russia. The Russian military is once again proving that it sees civilians as a [deliberately chosen] target in this war.”
Warehouses at Sonyachna Halereya were allegedly being used for the benefit of Ukraine’s armed forces, said Russian “war correspondent” Yury Kotenok. The Russian Defense Ministry has used this argument before to justify strikes on privately owned Ukrainian businesses. Ukraine, for its part, has cited a similar reason for attacking warehouses belonging to Wildberries, a Russian online marketplace.
Russian forces carried out the previous major strike on Kryvyi Rih on August 16, hitting the city’s industrial plants with missiles and drones. The attack killed two people and wounded 14 others. Ukraine’s largest mining and metallurgical plant, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, was reportedly damaged in the strike.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Ukraine intelligence alleges hidden Russian biolab site
articles.body:
- Ukraine's HUR intelligence agency alleges Russia operates a secret biological laboratory complex on Lisiy Island in Tver Oblast, an unverified claim.
- HUR links the site to a 2026 Russian cattle disease outbreak, though independently documented reporting places that outbreak in Siberia, far from Tver.
Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, the Main Directorate of Intelligence, known as HUR, said Friday that Russia has built a secret military complex of biological laboratories on an island in the Tver region, where it experiments with dangerous viruses and other pathogens on behalf of the armed forces.
HUR identified the facility as the “Center for Experimental Physiology,” located on Lisiy Island in the Vyshny Volochyok Reservoir, roughly 120 km (75 miles) northwest of Tver. The agency said the site operates under the cover of veterinary and physiological research. HUR did not publish documents, imagery, or other evidence to support the claim, and Russian authorities have not commented on it.
According to HUR, the waters around the island have been closed to fishing, swimming, and boating since 2023 under a designation as a “specially protected territory of regional significance.” The reservoir supplies drinking water to several towns, including Vyshny Volochyok, and feeds the Tvertsa River, a tributary of the Volga.
HUR said that if dangerous pathogens or chemicals from the laboratories entered the reservoir, the consequences of any resulting outbreak could be severe not only for the surrounding region but for Russia as a whole. The agency did not say it had evidence that such a release has occurred.
The agency said the facility was built on the personal order of Russian President Vladimir Putin as a project of particular importance, described internally as necessary to “ensure the defense capability and security of Russia.” HUR said the complex is formally structured under the Federal Medical-Biological Agency, a Russian federal body known as FMBA that oversees medical services for workers in nuclear, chemical, and other hazardous industries.
HUR said the site is under heightened security, including air defense units assigned to protect it from aerial attack, and that Russian Defense Minister Andrei Belousov has been made responsible for the facility’s security regime. The agency said Russian soldiers assigned to guard the site have privately expressed fear of exposure to unknown pathogens, without naming any individuals or providing direct statements from them.
HUR pointed to an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease among cattle that began in Russia in early 2026 as a possible, though unconfirmed, consequence of failed experiments at facilities like the one on Lisiy Island. That outbreak has been documented independently. It began in Siberia’s Novosibirsk region in February 2026, was initially attributed by Russian officials to pasteurellosis, and later spread west toward the Urals and the border with Kazakhstan and China, prompting mass culling operations, regional export bans, and a U.S. Department of Agriculture report questioning Moscow’s official explanation. Russian authorities have not confirmed foot-and-mouth disease as the cause, and independent reporting on the outbreak has focused on Siberian regions, roughly 2,500 km (1,550 miles) from Tver Oblast, with no established link to any laboratory facility.

articles.title: SBU urges citizens to be particularly vigilant ahead of, on Independence Day
articles.body:
Under conditions of full-scale war, Russians may use mass events for Ukraine’s Independence Day to conduct shelling, provocations, terrorist attacks, sabotage, cyberattacks, and other crimes, the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) warns.
"The Security Service urges citizens to be vigilant and act responsibly regarding their own safety. On the eve of and during festive events, several basic rules should be observed: do not ignore air raid sirens and locate the nearest shelter in advance; do not approach suspicious objects and do not attempt to move or inspect them yourself; in case of detecting suspicious individuals, objects, or other signs of potential illegal activity, notify law enforcement," according to a statement on the SBU Telegram channel.
Citizens are also reminded not to publish photos or videos indicating locations of military personnel, critical infrastructure facilities, checkpoints, air defense assets, etc.; not to share information regarding the aftermath of strikes, air defense operations, or movements of Ukrainian troops; and not to fulfill requests from unknown individuals proposing doubtful tasks, including taking photos or videos of specific facilities, delivering packages, or leaving objects in designated places, even if they present themselves as law enforcement officers.
"Separately, the SBU draws citizens’ attention to attempts by Russian special services to recruit Ukrainians for preparing terrorist attacks and committing acts of sabotage. If unknown individuals offer money for arson, property damage, placing unknown objects, gathering information on military facilities, or other illegal actions, do not agree to such offers and immediately report them to the SSU," the Service emphasized.
In case of receiving information regarding preparations for sabotage, terrorist acts, recruitment, or other activities that may pose a threat to state security, citizens are asked to contact the SBU via the hotline at 1516, report via the "Burn the FSB Agent" chatbot, or email [email protected].

articles.title: German missile-carrier drone completes first flight
articles.body:
- POLARIS Spaceplanes flew its COBRA prototype for the first time, covering more than 20 km with a takeoff mass above 600 kg.
- COBRA is being developed with Diehl Defence under the AirLAS program to carry and launch IRIS-T air-to-air missiles from an unmanned aircraft.
POLARIS Spaceplanes has flown its COBRA prototype for the first time, covering more than 20 km in what the German company described as a smooth flight.
The German aerospace firm announced the milestone in a social media post, saying additional test flights are planned in the coming months and that video footage would follow in coming days. COBRA has a takeoff mass above 600 kg and is being developed jointly with Diehl Defence under the AirLAS program, an effort to build an unmanned aircraft capable of carrying and launching IRIS-T air-to-air missiles.
COBRA is intended primarily for air defense missions. Diehl Defence and POLARIS have described AirLAS as a way to fire IRIS-T missiles from an airborne platform rather than a fixed ground launcher, extending the missile’s reach and giving forces a mobile, forward-deployed option for engaging aircraft, drones, cruise missiles, or helicopters.
Diehl and POLARIS signed an exclusive cooperation agreement at the Paris Air Show in June 2025 to develop AirLAS. The two companies publicly unveiled a demonstrator called the Cobra 600 at the ILA Berlin air show in June 2026. That aircraft measured 6 meters long, used a delta-wing, flying-wing-style airframe with wingtip stabilizers, and was shown carrying a single IRIS-T missile on a top-mounted pylon. The version displayed at ILA Berlin was powered by two JetCat P1000-PRO micro turbojet engines, each producing just under 250 pounds of thrust, though the airframe includes intake ports for two additional engines.
The IRIS-T is a short-range, infrared-guided air-to-air missile built by Diehl Defence and used across multiple European and allied air forces. It weighs 87.4 kg (193 pounds), has a stated top speed of Mach 3, and a standard operational range of about 25 km (16 miles) when fired from an aircraft. Ground-launched versions of the missile family, IRIS-T SLS and IRIS-T SLM, have shorter reach, with ranges of roughly 12 km and 40 km respectively, according to figures the companies have cited.
By putting the missile on an unmanned aircraft, Diehl and POLARIS have said AirLAS is designed to move the launch point closer to a target before firing, rather than relying only on a missile’s own range from a stationary position. The companies have said the platform is designed to be recovered and reused after a mission, or expended as a one-way system depending on the requirement.
POLARIS Spaceplanes was founded to develop reusable hypersonic spaceplanes and describes COBRA as a scaled-down derivative of that spaceplane work adapted for defense applications. The company, based in Bremen, has separately worked on programs including the AURORA multipurpose spaceplane and received funding from Germany’s Federal Office of Bundeswehr Equipment, Information Technology and In-Service Support for in-flight refueling technology intended to extend range and payload capacity on its vehicles.
The AirLAS program has not been the subject of a confirmed procurement contract from the German military or any other government to date. Diehl Defence has said at least one unnamed country has expressed investment interest in the project, though no purchase agreement has been disclosed.

articles.title: Trump warns of ‘economic D-Day’ against Iran, but Tehran is well acquainted with sanctions
articles.body:
Trump warns of ‘economic D-Day’ against Iran, but Tehran is well acquainted with sanctions
Oil tankers and vessels loaded with containers were seen at a standstill in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday. U.S. President Donald Trump has again threatened Oman as Iran says it is working with the Gulf Arab country on a plan to manage shipping through the strait. Fully reopening the waterway has been a key U.S. demand.
NEW YORK (AP) — Nearing the six-month mark of the Iran war and facing diminishing stockpiles of key weapons, the Trump administration is touting a crushing financial campaign against Tehran, promising an “economic D-Day” against a country that has withstood nearly five decades of punishing American sanctions.
With sparse details, President Donald Trump announced this week that the U.S. would be imposing an “unprecedented” level of economic warfare and isolation on Iran, aiming to force its leadership to cave to demands to end its nuclear program and fully reopen the crucial Strait of Hormuz to oil and natural gas tankers.
It reflects the dire reality Trump faces with an increasingly unpopular war he can’t seem to end just months before pivotal midterm elections that will decide whether his Republican Party keeps control of Congress. Whether out of desperation or strategy, the president is refocusing America’s might on bringing Iran to its knees through an accelerated sanctions campaign against one of the most economically penalized countries in the world.
In response to the threat, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted Friday on X the history of U.S. sanctions against Iran, saying, “We have seen this movie before. Same bull. Different bullies.”
The immediate reaction from Iran hawks has been praise and a call for patience as it plays out, while other analysts warn that Trump is refusing to learn the lessons of his predecessors.
In an interview Thursday on CNBC, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent offered a small glimpse of what may be ahead, threatening secondary sanctions on nations and companies that conduct business with Iran.
He did not reveal who would be targeted as part of this next phase of the administration’s Operation Economic Fury, which earlier had focused on entities and people who buy oil from or bank with Iran. China and India, however, are major buyers of Iranian oil.
“If you insist on doing business with them, then the U.S. Treasury and U.S. government will put its full might and force against you,” Bessent said. “It’s time for our allies and the rest of the world to make a decision.”
Some experts see ‘uncharted waters’ that could force Iran’s hand
Despite decades of U.S. sanctions against Iran, the Trump administration is arguing that it’s only a matter of time and that striking the right economic target would get Tehran to its breaking point.
Richard Goldberg, who coordinated efforts to put diplomatic pressure on Iran in Trump’s first term, said the consequences of U.S. strikes on Iran’s nuclear sites last year, the war this year and the American naval blockade on Iranian ports have created the perfect storm for capitulation — one that didn’t previously exist.
“I think we’re watching a strategy, whether it takes a short time or a long time, that is very much about fundamentally changing the future of the world by seeing the end of this regime,” said Goldberg, who is now at the hawkish Washington think tank Foundation for Defense of Democracies, or FDD.
“I caution everyone — including myself, who has worked on sanctions, who’s worked on financial warfare — to have the humility to admit that we are in uncharted waters,” he said.
He said the decision this week by the United Arab Emirates — once one of Tehran’s most important trading partners — to suspend trade with Iran over an alleged missile attack will only further isolate the government.
Beyond trade in domestically produced goods, the Emiratis had helped the country absorb some of the shocks caused by sanctions through its re-export hub.
Targeting allies and partners comes at a price
With nearly all of Iran’s energy, financial and transportation sectors already covered by U.S. sanctions, Trump’s aim appears to be to apply secondary sanctions on countries, including allies and partners, that have not cut all ties with Iran to starve the country of any remaining income it may still be receiving.
In many ways, it is a redux of Trump’s first-term maximum-pressure campaign, which he has ramped up during his second term to include military action.
But as Trump and his allies discovered during his first administration, it can be difficult to enforce secondary sanctions without harming U.S. interests and provoking reciprocal measures. There were numerous instances of the administration granting sanctions waivers to countries, particularly those that rely on Iranian oil for their energy needs.
“Trump’s strategy now rests on targeting Tehran directly by impeding its touch points and access to the formal financial system and international economy,” said Behnam Ben Taleblu, senior director of the FDD’s Iran program. “This will require making the Iran issue more important in U.S. bilateral relations with countries in Europe and Asia.”
Iran doesn’t see an ‘open door’ at the end of the sanctions campaign
Iranian officials and analysts have accused the Republican president of flip-flopping with his latest pivot to economic pressure against Tehran. Trump has long derided past leaders who used sanctions to limit Iran’s ability to pay for its military and nuclear development.
In a post last week on X, Esmail Baghaei, a spokesman for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, wrote that Washington’s pattern of retreating to sanctions when it doesn’t want to pursue diplomacy has proven to be futile.
“Iran has demonstrated over decades that it will not be strangled by these exhausted refrains,” he said. “The real risk is that American politicians, clinging to this bad habit, will instead strangle their own remaining chances of a less humiliating exit from a crisis of their own making.”
Ali Vaez, Iran director at the International Crisis Group, said the Trump administration’s decision to take its own maximum-pressure policy to new heights with military action seems to ignore years of U.S. foreign-policy lessons that show Iran does not respond well to pressure.
If anything, he says, the latest economic campaign has only “hardened Iran’s position.”
“I think (Trump’s) blind spot is the fact that the only thing that the Iranian regime views as more dangerous than suffering from U.S. sanctions is surrendering to U.S. terms,” Vaez said.
Plus, the past year of start-stop diplomacy has only worsened the already fragile dynamic between the longtime adversaries, Vaez says, adding that Iranian officials’ lack of trust in Trump and his mediators has created an untenable foundation.
“They believe that even if they capitulate to U.S. terms under economic duress, Trump would move the goalposts and ask for more,” he said. “And this is really the fundamental problem: Pressure without an open door is an exercise in futility.”
___
Associated Press writers Matthew Lee and Fatima Hussein in Washington contributed to this report.

articles.title: Ukraine’s new commander spoke with chair of NATO’s Military Committee. Result: body will visit Ukraine in October, for first time in eight years
articles.body:
NATO's top military body is coming to Ukraine for the first time in nearly a decade. NATO's Military Committee will visit Ukraine in October, the last such visit having been eight years ago, Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi said after his first conversation with Admiral Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, the committee's chair, the General Staff reported.
Coming early in Drapatyi's tenure as commander-in-chief, the plans on the first NATO Military Committee trip to Ukraine reflect an alliance drawing closer to a country that both receives its support and feeds back combat experience no other NATO member has.
Drapatyi briefed NATO on the front and Ukraine's priorities
Drapatyi laid out the war for the alliance's top soldier. He informed Cavo Dragone about the situation at the front and Ukraine's priorities: long-range strikes, flexible infantry tactics, and the robotization of the front line, according to the General Staff.
Air defense was a focus. Drapatyi stressed that protecting the skies is his priority amid the same interceptor-shortage problem that has left Ukrainian cities exposed to Russian missiles. He thanked the admiral for his consistent support, noting Cavo Dragone had visited Ukraine three times and seen the situation firsthand.
Ukraine frames itself as a contributor
Drapatyi cast the relationship as two-way.
"In October, we expect the NATO Military Committee in Ukraine. The last such visit was eight years ago. Ukraine not only receives support. We transfer combat experience that no one has today, and it works for the security of the whole Alliance," he said.
The admiral confirmed continued support
Cavo Dragone affirmed NATO's backing. He confirmed NATO's continued military support as Ukraine defends its sovereignty and territorial integrity, and said allies in Europe and North America are ramping up defense production, speeding deliveries, and supporting the transfer of needed equipment to Ukraine, he wrote on X.
"I have seen Ukrainian courage with my own eyes: soldiers holding the line with extraordinary bravery for their homes, their families, and their freedom," Dragone said.
He tied Ukraine's security to the alliance's own.
"Ukraine's security is our security, and we will continue to stand alongside Ukraine to help achieve a just and lasting peace," he added.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Ukrainian drones set Russia's Perm oil refinery ablaze
articles.body:
Key developments on Aug. 21:
- Zelensky confirms drone attack on oil refinery in Russia's Perm
- Russian double-tap strike on shopping center in Kryvyi Rih kills at least 14, injures more than 100
- Ukrainian attack on Russian air base damages Su-34 bomber
- Retired FSB general found dead in Moscow, Russian media report
- More than 80 Ukrainian soldiers deserted during training in Germany, media reports
President Zelensky confirmed a drone strike on Russia's Perm oil refinery overnight on Aug. 21.
Videos shared by the Ukrainian Telegram channel Exilenova+ purportedly show explosions and a fire in Perm, a city roughly 1,500 kilometers (930 miles) from Ukraine.
Exilenova+ said local residents reported a series of explosions at the refinery. OSINT analysts from ASTRA, an independent Russian Telegram channel, geolocated footage showing smoke rising near the Lukoil-Permnefteorgsintez oil refinery.
"We continue to use our long-range sanctions to return the consequences of the war to where it came from," Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Local authorities warned residents of incoming unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) around 6.30 a.m. local time. Around the same time, temporary restrictions were introduced at Bolshoe Savino airport in Perm, ASTRA wrote. These have since been lifted.
Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed its air defenses shot down 325 Ukrainian drones overnight.
read also
Russian double-tap strike on shopping center in Kryvyi Rih kills at least 14, injures more than 100
Russian forces launched a daytime drone strike on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih on Aug. 21, killing at least 14 people and injuring 121 others, including 22 children, local authorities said.
Zelensky said the drones struck in two waves, with the second strike taking place around half an hour after the first, when rescue services were already responding at the scene.
"An absolutely cynical and vile strike was carried out by the Russians against an ordinary shopping center in Kryvyi Rih," Zelensky said.
Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi Rih's Defense Council, said the second strike was carried out by a jet-powered Shahed-type drone, adding that the drones were flying at extremely low altitudes.
The Dnipropetrovsk Regional Prosecutor's Office reported that 14 people were killed. Vilkul said 121 people were injured, 29 of whom were in serious condition, including five children.
"There are people who have gone missing and cannot be contacted," Vilkul said.
"Bloody damn Russian bastards," he added.
Ukraine's Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets said Russia was deliberately striking places where civilians gather in broad daylight.
read also
Ukrainian attack on Russian air base damages Su-34 bomber
A Ukrainian drone attack on a Russian air base in Akhtubinsk overnight on Aug. 20 damaged a Russian Su-34 fighter-bomber, the General Staff said.
The Akhtubinsk air base is about 650 kilometers (404 miles) from the front line and is home to Russia's 929th State Aircraft Test Center of the Ministry of Defense, the General Staff reported. This institution is Russia's primary center for testing new weapons and aircraft.
Several Su-34 jets are based in Akhtubinsk. They are multifunctional fighter-bomber jets deploying different types of guided bombs (KAB) and high-explosive bombs (FAB).
read also
Retired FSB general found dead in Moscow, Russian media report
Retired Russian FSB Major General Igor Laptev, whose business supplied communications equipment to Russia's Defense Ministry and other state agencies, was found dead in his Moscow apartment, Russian media reported on Aug. 21.
The 83-year-old was found with a gunshot wound to the head in his apartment on Verkhnyaya Krasnoselskaya Street, according to Russian outlets Moskovsky Komsomolets and Izvestia.
The outlets, citing unnamed sources, reported that Laptev died by suicide on August 20.
Russian authorities have not publicly confirmed the reports, and the circumstances surrounding Laptev’s death remain unclear.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the claims.
read also
More than 80 Ukrainian soldiers deserted during training in Germany, media reports
Around 80 Ukrainian soldiers have deserted while undergoing military training in the German state of Saxony-Anhalt since 2022, with cases across Germany estimated in the hundreds, Die Zeit reported on Aug. 20.
The soldiers had been sent to Germany for training to fight Russia, but they left the training grounds unauthorized to avoid returning to Ukraine.
The report comes as Ukraine struggles with a worsening manpower shortage after more than four years of full-scale war, increasingly relying on mobilized recruits as the pool of volunteers shrinks.
More than 25,000 Ukrainian soldiers had undergone military training in Germany by early 2026, according to the Bundeswehr.
Germany provides training as part of the EU Military Assistance Mission for Ukraine (EUMAM UA), launched in 2022. By early 2026, 22 participating European countries had trained around 87,000 Ukrainian soldiers. The training includes instruction in operating military equipment, weapons handling, camouflage, and first aid.

articles.title: Ukraine Planned 1,000-Drone Swarm to Paralyze Moscow Airports
articles.body:
Ukraine drew up plans to unleash a swarm of up to 1,000 autonomous drones on Moscow’s airports in a bid to overwhelm Russian air defenses, cripple air travel and pressure the Kremlin back to negotiations.
The operation, codenamed “M&Ms,” was developed under former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov and envisioned sending hundreds of small, low-cost drones into Moscow in a single night, according to two sources familiar with the plan.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to The Atlantic report, the drones were designed to navigate and identify targets without human operators. Their onboard computers would contain detailed maps and images of designated targets, allowing the UAVs to compare live camera footage with data stored in their systems.
Once a target was identified, a drone would dive into it and detonate without requiring confirmation from an operator.
The goal: ground Moscow
The plan was designed to overwhelm Russian air defenses and disrupt Moscow’s four major airports – Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky – potentially for an extended period.
Ukraine hoped prolonged disruption would force international carriers, including Turkish Airlines and Emirates, to reconsider flights to Moscow, cutting off a key link between Russia’s political elite and the outside world.
The operation was also intended to create pressure on Russian authorities and push President Vladimir Putin back toward negotiations to end Russia’s war against Ukraine.
Mariupol Volunteer Safe After Risking Everything to Save Son Allegedly Threatened by Russia’s FSB
The plan was reportedly presented to President Volodymyr Zelensky in early 2026. He raised concerns about the potential risks to civilian aircraft, passengers and airport workers but allowed preparations to continue, according to The Atlantic’s sources.
Organizers also proposed warning civilian airlines ahead of the operation so they could avoid Moscow’s airports and evacuate aircraft before the drone swarm arrived.
Project halted after Fedorov’s exit
Preparations were halted in July following Fedorov’s resignation as defense minister.
The sources said Fedorov had spent much of the year developing the project, assembling programmers to build the AI-based navigation system and securing funding from Ukraine’s European allies for autonomous drones.
The project could still be revived.
Zelensky’s office, however, denied the operation existed, calling the report “complete nonsense.”
The official said Ukraine has only one objective involving Russian airports: forcing Moscow to repeatedly impose its “carpet” emergency protocol, which restricts air traffic during security threats.
Ukraine does seek to shut Russian airports down for prolonged periods or even completely, the official said, but lacks long-range weapons precise and reliable enough to strike airports without posing excessive risks to civilians.
Russian airports have already faced repeated disruptions linked to Ukrainian attacks.
According to Russia’s Federal Air Transport Agency, restrictions were imposed 114 times between June 28 and July 28. Moscow’s four main airports accounted for at least 17 temporary shutdowns during that period.
Across Russia, more than 290 similar disruptions were recorded during the first quarter of 2026.

articles.title: Russian Forces Launch 172 Attacks Across Front Line on Friday
articles.body:
Russian forces launched 172 attacks across the front line on Friday, Aug. 21, with the most intense combat reported on the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) detailed the strikes in its daily operational update, covering the 24-period ending at 10:00 p.m. local time.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the report, Russia carried out 75 airstrikes using 219 guided aerial bombs (KABs), deployed 6,751 kamikaze drones and shelled Ukrainian military positions and populated areas 1,939 times.
Russian forces launched 23 attacks on the Pokrovsk axis, including near Bilytske, Udachne, Muravka and Novopidhrodne, as well as toward Hannivka, Novyi Donbas, Svitłe, Shevchenko, Vasylivka and Serhiivka.
Two combat engagements were still underway at the time of the report.
Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka axes
The General Staff said preliminary estimates showed 35 Russian troops were killed and 14 wounded on the Pokrovsk axis.
The AFU reported destroying a tank, six vehicles, three artillery systems, a fuel depot, an ammunition depot and 27 Russian personnel shelters.
On the same axis, 416 Russian drones were destroyed or suppressed.
On the Kostiantynivka axis, 20 Russian assaults were repelled near Kostiantynivka, Ivanopillia, Illinivka, Novoselivka, Novomykolaivka, Shakhove, Sofiivka and Vilne, as well as toward Dovha Balka.
One combat engagement was reportedly ongoing at the time of the report.
Sloviansk, Lyman, and other axes
Russia reportedly launched 11 assaults on the South Slobozhshchyna axis toward Izbytske, Radkivka, Kovalivka, Okhrimivka and Mytrofanivka, with two attacks still underway at the time of the report.
Zelensky Informs UN Secretary-General Guterres About Russian Strikes
According to the General Staff, the AFU repelled four Russian attempts to advance on the Lyman axis and eight on the Sloviansk axis, where fighting was ongoing.
Three Russian attacks were reported on the Oleksandrivka axis, three toward Tsvitkove on the Huliaipole axis and two near Plavni and Mali Shcherbaky on the Orikhiv axis.
One engagement on the Orikhiv axis, in the Zaporizhzhia region, was still ongoing at the time of the report.
No offensive operations were reported on the Kupiansk and Prydniprovske axes, the General Staff said.
