articles.title: Zelenskyy called the strike on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih a terrorist attack and urged the world to increase pressure on Russia
articles.body:
Zelenskyy called the strike on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih a terrorist attack and urged the world to increase pressure on Russia
Kyiv • UNN
Russian drones struck a shopping and entertainment center in Kryvyi Rih twice, killing six people and injuring 96. Zelenskyy called for increased pressure on the Russian Federation.
President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy called Russia’s attacks on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih an act of terrorism and called on the world to respond by increasing pressure on the aggressor, reports UNN.
Details
Head of State Volodymyr Zelenskyy specified that the drones flew toward the city in two waves.
"The Russians carried out an absolutely cynical and vile strike on an ordinary shopping center in Kryvyi Rih. Half an hour after the first hit and the fire, there was a second strike on the emergency services," the Ukrainian leader wrote on his Telegram channel.
The President also expressed his condolences to the families and loved ones of those killed and injured.
He stressed that such strikes are simply acts of terrorism. And the world must respond to them accordingly—through real pressure on the aggressor.
In addition
Meanwhile, Dmytro Lubinets, the Verkhovna Rada Commissioner for Human Rights, stressed that the enemy deliberately strikes places where civilians gather in broad daylight.
"People came to the shopping center to go about their ordinary business: to shop, go to work, or spend time with their loved ones. For Russia, this has no significance whatsoever," Lubinets wrote on his official Telegram channel.
He summarized that the Russian army is once again proving that civilians are a deliberate target for it in this war against Ukraine.
What is known about the Russian armed forces’ strike on Kryvyi Rih on August 21
The Russians struck Kryvyi Rih with drones at 4:30 p.m. The target was the "Sonyachna Halereia" shopping mall in the Saksahanskyi district of the city. Immediately after the first strike, a massive fire broke out inside the premises. Two people, one of whom, according to local media reports, was a child, died at the scene. Dozens were injured.
Employees of all services immediately arrived at the scene: rescuers, medics, and law enforcement officers. They immediately began extinguishing the fire and providing assistance to the facility’s employees and shopping mall visitors. However, at 4:52 p.m., the building was struck a second time. This increased the number of victims and injured.
The enemy’s attack on the city continued until 5:28 p.m.
As of now, six deaths are known: five people died at the scene from their injuries, while a sixth resident, who sustained severe injuries, is in the operating room. Injuries were sustained by 96 residents of Kryvyi Rih, including children. Twenty injured people are currently under medical care, but their condition is serious.
The environmental situation in the city has deteriorated. Thick black smoke can be seen dozens of kilometers from the site of the incident. The smoke is pungent and has an unpleasant odor. Residents were asked to close their windows.
Meanwhile, in Russian media, the enemy began spreading its own version of events. The Russians claim that they directed UAVs at "military facilities." And, allegedly, because of the operation of Ukrainian air defenses, the drones deviated from their course and "suddenly" fell onto the roof of the shopping mall.

articles.title: Iranian families struggle to afford the basics as US ratchets up economic warfare
articles.body:
Iranian families struggle to afford the basics as US ratchets up economic warfare
TEHRAN, Iran (AP) — Tehran’s grocery stores are well-stocked, but many families can barely afford the basics. Unemployment is soaring and those with jobs are working more hours for money worth half as much as a year ago, putting food, medicine and everything else — except for heavily subsidized gasoline — further out of reach.
“We have virtually given up on many things,” said Ahmad Karimi, 52, a taxi driver and father of two who has been working 15-hour days to make ends meet. “We’re cutting out fruit, we’re cutting out protein, we’ve given up leisure, we even work on weekends.”
Nearly six months into the war with the United States and Israel, the Iranian economy is taking a beating under the force of sanctions and a naval blockade that is making it extremely difficult for the country to export oil, its most valuable product.
Whether this intensifying economic pressure will translate anytime soon into military or political concessions from Iran remains to be seen — but some experts are skeptical. Since the war began, Iran has been attacking oil-rich neighbors and U.S. bases in the region, and disrupting shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, its biggest strategic advantage.
Iran is trying to use this retaliatory pressure — which is driving up energy prices globally — to bring the war to an end on the best terms possible. It is pressing for sanctions relief, and seeking enough control over the strait to demand payment from ships passing through to deliver energy and other goods.
The Trump administration — which is stuck fighting over a waterway in a war that was launched to curb Iran’s nuclear program — is now promising to deliver even tougher sanctions to try to squeeze the Islamic Republic into submission. But experts say U.S. President Donald Trump may be underestimating how long Iran can hold out.
Iran has been subject to Western sanctions for years and has become deft at partially circumventing them. It has expanded domestic production, used informal cross-border trade networks, bought restricted goods through third countries, and used a shadow fleet to transport its oil.
“Iran’s resistance capacity not only avoids collapse, it also prevents the economic pain from translating into the political pressure and changes that the U.S. expects,” said Hadi Kahalzadeh, an expert on Iran’s economy at Brandeis University.
Iran’s economic strains carry an ‘emotional toll’
Tehran’s sprawling Grand Bazaar is regularly packed with shoppers hoping to find more affordable staples than at the country’s grocery stores, where rice is 60% more expensive and beef is 150% more expensive than before the war.
A mother of two from northern Iran posted a photo on X this week after purchasing milk, eggs, toilet paper and a few other items, but no meat. She complained that it cost 89 million rials (about $65).
“Buying basic necessities has become our main priority, and our shopping basket has gotten smaller and more limited,” the 41-year-old told The Associated Press on condition of anonymity for fear of retribution.
“The emotional toll and the pressure we’re under are another story,” she said. “Every time we have to say no to our children, every time we have to go back and forth over a decision, whether it’s a class you’d love your children to take or something they really want you to buy for them, it’s genuinely exhausting.”
By the end of the year, inflation in Iran is expected to rise nearly 70%, according to the International Monetary Fund, and the country’s economy — devastated by a decade of sanctions before the war — is forecast to shrink by more than 5%.
While gasoline has remained cheap thanks to government subsidies, even that might not last forever as supplies get tighter. A presidential aide told Iranian state television last week that the country is now using more gasoline each day than it produces and may need to raise prices — something that in the past has led to widespread protests.
Iranians turn some anger toward countries behind sanctions
Iran’s theocratic leaders were already facing economic discontent before the U.S. and Israel started the war on Feb. 28. Protests had spread across the country at the beginning of the year before they were violently put down, with thousands killed and tens of thousands believed to have been arrested.
Many Iranians have now turned at least some of their economic frustrations toward the countries behind the sanctions and the attacks that have destroyed factories and critical infrastructure and killed scores of civilians, said Hassan Golmoradi, a Tehran-based economist.
“Despite the hardships and difficulties, they have shown considerable patience in putting up with the resulting economic pressures,” Golmoradi said.
Iran’s leaders have said it is a treasonous offense — punishable by death — to take part in anti-government protests.
“They do suffer, but they do not think that by joining violent protests they can achieve something for themselves and their families,” said Mohammad Farzanegan, a professor of Middle Eastern economics at the University of Marburg in Germany.
Trump is threatening tougher sanctions
On Wednesday, Trump vowed on social media to unleash against Iran the “most crushing economic operation ever taken against any country.” He also threatened secondary sanctions on nations and companies that continue to do business with Iran.
The United Arab Emirates, which for years had enabled Iran to circumvent sanctions and receive goods from other countries, announced this week it was suspending all trade with Tehran. Trump had called the leader of the UAE, Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, the day before the announcement.
With the economic struggles, the elected government of Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said it favors a negotiated end to the war. “What concerns us is people’s livelihoods and their economic situation, and we are doing everything we can to deal with it,” he told reporters last week.
But the most powerful force in Iran remains the paramilitary Revolutionary Guard, which has only become stronger after withstanding U.S. and Israeli airstrikes that killed Iran’s top leaders during the war’s opening salvos. The Guard is pressing for greater concessions from the U.S., including Iranian control over the Strait of Hormuz and financial compensation for the war.
With negotiations to end the war stalled, Iran’s hard-liners believe their country can endure the conflict’s economic pressures longer than their adversaries.
Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, this month appointed a former Revolutionary Guard commander to head Iran’s powerful Supreme National Security Council, a sign that he favors the hard-line approach.
A taxi driver says something has to give
Official government statistics put Iran’s unemployment rate at 9.1%, though state-affiliated media outlets have said the real figure is most likely many times higher. A Labor Ministry official said last week that by late May, just three months into the war, more than 1 million jobs had been lost.
In a sign that Iran’s leaders are at least somewhat concerned about public opinion, the government has refrained from enforcing mandatory hijab regulations as harshly as it had been — a social freedom that has long been sought by many.
But these days many Iranians are focused on how their lifestyles are restricted economically.
Karimi, the taxi driver, said Iran’s leaders will need to do something soon to alleviate the financial pressures he and others are feeling.
“The people won’t be able to continue living like this,” he said. “We’re simply breathing, surviving, and trying to make it from one day to the next.”
___
Rising reported from Dubai, United Arab Emirates.

articles.title: Editor of military news outlet that first revealed US aircraft carrier crisis says he was fired over interview – live
articles.body:
Editor of military news outlet that first revealed US aircraft carrier crisis says he was fired over interview – live
Erik Slavin says he was dismissed for insubordination after objecting to potential censorship in wake of furor sparked by reported conditions on USS Abraham Lincoln
Stars and Stripes editor says he has been fired for insubordination after doing interview
In an update to my earlier post, the Pentagon is confirmed to have fired the editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes, Erik Slavin, as well as its publisher, Max Lederer, and a reporter, Slavin has told the Associated Press.
Slavin said he was dismissed for insubordination after an interview he gave that objected to any potential censorship by the US military.
He told the AP he was fired “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line”. He added that he stands by the principle “that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent”.
Earlier this week, Lederer announced his retirement effective at the end of September. He too received a separation notice, according to Slavin, as did the Middle East reporter Lara Korte.
Trump touts his ballroom while rallying for Darline Graham
The president is now speaking at a rally in support of the Senate campaign of Darline Graham, the sister of the late senator, Lindsey Graham.
After a few minutes of praise for her campaign, Trump began discussing his ballroom project, saying he was in a “very good mood” after US supreme court chief justice John Roberts issued an order in his favor earlier today. The order allowed the White House to continue construction of the ballroom, a top Trump priority, while appeals challenging the project are ongoing.
At the rally, Trump described the ballroom as a “beautiful, magnificent complex, being built on the hallowed grounds of our cherished White House”. He said the ballroom was “so vital for national security” and would be “the greatest of its kind anywhere that’s ever been built”.
Trump shows reporters pro-Trump headlines from pro-Trump media
Concerns about the narrow, partisan nature of the media consumed by the president of the United States have spiked in recent days amid new attention to the role Donald Trump’s aide, Natalie Harp, plays in limiting what he sees, by printing out mainly flattering headlines and posts for him from the internet for him to read.
Trump himself accidentally offered up evidence of just how skewed his media diet is on Friday, when he used a few minutes with reporters to hold up a print-out of what he cast as important media headlines before boarding a flight to South Carolina for a rally in support of the Senate campaign of late Lindsey Graham’s sister, Darline.
“So, here are some headlines,” the president said after asking his press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, to hand him a print-out that displayed nine headlines, but no indiction of where they were published. “These are incredible headlines that just came out over the last 24 hours.”
“It’s probably easier if I show them to you than reading them,” Trump said, holding up the sheet of paper in front of photographers in the White House pool.
He then boasted about the headlines, which were largely taken from partisan, right-wing outlets that openly support him and simply repeated his administration’s claims.
Two of the headlines came from Breitbart, the far-right website its former editor Steve Bannon once described as a “platform for the alt-right”. Two came from outlets owned by Trump supporter Rupert Murdoch: the New York Post and Fox News. One was an opinion piece from a former Trump campaign spokesman published by the Daily Signal, a website founded by the Heritage Foundation, the right-wing think tank behind Project 2025. One came from Voz, a conservative news site aimed at Latinos founded in 2022 by pro-Trump executives.
The other three headlines came from avowedly non-partisan news outlets, Axios, CNN and the Washington Post, but in all three cases the headlines simply presented what looked like good news that the administration took credit.
As we reported last week, when Trump held up the Washington Post headline “Prescription drug prices record sharpest drop in more than 60 years”, the president apparently failed to read the article below, since it reported that independent experts actually attributed the price drop to Joe Biden, not Trump.
The secretary of the US Army, Dan Driscoll, is expected to step down from his role by the end of the year, after months of tension with the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, the Wall Street Journal reported on Friday.
Driscoll, a friend and Yale Law school classmate of vice-president JD Vance, reportedly angered Hegseth near the very start of his tenure at the Pentagon when he offered to set up a visit by Vance and Donald Trump.
The departure, as the US is engaged in a war with Iran, would further deplete the US Army of Senate-confirmed leaders. In April, Hegseth fired the Army’s chief of staff, General Randy George and a replacement has yet to be nominated.
Trump again denies that taxpayers will fund his ballroom, despite evidence it will drain hundreds of millions from US budget
Speaking to reporters on his way to a political rally in South Carolina, Donald Trump was asked if he could “guarantee that no tax money will be used in the construction of the ballroom?”
The president replied, as he has for over a year, by insisting that the project would be entirely paid for by private donations, despite multiple reports that the project will drain hundreds of millions of taxpayer dollars from federal agencies.
“We’re spending hundreds of millions of dollars on the ballroom and it’s all from people like me and great companies that are putting it up. It’s going to be close to $400 million and it’s all paid for by patriots and patriotic companies,” Trump said. “No taxpayer money for the ballroom at all.”
But the Washington Post reported in June that Trump’s claim is simply untrue. A project summary prepared by the ballroom contractor obtained by the Post showed that the total construction was expected to cost $600m, with more than half of the funds coming from taxpayers.
Two days later, the New York Times revealed that the Trump administration had shifted over $350m from the Secret Service’s budget to White House to pay for a secure military bunker underneath the luxury ballroom.
Trump thanks supreme court for allowing work to proceed on his 'Military/Ballroom Complex'
In a social media post on Friday, Donald Trump thanked the supreme court for allowing work to proceed, for now, on what he has taken to calling his White House “Military/Ballroom Complex”.
The president’s brief post was packed with misleading or false claims about the order and the ballroom he razed the entire East Wing of the White House to start building.
“We are grateful for the Decision of the United States Supreme Court”, Trump wrote, mischaracterizing the single-sentence order from one justice, John Roberts, as a decision of the court. In fact, Roberts only lifted a preliminary injunction from a lower court that had blocked above-ground work on the ballroom to give the full supreme court time to reach a final decision on whether the president can complete the project.
“The Military/Ballroom Complex being built on the hallowed grounds of the White House, which is so vital for National Security, will be THE GREATEST OF ITS KIND!” Trump continued, continuing to cast the creation of a vast reception hall on the White House grounds as somehow motivated by a concern to increase security around the presidential residence.
A White House bunker beneath the East Wing, demolished by Trump in his rush to construct his ballroom, does need to be replaced, but he is simply solving a problem he created. Trump was reportedly rushed into the bunker by the Secret Service in 2020, as protesters rallied to decry police violence against Black Americans after the murder of George Floyd.
“It is something that Presidents have wanted for 150 years, and that the Military has been seeking for the last 100 years,” Trump continued, repeating an entirely unsourced claim he has been making for more than a year now.
“Their wish will soon be fulfilled! Construction is under budget and ahead of schedule,” he concluded. Although this is a claim Trump has been making about building projects since his days as a real estate developer, it is clearly not true that construction of the ballroom is “under budget” given that the White House first said the ballroom would cost approximately $200m when it was unveiled in July 2025, before the president started calling if a $400m project, and the contractor hired for the ballroom reportedly told the White House in March that the project cost had soared to $600m, according to a document obtained by the Washington Post.
Senator Chuck Schumer, who leads the Democratic minority in the Senate, denounced the supreme court order Trump hailed.
“The MAGA Supreme Court is rubber stamping Trump’s vanity-driven, gilded corruption,” Schumer posted in response to the news.
“As costs skyrocket, the administration is wasting money on an endless and illegal war, corporate giveaways, and Trump’s pet projects,” Schumer added. “We will continue to fight this flagrant waste of taxpayer money relentlessly in the courts.”
Stars and Stripes editor says he has been fired for insubordination after doing interview
In an update to my earlier post, the Pentagon is confirmed to have fired the editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes, Erik Slavin, as well as its publisher, Max Lederer, and a reporter, Slavin has told the Associated Press.
Slavin said he was dismissed for insubordination after an interview he gave that objected to any potential censorship by the US military.
He told the AP he was fired “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line”. He added that he stands by the principle “that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent”.
Earlier this week, Lederer announced his retirement effective at the end of September. He too received a separation notice, according to Slavin, as did the Middle East reporter Lara Korte.
Trump threatens think tank with $5bn lawsuit over report that found 'no evidence' that his national guard deployments had affected crime rate
The New York Times (paywall) reports that Donald Trump has threatened a prominent progressive think tank with a $5bn lawsuit over a report that found the president’s expensive deployment of the national guard and other federal agents has done little to reduce violent crime in Washington DC and other cities.
Trump regularly touts his supposed success in taking DC “from high crime to no crime”. For instance, a few weeks ago he told reporters in the Oval Office: “This was the crime capital, frankly, of the world. It was the most unsafe capital of any country in the world. Now, it’s one of the safest, and it’s one of the safest places in the United States.”
Last month, the Center for American Progress published findings that Trump’s deployments had failed to reduce violent crime despite its claims of success. The analysis highlighted that violent crime rates had already dropped before Trump took office again, and said his administration “is using these declines to justify expanding policies that are unpopular, ineffective, and costly”.
It’s summary reads:
Even though the data clearly show that violent crime and homicides were already dropping in American cities in 2023 and 2024, the Trump administration has continued to threaten city and state leaders and argue that its extreme actions, such as deploying the National Guard to support law enforcement operations, are improving public safety.
However, new Center for American Progress analysis finds no evidence that National Guard deployments have reduced violent crime. Moreover, if these deployments are extended and continue through the end of 2026, they could cost American taxpayers more than $1.7 billion.
This left the administration displeased. Per the NYT’s report:
On Monday, one of Mr. Trump’s personal lawyers, Alejandro Brito, wrote a letter to the center warning that he would file the suit if the group did not fully retract the report, which was published on its website on July 13. The letter, viewed by The New York Times, was addressed to the group’s president and chief executive, Neera Tanden, a longtime Democratic official who served as a senior adviser to President Joseph R. Biden Jr., and to several of its board members.
Mr. Brito claimed that the report about the National Guard was full of malicious and false statements. He gave Ms. Tanden and members of her board until 5 p.m. on Friday to retract it and apologize to Mr. Trump.
Tanden hit back, telling the Times in a statement that the center would “neither cower nor bend in the face” of legal action. She also defended the report, asserting that while its findings might have been “inconvenient to the Trump administration”, they were “grounded in rigorous, evidence-based research and analysis”.
She added:
This threatened lawsuit’s attack on facts and evidence is baseless.A fundamental protection of the First Amendment is to allow for the publication of facts and analysis that is contrary to the arguments and claims of any administration.A lawsuit is a transparent attempt to silence us.
Pentagon moves to fire publisher and editor of Stars and Stripes - report
The Pentagon has moved to fire both the publisher and the editor in chief of Stars and Stripes, the leading US military news outlet partly funded by taxpayers, for alleged insubordination, CBS News reports.
Separation notices were delivered today, and give publisher Max Lederer and editor-in-chief Erik Slavin five days to appeal their dismissals, according to people familiar with the matter who spoke to CBS News. The cause cited was insubordination, one of the people said. They did not elaborate on the details of the alleged insubordination.
Lederer, the publisher of the military daily for 19 years, had this week told colleagues he planned to retire on 30 September, citing fundamental differences with the Trump administration.
“It has become clear that my philosophy of leadership, and my understanding of value and mission of the Stars and Stripes, differ in fundamental ways from the direction of the leadership of the Department of Defense,” Lederer said in a letter to staff, which was posted on X.
This comes days after the outlet revealed, along with the Navy Times, the deteriorating conditions and mental health crisis for service members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which is on a record-breaking nine-month deployment in the Middle East as part of the US-Israel war on Iran.
It is unclear whether that reporting is linked to the reported discussions inside the Pentagon. But Slavin has spoken publicly about disagreements with Pentagon leaders.
As my colleague Edward Helmore notes, Slavin hinted at tensions with the military brass just last month when he said the “foxhole” he would be willing to die in would be over editorial independence from the Pentagon, which provides about 65% of its funding.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon spokesperson, Sean Parnell, posted on X: “We are bringing Stars & Stripes into the 21st century. We will modernize its operations, refocus its content away from woke distractions that syphon morale, and adapt it to serve a new generation of service members.”
Further to our earlier posts on the backlash over reports that a navy aircraft carrier set to honor a Black war hero may, instead, be named after Donald Trump, it seems worth noting that in Trump’s executive order last week, when he demanded that a new aircraft carrier under construction be redesigned to install steam catapults to launch fighter jets, there was no mention of the fact that the ship was to be named the USS Doris Miller, in honor of a Black hero of Pearl Harbor. The order did not refer to the ship at any point as the USS Miller, a name chosen by the navy during Trump’s first term, but instead used just the ship’s hull number, CVN-81.
Supreme court chief justice allows work on Trump’s $400m White House ballroom to continue for now
Chief Justice John Roberts is allowing the White House to continue construction on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m ballroom project for now, the Associated Press reports, as the supreme court considers the Trump administration’s emergency request to intervene in lawsuits over the project.
The brief, one-page document does not detail Roberts’ reasoning or lay out a timeline for a fuller decision from the high court.
Lower courts had ordered a halt to the project, finding that it must have congressional approval. That ruling was set to take effect today.
When Trump first announced the plans for a new ballroom, he did not emphasize national security.
He also said the project would be funded by private donations, including from himself. But in June it was revealed that the administration had quietly redirected $352m in federal funds designated for the Secret Service toward the project, after Congress explicitly refused to provide $1bn in funds for it.
Migrants reportedly flown to Equatorial Guinea after resisting Liberia deportation under Trump deal
Five people whom the US attempted to deport to Liberia this week resisted getting off the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea, another African country to which the Trump administration is removing migrants it cannot legally send home, two sources familiar with the matter have told Reuters.
The incident represents an early snag in Washington’s plan to send up to 1,200 so-called third-country deportees to Liberia, one of the largest such deals it has struck in Africa despite criticism from immigrants’ rights advocates.
Third-country deportees have, in most cases, obtained legal protection against repatriation after US immigration judges ruled they risked torture or other abuses in their home countries.
Liberia announced on Tuesday that it had agreed to receive deportees and that the first group of 20 would arrive on Thursday. But a Liberian official, speaking on condition of anonymity because of the sensitivity of the matter, told Reuters today that only 15 deportees disembarked.
At least five others - three Cuban men, one Brazilian man and one Cameroonian woman - refused to get off the plane in Liberia, according to three sources familiar with the incident, one of whom was a Honduran deportee on the flight.
Authorities then told them they would be flown to the US, but the plane instead headed to Malabo, in Equatorial Guinea, where the five were forced to disembark against their will, two of the sources said.
Liberia’s information ministry did not respond to a Reuters request for comment on Friday.
The five are now being held with more than 30 other migrants whom the Trump administration had previously sent to Equatorial Guinea under a deal that, like others in Africa, has been denounced by human rights groups and advocates who say many of the deportees are ultimately repatriated.
In May, human rights experts at the United Nations issued a rare public appeal to Equatorial Guinea, urging the country to halt its plans to return US deportees to their home countries, where they face political violence, torture and death.
The US state department said it remained “unwavering in our commitment to end illegal and mass immigration and bolster America’s border security”.
A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said all the migrants “were deported to a safe third country”, adding: “If a judge finds an illegal alien has no right to be in this country, we are going to remove them. Period.”
Thomas Bledsoe told CNN the potential move is “quite a shock” and that the family were not notified beforehand. “Not only was it a shock, but it was also shocking that we found out from a new outlet [and not] from the Navy,” he said.
But this isn’t just about a name on a ship, he added.
It’s about an opportunity and a goal. It’s about what it means to be an American and it’s also about how we as a community can grow as one.
Less than three months to go until the midterms, voters are thinking about grocery prices, the Iran war and… datacenters.
This week, Jonathan Freedland speaks to historian Jill Lepore about how this latest AI backlash could influence those all-important elections in November. Are we seeing the beginning of the end of the ‘artificial state’?

articles.title: NATO conducted unannounced large-scale exercises near Kaliningrad amid rising tensions with the Russian Federation
articles.body:
NATO conducted unannounced large-scale exercises near Kaliningrad amid rising tensions with the Russian Federation
Kyiv • UNN
The alliance deployed up to 50 aircraft on the eastern flank, including F-35s, AWACS and electronic warfare aircraft. Poland is strengthening its monitoring of Russia's activity.
NATO conducted a series of unannounced military exercises this week near Kaliningrad and on the Alliance’s eastern flank, involving reconnaissance aircraft, tankers, F-35 fighter jets and other advanced air assets. This was reported by the Lithuanian broadcaster LRT, writes UNN.
Details
Dozens of NATO aircraft carried out missions over Poland, the Baltic states and other areas of the eastern flank. They included AWACS radar reconnaissance aircraft, tanker aircraft, reconnaissance planes and an American electronic warfare aircraft capable of disrupting the enemy’s communications.
According to NATO, the exercises had been planned in advance and were not a response to a new threat from Russia. At the same time, what was unusual was that the Alliance did not announce them beforehand. Unofficial estimates suggest that up to 50 aircraft may have participated in the exercises.
Poland strengthens monitoring of Russia’s actions
Former Polish military general Roman Polko said that the current exercises differed in scale and intensity.
These NATO exercises show that the organization takes the Alliance’s northeastern flank seriously. They are much more intensive than previous ones and are conducted at various levels, covering all domains
Polish Deputy Defense Minister Cezary Tomczyk said that Warsaw was closely monitoring Russia’s military activity in Kaliningrad, Belarus and on the territory of the Russian Federation.
Russia is arming itself against NATO. Perhaps not because it has decided to start a war, but because it wants to show how strong it is. It wants to show that it has not yet said its final word in the war in Ukraine. We are monitoring very closely – using military and civilian intelligence, as well as satellite imagery – what Russia is doing in Kaliningrad, Belarus and Russia itself
Poland is simultaneously strengthening its land border with the Kaliningrad region together with German and American troops. As part of the "Eastern Shield" project, tank obstacles, fences and surveillance systems are being installed.

articles.title: Former Air Force Secretary James G. Roche Dies at 86
articles.body:
James G. Roche, the 20th Secretary of the Air Force who led the department from 2001-2005, died Aug. 4. He was 86.
As Secretary, Roche led the Air Force through the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks and subsequent preparations and campaigns in Afghanistan in 2001 and Iraq in 2003. During his tenure, he pushed for tighter synergy between the Air Force’s air and space activities, improved readiness, a shift from platform-based acquisition to capabilities- and networks-based systems, and setting the Air Force on a course to adopt combat drones partnered with piloted aircraft; a concept now coming to fruition in the form of Collaborative Combat Aircraft.
Though nominated by President George W. Bush to be Army Secretary in 2005, Roche withdrew his name from consideration when it became apparent that congressional opponents would block his confirmation indefinitely. At issue was Roche’s promotion of a plan to replace the Air Force’s oldest aerial tankers with aircraft leased from Boeing. One of Roche’s acquisition officials acted improperly in pursuit of the idea: that official went to jail and another resigned, but Roche himself was not found to have acted criminally.
Born in Brooklyn, N.Y., in 1939, Roche earned a bachelor’s degree in humanities from Chicago’s Illinois Institute of Technology in 1960 and took up a Navy commission through the ROTC. In 1966 he completed a master’s in operations research from the Navy postgraduate school in Monterey, Calif. , and earned a doctorate in business administration from Harvard in 1972.
Roche served 23 years as a Navy officer, during which he commanded the guided missile destroyer USS Buchanan. While in uniform, he worked on the Senate intelligence committee and served as deputy to Andrew Marshall, the Pentagon’s Director of Net Assessment. Retiring as a captain in 1983, he then headed the Democratic staff of the Senate Armed Services Committee for a year, moving to Northrop in 1984. He headed the company’s analysis center in Washington for five years, then became a vice president and assistant to Northrop CEO Tom Jones. A series of executive positions with Northrop followed: first as VP and then chief of advanced development and planning, then as president of Northrop’s Electronic Sensors and Systems sector until his appointment by Bush to be Air Force Secretary in 2001.
In the months leading up to the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks, Roche moved to enhance the appeal and quality of life for enlisted Airmen by improving their educational opportunities and living conditions. He insisted the Air Force’s air and space capabilities needed to be more closely aligned: he set in motion plans to integrate air- and space-based sensor and communications networks, and expanded the integration of space capabilities with field units. He also moved to improve readiness through more exercises and more funding for spare parts.
Roche also took a cue from Chief of Staff Gen. John Jumper to pursue unmanned combat aircraft. In 2000, Jumper, as head of Air Combat Command, had directed the arming of MQ-9 Predator reconnaissance drones, tests of which began in early 2001. Roche saw armed, self-directed drones as certain to be an important part of the Air Force’s future. He began to promote the idea—pushing for further development of experiments like the X-45 Unmanned Combat Aircraft Vehicle, already underway—and in several speeches and internal messages told Air Force leaders to anticipate and begin preparing for the day when unmanned combat aerial vehicles, or UCAVs, would fly alongside piloted aircraft or pursue combat missions independently.
While successful, the UCAV experiment did not become a top Air Force acquisition priority until Air Force Secretary Frank Kendall formally started the CCA program in 2022. It is likely the Air Force’s UCAV program transitioned to classified efforts in the intervening years. Roche frequently touted combat UAVs as assets that did not tire and could undertake long missions without degraded “acuity.” He also noted that if a drone is lost in combat, “you don’t have to write a letter to the mother of a computer chip.”
In the immediate aftermath of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, Roche put greater emphasis on the Air Expeditionary Forces concept, already then taking shape, pumping more people, aircraft, and logistical backing into the construct, and shifting emphasis from stateside garrison activities to forward deployments. He pushed the deployment of unmanned aircraft like the RQ-4 Global Hawk and MQ-1 Predator into the Southwest Asia theater, even though both were still considered experimental. Along with the Army, he fostered greater field cooperation between the services, putting airmen in Army ground units to facilitate air attacks and close air support.
Roche also increased the use of the Air National Guard and Air Force Reserve in the Afghanistan campaign, integrating those units more closely with the Active-Duty force; leading to a day-to-day operational dependency on reserves that the Air Force still maintains.
In addition, Roche advocated creation of more Air Operations Centers as a way to develop Air Force and joint networks and integrated capabilities, and moved to add more Air Force special operations capabilities to aid the other services.
Soon after 9/11, Roche was favorably inclined toward a plan suggested Sen. Ted Stevens (R-Alaska) to rapidly obtain additional aerial refueling capability by leasing such aircraft from Boeing, which had built the KC-135 and KC-10 tankers. The idea was that leasing the aircraft would allow them to be acquired through operations and maintenance accounts rather than through an outright acquisition program at a time when the Air Force was strapped for modernization dollars. It was also thought that a lease would bring the jets online faster than a straight buy. For his part, Stevens saw the idea as a way to help prop up Boeing and the U.S. airline industry, which had taken a body blow in canceled orders due to the terrorist attacks, which had caused a precipitous drop in air travel.
Roche favored quickly awarding a contract to Boeing both as a boost to the U.S. industrial base and because Boeing alone had a recent design for a boom-type refueling system. However, European airliner maker Airbus/EADS persuaded members of Congress that it could quickly certify its own boom and create a production line in the U.S. and should be allowed to compete for the work. Those members and others succeeded in getting the Air Force to agree to a “best value” competition, since EADS could not compete on unit price alone, given that its A330 aircraft was much larger than Boeing’s 767-based tanker.
In emails that came to light through subsequent investigations, it was clear that Roche favored a sole-source Boeing approach. He also had a personal animosity toward Ralph Crosby—a former Northrop rival—who was then head of EADS North America. Roche disparaged EADS’s offering of the Airbus A330 tanker as a mostly European product with only a “Made in America” sticker on it.
Roche also reportedly had an ongoing feud with Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) dating back to their Navy days, and McCain, a powerful voice on the Senate Armed Services Committee, made the tanker lease a personal crusade, publicly criticizing it as a “sweetheart deal” for Boeing that would cost the government far more than a straight purchase. He demanded numerous investigations of the plan.
Darleen Druyun, who had been the Air Force’s Principal Deputy Assistant Secretary for Acquisition and Management for 10 years, was zealous in promoting the Boeing lease. Several investigations determined that Druyun passed information to Boeing about EADS’ proposal and had demanded from Boeing an executive job for herself and jobs for other family members in exchange for giving Boeing favorable terms on the lease and overall favorable treatment on the competition. She also collaborated with Boeing to give the company favorable terms on launch vehicle contracts and steered the initial Small Diameter Bomb contract to the company. Druyun was arrested and eventually served nine months in prison, but it was determined Roche had not directed her to commit the contracting crimes and was unaware of her activities. One Boeing executive also went to jail and longtime Boeing CEO Phil Condit resigned. Boeing had to pay a $615 million fine. Druyun’s immediate boss, Marvin Sambur, resigned his post, but was not found to have participated in Druyun’s scheme.
McCain and other Senators held up promotions of several senior Air Force officers while demanding information and awaiting investigation results on the tanker lease, which the Air Force finally abandoned in fall 2004. Instead, it decided to buy 100 tankers, but that plan went through extensive modifications and reruns of a competition until Boeing was finally awarded a contract in 2011 for 179 KC-46 tankers.
Soon after the lease plan imploded, Bush nominated Roche to take on the post of Secretary of the Army, but he withdrew his name from nomination when it became clear his confirmation would be blocked indefinitely by tanker foes in Congress. He said it was unfair to make the senior officers awaiting promotion to wait while his issues were resolved. He announced his resignation from the Air Force in November 2004, and departed the job at the beginning of the second Bush term, in January 2005. Roche said he had always planned on serving only one term and allowed some overlap of his successor with the term of Gen. John Jumper.
Roche himself was found to have committed an ethics violation by sending an email recommending a person for a job with Northrop. While the recommendation itself wasn’t an ethical violation, Roche’s use of his official email, which bore his government title and potentially implied government endorsement, constituted the infraction. Defense Secretary Donald Rumsfeld considered the mistake inadvertent and did not pursue any sanctions.
In retirement, Roche served on the board of Orbital Sciences Corp./Orbital ATK until it became part of Northrop Grumman. He was also a member of the Council on Foreign Relations and the Washington Institute for Near East Policy.
Ret. Lt. Gen. David Deptula, head of AFA’s Mitchell Institute for Aerospace Studies, worked for Roche during the Air Force’s 2001 Quadrennial Defense Review.
“Secretary Roche’s impact on our national security cannot be overstated,” Deptula said. “Whether in uniform, in industry, or as Secretary of the Air Force, he was a most innovative, dedicated, and driven individual. He didn’t simply receive briefings—he understood the issues at a fundamental level, challenged assumptions, and pressed those of us on his staff to advance our thinking about air and space power. His command of strategy and policy, coupled with his deep interest in science and technology, was second to none. He made the Air Force and the nation stronger, and had a significant impact as a result.”
Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth S. Wilsbach wrote on social media that Roche “led our Department … through one of its most consequential moments following September 11th, cementing air and space power as the linchpin of the Joint Force.”
The current Secretary of the Air Force, Troy Meink, wrote that Roche’s “leadership and commitment helped strengthen the Joint Force, leaving a true impression on our nation.”

articles.title: Russia asked the UN for a treaty against ‘extremism,’ ‘subversion,’ and ‘discrediting the authorities.’ Instead, it got one that covers hacking and fraud.
articles.body:
Russia asked the UN for a treaty against ‘extremism,’ ‘subversion,’ and ‘discrediting the authorities.’ Instead, it got one that covers hacking and fraud.
Ratified with reservations?
By the end of 2026, a major new international treaty will be submitted to the State Duma for ratification: the United Nations Convention against Cybercrime. Russia does not agree with every provision in the document — even though Russia was the one that initiated it. So the convention will be ratified with reservations. How substantial those reservations will be, we don’t yet know.
What is this convention, anyway?
It creates a single framework for international cooperation against crime on the internet. The treaty gives investigators in one country a legal way to obtain help from their counterparts abroad with:
- “the freezing, seizure, confiscation, and return of proceeds” from a defined list of crimes
- “the collection, obtaining, preservation, and sharing of evidence in electronic form”
To make sure evidence can be collected and preserved, every state that ratifies the convention must develop the capacity to intercept internet traffic in real time itself and store it for at least 90 days. Or hand that job to someone else — internet service providers, for example.
This sounds like Russia’s “Yarovaya law.” Is the whole world about to adopt it?
It does sound a lot like it.
The “Yarovaya law,” passed in Russia 10 years ago, required telecom operators and ”organizers of information dissemination” to:
- Store all of their users’ text messages, voice data, images, sounds, video, and other communications for six months
- Store the accompanying metadata — that is, information about the receipt, transmission, delivery, and processing of messages — for three years
But the new convention does not oblige countries to intercept and store every citizen’s internet traffic. They only have to be able to help their foreign counterparts with individual requests — such as setting up surveillance of a particular user.
Weren’t law enforcement agencies in different countries already cooperating?
They were. Back in 2001, the Convention on Cybercrime — also known as the Council of Europe’s Budapest Convention — was adopted. Formally it’s a regional treaty, but 82 countries around the world have joined it. Besides European countries, they include the United States, Canada, Israel, Brazil, Nigeria, the Philippines, and many others.
How does cooperation under the Budapest Convention work?
The Budapest Convention also requires its parties to adopt “legislative and other measures” to intercept traffic (and the metadata on that traffic) in real time.
It, too, allows a country to refuse to hand over data on the grounds of political persecution. And it mentions the obligation to protect human rights and freedoms, with references to the corresponding European Convention and to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights adopted by the UN.
Russia took part in the preparation of the Budapest Convention but became the only Council of Europe member that never signed it. Alexander Seger, the former executive secretary of the Council of Europe’s committee on the Budapest Convention, has maintained that formally this happened because of a misreading of one of the treaty’s articles. Russia’s representatives concluded that it infringed on the country’s sovereignty.
In the end, Russia drew up a convention of its own to replace that one — and proposed it as the basis for a global UN convention.
And the new convention really was adopted at Russia’s initiative?
Yes. The document was first announced 10 years ago, in July 2016, at an international forum for the heads of security and intelligence agencies. It was held in St. Petersburg under the auspices of the FSB. Here is how the Russian security service described the event:
The key theme of the forum was the problem of the use of information and communications technologies (ICT) for terrorist purposes, since the internet and the media space are the principal instrument for spreading terrorist ideology. The Russian side presented a draft Convention on Combating Cybercrime for discussion.
Note the name of that draft. Russia itself would later object to exactly this wording.
- The first public draft text of the convention, presented by Russia’s permanent representative to the UN in October 2017, already had a different name: the “Draft Convention on Cooperation in Combating Information Crime.”
- And in December 2019, when the UN General Assembly passed a resolution on Russia’s initiative calling for a new convention to be drafted, the wording changed once more — to ”countering the use of ICT for criminal purposes.”
What’s the difference? What didn’t Russia like about the term “cybercrime”?
Cybercrime is a fairly narrow term, one that limits the document’s reach to going after hackers. Russia’s goal from the start was different: to cover as many crimes as possible that had any connection at all to the internet. The scope of the original 2017 draft, for instance, extended even to administrative offenses.
In the 2019 General Assembly vote, the countries that voted against the resolution were mainly Western ones — European Union member states, the United States, Canada, Britain, and Japan. Russia was backed by countries in Africa and Asia, among them Iran, China, North Korea, and Syria.
Human rights organizations came out sharply against the convention: Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International, Access Now, the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and others. Their experts warned explicitly of the risk that dissidents, journalists, and independent security researchers would be targeted. The organizations called for narrowing the convention’s scope and, conversely, expanding the human rights protections in it. Or, failing that, for rejecting the “Russian” document outright.
But did Russia get the version it wanted?
Not quite. Western countries joined the drafting process — and managed to shape the final text. The parties had to work out compromises on a number of points, including the title, which ended up in two parts and rather unwieldy:
United Nations Convention against Cybercrime; Strengthening International Cooperation for Combating Certain Crimes Committed by Means of Information and Communications Technology Systems and for the Sharing of Evidence in Electronic Form of Serious Crimes
Russia objected to the final title and said it would issue a separate statement to that effect when it ratifies the convention.
So which reading won out? The Russian one or the Western one?
Hard to say for certain.
On one hand, the exchange of digital evidence covers any “serious” crime — one that carries a maximum sentence of at least four years in prison. Which means that if both countries treat an act as a “serious” crime, an investigator can ask colleagues abroad to intercept a suspect’s traffic. You could call that a diplomatic win for Moscow.
On the other hand, the final list of “cybercrimes” shrank considerably. Compared with the Russian draft of 2021, the following were struck from the convention:
- inducement to suicide or driving a person to suicide;
- crimes involving drawing minors into unlawful acts that endanger their life and health;
- creating and using digital information to mislead users;
- incitement to subversive or armed activity;
- crimes related to terrorist activity;
- crimes related to extremist activity;
- crimes related to the distribution of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances;
- crimes related to illegal arms trafficking;
- the rehabilitation of Nazism or the justification of genocide or crimes against peace and humanity;
- the illegal distribution of counterfeit medicines and medical devices;
- the violation of copyright and related rights using ICT.
Under the final version of the document, countries will not be able to obtain the seizure or confiscation of proceeds from these acts. Given that Russia and some other countries often use accusations of “extremism,” “terrorism,” or “subversive activity” as a pretext for going after political opponents, they did not gain a new tool for pressuring “enemies of the regime.”
- Illegal access
- Illegal interception
- Interference with electronic data
- Interference with an information and communications technology system
- Misuse of devices
- ICT system-related forgery
- ICT system-related theft or fraud
- Offenses related to online child sexual abuse or child sexual exploitation material
- Solicitation or grooming for the purpose of committing a sexual offense against a child
- Non-consensual dissemination of intimate images
- Laundering of proceeds of crime
Is the shorter list of crimes the only thing Western countries managed to affect?
No. The final version of the text, for example, still mentions the protection of human rights. Iran, with support from Russia, Syria, and several other states, tried to scrub those mentions from two articles of the convention, but both times more than 100 countries voted against doing so.
Iran proposed deleting half of this article of the convention:
Article 6. Respect for human rights
2. Nothing in this Convention shall be interpreted as permitting suppression of human rights or fundamental freedoms, including the rights related to the freedoms of expression, conscience, opinion, religion or belief, peaceful assembly and association, in accordance and in a manner consistent with applicable international human rights law.
And another article in its entirety:
Article 24. Conditions and safeguards
1. Each State Party shall ensure that the establishment, implementation and application of the powers and procedures provided for in this chapter are subject to conditions and safeguards provided for under its domestic law, which shall provide for the protection of human rights, in accordance with its obligations under international human rights law, and which shall incorporate the principle of proportionality.
2. In accordance with and pursuant to the domestic law of each State Party, such conditions and safeguards shall, as appropriate in view of the nature of the procedure or power concerned, include, inter alia, judicial or other independent review, the right to an effective remedy, grounds justifying application, and limitation of the scope and the duration of such power or procedure.
3. To the extent that it is consistent with the public interest, in particular the sound administration of justice, each State Party shall consider the impact of the powers and procedures in this chapter upon the rights, responsibilities and legitimate interests of third parties.
4. The conditions and safeguards established pursuant to this article shall apply domestically to the powers and procedures provided for in this chapter, both for the purposes of domestic criminal investigations and proceedings and for the purposes of international cooperation by the requested State Party.
5. Judicial or other independent review referred to in paragraph 2 of this article means review at the domestic level.
The same countries — Iran, Russia, Syria, and a couple of dozen others — tried to strip out the mechanism that lets a state refuse to cooperate, if a request is being used for political persecution, for instance. That amendment failed as well, and an important provision survived in Article 40:
22. Nothing in this Convention shall be interpreted as imposing an obligation to afford mutual legal assistance if the requested State Party has substantial grounds for believing that the request has been made for the purpose of prosecuting or punishing a person on account of that person’s sex, race, language, religion, nationality, ethnic origin or political opinions, or that compliance with the request would cause prejudice to that person’s position for any one of these reasons.
Is Russia satisfied with the version that emerged?
No. Which is why it plans to attach reservations when it ratifies.
What’s more, Russia managed to secure a rather unusual decision. The UN General Assembly has already ordered preparatory work to begin on a draft protocol “supplementing the Convention and addressing, inter alia, additional criminal offenses, as appropriate.”
And countries will start discussing that protocol before the convention has even entered into force. The first of two 10-day sessions will be held in January 2027 in Vienna, the second in 2028 in New York.
Russia may try to use this gambit again to widen the list of criminalized acts to include any offense that can be committed with ICT. Justifying and promoting “terrorism” and “extremism” (backing the Anti-Corruption Foundation, say), public calls for sanctions [against Russia] or against particular officials, spreading “fakes,” and “discrediting” the army and the authorities, for example.
So when will the new convention take effect?
Three months after 40 states ratify the text.
For now, it’s hard to predict when that will happen. Nearly 10 months have gone by since the official ceremony in Hanoi that opened the convention for signature. In that time, the convention has drawn 81 signatures but only three instruments of ratification — from Azerbaijan, Vietnam, and Qatar.

articles.title: The Atlantic: Zelensky authorized a plan to swarm Moscow’s airports with 1,000 drones — after warning it could harm civilian aircraft and passengers. His office calls the account ‘total nonsense.’
articles.body:
The Atlantic: Zelensky authorized a plan to swarm Moscow’s airports with 1,000 drones — after warning it could harm civilian aircraft and passengers. His office calls the account ‘total nonsense.’
Ukraine’s military drew up plans to strike Moscow’s airports with a swarm of 1,000 small AI-guided drones, two sources told The Atlantic on condition of anonymity.
The swarm was meant to shut down the airports for an extended period, forcing the foreign airlines still flying to Moscow to suspend service. Members of the Russian elite, no longer able to travel abroad, would then put additional pressure on the administration of Russian President Vladimir Putin, forcing it to return to peace talks, The Atlantic said.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was briefed on the plan, worried that civilian aircraft, passengers, and airport staff could be harmed. He authorized preparations anyway, seeing the operation as another source of leverage over the Russian authorities, according to the magazine.
Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s defense minister at the time, was the driving force behind the preparations. He secured financing from Western allies to mass-produce the drones and helped assemble a team of Ukrainian programmers to build an AI targeting system.
The operation’s development, The Atlantic’s sources said, advanced far enough to earn a code name of its own, M&Ms — what The Atlantic described as “a reference to the many small, cheap, and nearly identical drones that the mission would require.”
Preparations were halted after Fedorov’s dismissal. One of the magazine’s sources said reviving the project with a new team would be “technically possible” but would take about three months.
Ukraine’s presidential office, however, denies preparing any drone-swarm attacks on Russian airports. “That’s total nonsense,” a representative said. The Ukrainian military’s only objective when it comes to civilian airports, the representative said, is to force Russia to keep declaring “Carpet,” the emergency protocol that clears the country’s airspace, thereby disrupting flight schedules.
The war in photos
Russian forces carried out a combined missile-and-drone strike on Kyiv overnight into August 20. Zelensky called it one of the most cynical, calculated, and large-scale attacks. The attack killed at least 15 people and damaged dozens of buildings, among them homes, a school, and a kindergarten. Russian forces struck Kyiv again with drones that evening. Many Kyiv residents take shelter in the metro during Russian attacks.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
If you find any errors in this translation, please contact us at [email protected].
To read Meduza’s exclusive content in English, please subscribe to our newsletter.

articles.title: Ukraine planned 1,000 AI-guided drones a night to shut Moscow airports, Atlantic reports
articles.body:
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy allowed preparations for an AI-guided drone campaign against Moscow-area airports, The Atlantic reported on 20 August, citing two anonymous sources with direct knowledge of the proposal.
The reported plan sought to keep civilian flights grounded long enough to pressure Russia’s elite. Had it proceeded, it would have moved Ukraine toward large-scale autonomous strikes, raising questions under the laws of war about attacks without human confirmation. The Atlantic's disclosure follows months of reported Ukrainian attacks that repeatedly forced Moscow-area airport closures and sent increasingly large drone swarms toward the capital.
How the drone operation would have worked
Code-named M&Ms, the operation called for as many as 1,000 drones to fly toward Moscow-area airports each night and overwhelm Russian air defenses, one source said.
Onboard cameras would compare live views with preloaded maps and target images. They would also allow the drones to strike without pilot confirmation and to navigate without a remote-control link that is vulnerable to Russian electronic jamming, the sources said.
One source said prolonged airport closures were intended to pressure Kremlin-linked elites and push Vladimir Putin toward negotiations.
The plan was presented to Zelenskyy during the winter of 2025–26, The Atlantic reported. Preparations stopped after Zelenskyy dismissed Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whom The Atlantic described as the operation’s mastermind, in July, both sources said. One source said another team could revive the project within about three months.
Both sources said Zelenskyy allowed preparations despite concerns that a drone could hit a civilian airliner. Planners proposed warning airlines, according to one source.
A Zelenskyy spokesperson declined to comment. Another unnamed presidential office official called the report “total nonsense,” saying Ukraine lacked long-range weapons reliable enough to strike the airports without posing undue risks to civilians.
Previous Ukrainian strikes on Moscow
The alleged M&Ms operation never launched, but other reported Ukrainian drone attacks repeatedly disrupted Moscow’s airports.
From 5 to 7 May 2026, restrictions imposed amid reported Ukrainian drone attacks delayed more than 450 flights at Moscow airports. Limits at Vnukovo remained in place for nearly 18 hours, EP reported, citing the independent Russian investigative outlet Agentstvo.
Earlier this week, Russian authorities claimed that 620 drones flew toward Moscow in one night, EP reported. The Atlantic placed Russia’s nationwide interception claim for that night at 791 drones. Ukraine’s military did not claim the attack.

articles.title: 160 grams, 118-km link, and jam-resistance by frequency-hopping: Ukraine’s answer to drone war’s connectivity problem
articles.body:
A Ukrainian company has built a drone link designed to keep working when the enemy tries to jam it. Ukraine's defense-tech firm Rise Technologies has developed the Nakande digital communication system, designed for rapid integration into small and large FPV drones, bombers, and fixed-wing platforms, commercial director Viktor Chuikovskyi says, Defender Media reports.
The system attacks the connectivity problem that jamming creates for Ukraine's drones. On a front saturated with electronic warfare, drones that lose their radio link become useless, and Nakande answers that by constantly hopping frequencies to find clear air.
How the frequency-hopping works
Nakande's defining feature is its ability to change frequency. It hops across a tuning range of up to 1,000 MHz, monitoring channels within that band, finding a freer stretch, and automatically switching to it, Chuikovskyi said, which lets operators keep their link to drones amid electronic warfare and a congested radio spectrum.
That is the core countermeasure to jamming. By moving to whatever frequency is clear rather than staying on one the enemy can block, the system stays connected where a fixed-frequency link would be jammed dead.
What the link carries
Nakande's airborne module weighs 160 grams, supports 2×Ethernet and MAVLink, and combines control, telemetry, and video in a single secure link, with a downlink up to 5.2 Mbit/s that the maker says delivers clean video and a compressed 4K stream, protected by AES-256 encryption.
It is built for fast, flexible setup. The ground station deploys in under five minutes. Its standard IP architecture allows the operator, antenna, and control point to be separated over Ethernet, fiber, or VPN, and a single ground station can connect 50 to 100 modules.
It held a link past 100 kilometers
Nakande has been tested in combat, the maker says. It passed bench, field, and combat checks, with a dedicated range class up to 60 kilometers for FPV drones, and in testing its maximum configuration, held a link at 118 kilometers, Chuikovskyi said.
The company did not disclose the module's price but said it is several times lower than foreign equivalents.

articles.title: Russian drone strike on Kryvyi Rih shopping center kills 15, injures 130. Second attack targeted rescue workers 30 minutes later
articles.body:
Editor's note: This is a developing story.
A Russian drone attack on a shopping center in Kryvyi Rih on 21 August killed at least 15 people and injured 130, including 23 children, local authorities said.
The attack struck the shopping mall during the day, setting shops inside the building on fire, regional military administration head Oleksandr Hanzha said.
The attack came in two waves, with the second strike hitting emergency responders about 30 minutes after the first strike caused the fire, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Twenty-nine people remain in serious condition, including five children, according to Head of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council Oleksandr Vilkul.
One of the victims died in hospital from severe injuries sustained in the attack, bringing the death toll to six, according to Hanzha.
Second strike hit emergency responders
The second wave came as emergency crews were responding to the fire caused by the first strike.
Zelenskyy called the attack “simply an act of terrorism” and said the international community should respond with real pressure on Russia.
“For peace to be possible, Russia needs to face real accountability,” Zelenskyy said.
Kryvyi Rih, in central-southern Ukraine, has faced frequent Russian missile and drone attacks throughout the full-scale war, with repeated strikes causing heavy civilian casualties.
Russian channels acknowledge strike on civilian target
Russian military Telegram channels described the shopping center as a target shortly after the attack, according to Kryvyi Rih Times.
One Russian channel claimed that a “Geran-4” jet-powered drone had been used to strike the shopping and entertainment complex and said the “target was hit” before noting that a fire had broken out inside the building.
The channel also published the precise coordinates of the shopping center.
The posts did not provide evidence that the shopping center was a legitimate military target.
Russian forces have repeatedly used drones and missiles to strike Ukrainian cities and civilian infrastructure throughout the full-scale invasion.
Russian attacks across Dnipropetrovsk Oblast
Russian forces attacked four districts of Dnipropetrovsk Oblast nearly 60 times on 21 August using drones, artillery, and an aerial bomb, Hanzha said.
In addition to the attack on Kryvyi Rih, Russian strikes hit communities in Nikopol, Synelnykove, and Kamianske districts, damaging apartment buildings, private homes, and cars.
Three people were injured in Nikopol district, while two others were injured in Synelnykove district. Several of the injured were hospitalized, Hanzha said.
The attacks also damaged private homes in Synelnykove district and caused a fire in the Krynychanska community of Kamianske district.
