articles.title: ‘I don’t think beyond tomorrow’: How people in occupied Crimea are surviving one of the hardest summers of the war
articles.body:
‘I don’t think beyond tomorrow’: How people in occupied Crimea are surviving one of the hardest summers of the war
This summer in occupied Crimea has been one of the hardest in decades: Crimean cities are regularly shelled by Ukraine, there are few tourists, prices are rising, and there are regular outages of electricity, water, and gasoline. The Bereg cooperative talked to Crimean residents living in different parts of the region, from Dzhankoi to Alupka, about how they’re surviving and why they don’t even consider leaving. Meduza is publishing this piece in full.
The names of the people in this story have been changed for their safety.
‘We live like this: we buy a piece of meat at the store, cook it right away, and eat it’
Iryna
Dzhankoi; about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I’m from the Kherson region, but I moved to Dzhankoi in 2023. I don’t have any relatives here. We [my husband and I and our two children] moved on our own. We live in a two-story house in Dzhankoi, and when there are strikes, we go down from the second floor and sit in the bathroom.
Strikes happen regularly here. Drones target electrical substations and are shot down right over residential neighborhoods. In May, one hit a house, killing five people, damaging nearby buildings, including stores, and blowing out windows and doors. Since then, drones have also struck the railway station and a substation. Coming from the Kherson region, though, I’ve long since gotten used to all this.
We had no power for two weeks starting July 6. Now it’s back for four hours a day, at just 95 volts — not enough to run a refrigerator or washing machine. The only thing we can manage is charging a phone. We live like this: we buy a piece of meat at the store and cook and eat it right away. It’s not like before, when the refrigerator was always full. And now we wash our clothes by hand.
Authorities promised a [one-time] payment of 15,000 rubles per person to anyone who went without power for more than 48 hours. I applied on July 12, and it’s still under review, even though I’ve seen reports that other people have already been paid.
My older child used to go to daycare, but it closed for two weeks of repairs at the start of summer. It was supposed to reopen on July 1 but never did — all the daycares are now closed because of the power situation. Only emergency programs remain open, for children whose parents work and have no one else to watch them.
We bought an inverter generator for 25,000 rubles, which we turn on in the evening so our son can watch cartoons for a couple of hours. Our daughter, who’s a year old, is afraid of the dark, so turn on a lamp for her before bed to help calm her fears.
Water runs from 6 p.m. to 10 a.m., but the pressure is too weak to wash properly. It’s only strong enough at 3 a.m., so that’s when you wash your hair.
Gas right now [August 10] costs 190 rubles for 95 octane and 150 rubles for 92 octane, though it’s also sold for as much as 300 rubles, with lines stretching for kilometers. My family doesn’t have a car, but I know the going rate because a friend of mine paid that price.
Every product is still available in stores, but prices have risen sharply for staples like bread, sunflower oil, and sugar. A kilogram [2.2 pounds] of sugar used to cost 70 rubles; now it’s 100. Supermarkets bought powerful generators so shoppers could still get butter, sausage, and cheese, and customers can charge phones and power banks inside — the same goes for the city administration building and the local history museum. Walk down the street now and you’ll hear an incredible noise from all the generators.
I’m on maternity leave, and my husband used to work as a freight forwarder, but the company shut down until September. People think everything will get better in the fall, but I wonder what exactly they expect to change come September. Nobody really knows.
In any case, my husband found another job and is now doing an internship. Work is hard to find right now — the Dzhankoi dairy plant and several other companies have closed — and some of our acquaintances are simply staying home.
We’re planning to stay in Dzhankoi — I don’t see the point in fleeing somewhere else, since even a place like Krasnodar gets hit too. What makes me angriest is that the [city] administration isn’t doing anything about the power, while in Krasnoperekopsk, Armiansk, and Krasnohvardiiske, everything has already been fixed and the power is back on. We’re told the electricians are working around the clock, but I don’t believe it. By now, with all the time that’s passed, they could have restored so much of the power supply that I honestly don’t know what to say.
‘Every day, the standard of living falls lower and lower’
Ihor
Sevastopol; about 220 kilometers (137 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I don’t have a car, so the fuel crisis hasn’t hit me the way it has drivers, but it’s still affected me, as supply issues have pushed up prices at supermarkets. At Yeda Voda, for example, shelves were half-empty in early August. There’s also a big problem with Ozon, which has stopped accepting orders from Crimea; [local media] report that its warehouses are overflowing and nothing is being delivered.
Power is cut every day, sometimes for up to eight hours. Usually there’s no electricity from 6 to 8 a.m., then it comes on for four hours before going off again for another four. I work from home, so all of this is genuinely disruptive, and I rely on mobile internet to get by. I haven’t bought a generator since it’s impractical in an apartment, and gas is expensive anyway.
I don’t go to the beach — that’s just how much of a typical local I am. But even on the street, I notice fewer people and cars than last year. Every day, the standard of living falls lower and lower.
Sometimes strikes happen almost every day; other times there’s a lull for about a month. A missile recently hit near my house at 5 a.m., and it was terrifying. At moments like that I hide in the bathroom, though if it hits the house directly, nothing will help, since we have gas. Just as you start getting used to it, another strike comes, and it’s frightening all over again.
I have plenty of reasons not to leave. Just when it seems like it’s time to pack up, something happens [in my personal life] that makes leaving impossible. Plus, I don’t know where I’d go — so for now, I’m staying put.
I just wish Ukraine would come back and life could return to normal. Of course, it will never truly be like before, but at least this whole situation would somehow be resolved.
‘My husband’s workweek was cut from five days to three’
Inga
Ukromnoye, Simferopol district; about 130 kilometers (81 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I live with my husband and our three children. Overall, the power situation is manageable, but on days when it’s out for 5–6 hours, food in the freezer thaws and spoils. Our water comes from a well, so when the power goes, so does the water — we stock up whenever it’s running. We bought a 75,000-ruble generator for the house, essentially a battery that charges up and then supplies electricity.
My husband works in a neighboring village, where the power is often out for entire days, coming and going unpredictably. His company installed a generator too. His workweek was cut from five days to three, and we lost a third of our income. He’s currently our family’s only breadwinner, and I’m afraid he could be out of work entirely by winter if things keep going this way.
Supermarket prices have gone up by 30%. Cheaper chains like “Ambar” have half-empty shelves, though other stores still have a decent selection.
We’ve driven to the mainland three times for gas, buying 200 liters (53 gallons) each trip — it’s cheaper, and the fuel quality is better there.
During shelling we hide with the kids in the bathroom, though it’s been quiet lately. Our oldest, 17, understands everything and is scared just like we are. The middle child, 7, mostly sleeps through it, and so does the youngest, who’s a year old.
We thought about leaving at one point, but for now we’ve decided to stay. With three kids it’s complicated — our oldest is entering his final year of school, and the middle child is just starting. We’ve decided to get through the winter here and see what comes after that.
‘How my animals and I will stay warm this winter is a mystery’
Anna
A village in northwestern Crimea
The district where I was born and still live borders Ukraine by sea. I moved to the district center when I was young, then came back in 2014.
My return coincided with the neighboring state [how Anna refers to Ukraine] declaring a blockade of the peninsula. Many vacation resorts around the village closed as a result, since visitors stopped coming, and the dogs that had guarded those resorts were abandoned. They ran into the village looking for food among the people there.
I felt sorry for them, so I started feeding some and tried to find homes for others through social media, but I wasn’t able to place a single one.
It had the opposite effect: once people saw my posts, they started bringing animals to me from all over the district. Someone once just walked up and tied an adult dog to my fence. Others brought me animals found on the road with broken legs, or rescued from conflict zones. Several small puppies were pulled out literally from under a lawnmower.
In total, I now have 90 cats and 30 dogs. My property has no kennels or other special facilities — they all live with me at home, with some staying with relatives and others at abandoned vacation resorts. I’m a pensioner, and almost nobody helps me. It’s impossible to support that many animals on a single welfare payment, so I rely on people who care to pitch in.
The power problems started sometime in July, though I don’t remember exactly when, since I spend all my time busy with the animals. At first there was no electricity for two days, then it came back briefly before going out again for another two days. Then something serious happened, and we went five days without electricity, water, or gas.
Since I usually feed the animals porridge instead of store-bought pet food, I had to cook for myself and for them over an open fire. Fortunately, the administration brought me and other village residents a free gas canister in early August, but I’m almost afraid to even look at it or breathe on it — I’m trying to conserve it.
We recently bought an electric hot plate and cook on it whenever there’s power. Today [August 10] there was no power at all, so I had to give the animals dry food. The electricity now gets turned on and off at random, with no schedule at all, but we’ve adapted.
I used to buy pet food from Wildberries and Ozon, but now they refuse to deliver here. It’s more expensive at the store, and the nearest one is 25 kilometers (16 miles) away — I don’t have a car, but people help out.
When there are strikes, the animals get anxious. The dogs often start barking even before a drone alert comes in. I head for the bathroom, and the dogs and cats scatter to their hiding spots.
I’ve never even considered leaving the village. My relatives once told me, “If there’s an evacuation, leave them all behind. Health comes first.” But where would I abandon them all? Are they supposed to just die here alone? I’m not going anywhere.
I don’t make big plans — I don’t think beyond tomorrow, and I just deal with things as they come. Winter worries me because we rely on electric heaters. In past winters, only the cats had heating, since they live with me indoors, but heating with convection heaters is expensive, so we saved however we could. Of the eight heaters we needed, only three worked, and five were broken. Building warm enclosures for all the animals is my biggest dream.
How my animals and I will stay warm this winter is a mystery. The other villagers have stoves they can heat with coal and firewood, but no one can imagine how much that will cost.
I try to distance myself from the situation we’re in. I do my own thing, and I’m grateful to the animals for keeping me distracted.
More than anything, I want peace.
‘If the accumulated problems aren’t solved urgently, there will be a revolt’
Oleh
Dzhankoi; about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from mainland Ukraine
I live in Dzhankoi. We had no electricity at all from July 5 to 16. Starting July 17, power was supplied irregularly for 2–4 hours a day, at a catastrophically low voltage of 120–140 volts, or 150 if we were lucky. In some villages, it doesn’t even reach 100 volts.
At that voltage, basic appliances like refrigerators and washing machines would either fail to turn on at all, in the best case, or literally burn out in the worst. I was careful with mine — or maybe just lucky — and nothing burned out. To avoid the risk, I bought a voltage stabilizer, but it doesn’t help much, since most models don’t work at input voltages below 150 volts.
In August, daytime temperatures in Crimea reach nearly 40 degrees Celsius (104 degrees Fahrenheit), so without a refrigerator, food spoils within hours, and I had to forget about air conditioning entirely. A neighbor with a generator saved me by running power to my refrigerator for four hours a day. Stable power was restored in Dzhankoi on August 12, though in the surrounding villages, the situation still leaves much to be desired.
I live on the first floor and have been lucky with water — it’s almost always available. It’s much harder for village residents and for Dzhankoi residents on higher floors, since the water supply depends on electricity. For them it often comes out as a thin trickle for 2–3 hours, and sometimes there’s no water at all for a whole day.
Food prices have risen noticeably. Perishable goods like vegetables, fruit, and sausages have disappeared from stores, though everything else is still available.
Overall, people are desperate — they’ve been pushed to the limit. If the accumulated problems aren’t solved urgently, there will be a revolt.
I’ve thought about moving, but for now, that’s all it is — a thought.
‘I’m getting by however I can, and I’m not planning to leave’
Anton
Alupka; about 980 kilometers (609 miles) from mainland Ukraine
Starting around July 21, the city went four days straight without power. Now it’s supplied from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. Conditions are worse in other cities, but we may get more [electricity] because we have no gas.
I recently passed through Yalta and saw people crowding outside supermarkets to charge their phones, since the stores had put out extension cords. We’ve had something similar here too, but only during total power outages.
I have a car and a scooter, but I haven’t been to a gas station in a while. I only heard that [Kremlin-appointed Crimea head Sergey] Aksyonov [as of August 4] set the price of 92-octane gasoline at 100 rubles. In early July, I drove to the mainland and brought back 100 liters (26 gallons) of gasoline, waiting in line eight times at four different stations over the course of a day. People around me were tense and angry.
The last time I filled up was in early August, at 190 rubles, with no lines at all. I just drove up and that was it. The most I’ve ever paid was 275 rubles, and resellers have charged as much as 350, even 500 rubles. But what choice do you have?
I ride a motorcycle to work now to save fuel. Since the start of August, I’ve been working as an assistant at a private villa. Before that I worked at a factory, but construction was frozen due to logistics problems along the “Novorossiya” highway.
I used to give tours for tourists every summer, and my pay depended on how much work I did. This year there are no tourists at all, so I didn’t even bother trying.
These days I hardly go anywhere except work — only on weekends do I treat myself to the beach. Everyone there is local; I can tell from the license plates.
In Crimea they banned riding motorcycles from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m., saying they sound like drones — they can tow your scooter to an impound lot and fine you 30,000 rubles. I once got lost near Sudak and had to sleep on a mountain pass; luckily, I had a sleeping bag and a hammock with me, and something was being bombed in the distance all night. Now I always race home by 9:30 to make it in time.
Drones almost never fly over Alupka. There was only one time, [July 22], when I heard explosions at night, after which the power went out. But near Sevastopol, where I vacationed last year, there was constant cannon fire. It was scary.
Because of the power outages, various products disappeared from supermarkets for a while — dairy, for example — but now there are almost no empty shelves anywhere. The one thing I’ve noticed missing is cigarettes. At Yeda Voda, 70% of the products are gone. Only vodka is left. Other stores bought generators and reorganized how they operate.
At the store near my house, while there was no power, employees would unscrew the cap off a bottle of water I wanted to buy, keep it, and screw on a different one. That way, once the power came back, they could scan the item into the Chestny Znak system. Sellers also copied barcodes into a notebook by hand.
Prices have gone up by about 30%. I used to buy the “Adrenaline” energy drink for 110 rubles; now it costs 160. Camping gas canisters have gotten a lot more expensive too — they used to cost 100 rubles, peaked at 250, and now sell for 170. These canisters are the main lifesaver for people when the power goes out.
I’m getting by however I can, and I’m not planning to leave. My mother is here, and I don’t want to abandon her. The mood, of course, isn’t great, but we’re living one day at a time. Back in late May there was still confidence that the tourist season would take off and we’d be able to earn good money. This summer, there’s no hope of that.
Winter is coming soon, and I hope I’ll be able to earn at least a little money to buy alternative energy sources — a big gas canister, say — so I’ll have something to cook and heat the apartment with.
I really want all of this to end.

articles.title: Russia’s missile tests around disputed islands anger Japan
articles.body:
Japan has criticised missile tests carried out by Russia’s navy around the disputed islands visited by Vladimir Putin last week amid continuing tensions between the two countries.
Russia’s Pacific fleet said on Thursday that it had fired Bastion surface-to-ship missiles from Etorofu, the largest island in the disputed archipelago, simulating an attack on enemy vessels, hitting all of its targets approximately 300km away.
Officials said the drills included a nuclear-powered submarine and a guided-missile cruiser, according to reports.
Putin sparked a tit-for-tat summoning of ambassadors in Tokyo and Moscow with his first visit last week to Etorofu, the largest of the group of four islands. They are referred to as the Northern Territories or Four Northern Islands in Japan, and as part of the Kuril Islands in Russia.
Toshimitsu Motegi, Japan’s foreign minister, said on Thursday during a trip to Oman: “We cannot tolerate moves to strengthen military power on the Four Northern Islands because they go against our country’s stance [on the territories].”
Territorial rows over the islands go back to the 19th century. The Soviet Union seized them from Japan at the end of the second world war.
Exercises by the Russian fleet began on 4 August and Japan was informed in advance that they would include live-fire drills. Japan lodged a protest against the large-scale manoeuvres on 5 August.
According to the Russian news agency Tass, the drills involved “approximately 60 surface ships, submarines, and support vessels, about 30 aircraft, helicopters, and unmanned aerial systems of the Pacific fleet’s naval aviation, as well as over 13,000 service members”.
Putin observed some of the exercises from the Varyag on 12 August as part of his trip to the disputed islands and to Sakhalin, the large undisputedly Russian island north of Hokkaido.
“The region is unfortunately becoming increasingly prone to conflict, with Nato seeking to gain a foothold here and the emergence of new military and political blocs,” said Putin, speaking aboard the flagship. “There are efforts and plans to deploy new weapons systems here, which creates threats for our country.”
The Russian drills are scheduled to continue through 29 August.

articles.title: The Atlantic: Zelenskyy was reportedly offered plan to strike Moscow airports with drones
articles.body:
The Atlantic: Zelenskyy was reportedly offered plan to strike Moscow airports with drones
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was reportedly offered a plan in early 2026 to launch large-scale drone strikes against airports in Moscow and Moscow Oblast.
Source: The Atlantic, citing two people familiar with the situation
Quote: "Early this year, Ukrainian officials came to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy with a risky new plan to end the war with Russia. It would require expanding their bombing campaign to include a set of targets and a class of weapons they had long avoided."
Details: According to two sources cited by The Atlantic, officials proposed expanding Ukrainian strikes to Moscow's airports using drones equipped with artificial intelligence. The aim would have been to disrupt the operations of international airlines flying to and from the Russian capital.
If conducted, the plan would have been unprecedented in the history of warfare. It envisaged swarms of autonomous drones equipped with AI-based navigation systems independently locating and striking targets without being controlled by an operator.
According to the journalists, similar systems have been tested by various countries, including the US, in recent years. Meanwhile, the legality of their use is the subject of an ongoing debate because of the potential for violations of international humanitarian law. No country has yet used such systems in combat.
The Atlantic reported that the plan was presented to Zelenskyy in the winter. The Ukrainian president expressed serious concern about the potential threat to civilian aviation, including the risk of accidentally striking a passenger aircraft or killing civilians near the airports.
Despite these concerns, Zelenskyy, seeking a way to put pressure on Russia and revive the peace process, allowed preparations for such strikes to continue for some time, The Atlantic said.
The Atlantic reported that by mid-spring, preparations had progressed sufficiently far and the project had been given the name M&M's.
The Atlantic said former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov played a key role in the project. According to the sources, he was involved in assembling a team of developers, developing AI-based guidance systems and seeking funding to produce large numbers of autonomous UAVs.
However, preparations for the operation were subsequently halted.
A representative from the Office of the President of Ukraine denied the information in comments to The Atlantic, calling the claims false.
There is currently no official confirmation that such a plan was developed or existed.
Background:
- Moscow and Moscow Oblast have come under repeated drone attacks in recent months. For example, on the night of 18-19 August, Russian authorities again reported a drone attack on Moscow.
- On the night of 17-18 August, the Russian authorities reported that more than 600 drones were heading towards Moscow.
- On the afternoon of 18 August, Russia's Defence Ministry claimed that more than 1,600 drones had been shot down over a 24-hour period, along with 10 guided aerial bombs and two HIMARS rockets.

articles.title: Days After Putin’s First Visit, Russia Fires Missiles Near Islands Claimed by Japan
articles.body:
- Category
- World
Days After Putin’s First Visit, Russia Fires Missiles Near Islands Claimed by Japan
Days after Putin’s first-ever visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, Russia staged rare missile drills nearby—using a nuclear submarine, a missile cruiser, and a Bastion coastal system in a fresh show of force toward Japan.
Russia has carried out rare missile drills involving naval vessels and a ground-based launcher near the disputed southern Kuril Islands, adding to already heightened tensions with Japan, Bloomberg reported on August 21.
Russia’s Pacific Fleet said missiles were launched from a nuclear-powered submarine, a missile cruiser, and a Bastion coastal defense system operating in the area of the southern Kurils. The fleet did not specify when the exercises took place.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Russian military, the missiles were fired at targets located more than 300 kilometers, or about 186 miles, away and successfully struck them.
The Pacific Fleet did not disclose the exact location of the drills. Russia has, however, deployed Bastion coastal defense batteries on Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu, since 2016.
The exercises drew a sharp reaction from Tokyo.
“Russia’s military buildup on the four Northern Islands runs counter to Japan’s position and is unacceptable,” Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi told reporters.
The southern Kuril Islands have remained under Russian control since Soviet forces seized them from Japan in the final days of World War II. Tokyo continues to claim Iturup, Kunashir, Shikotan, and the Habomai islets, collectively referring to them as the Northern Territories.
The missile drills came only days after Russian leader Vladimir Putin made his first visit to the disputed territory, traveling to Iturup last week. Japan formally protested that visit as well.
The long-running territorial dispute has prevented Russia and Japan from signing a formal peace treaty since World War II.
The latest military activity also comes as Japan continues to support Ukraine against Russia’s war of aggression, including through sanctions on Moscow.
Tokyo has also provided Ukraine with non-lethal military assistance, including body armor and vehicles.
During his recent visit to Russia’s Far East, Putin accused Japan of changing its approach toward Moscow without provocation. He criticized Japanese sanctions and pointed to defense documents in which Tokyo identifies Russia as a serious security threat.
The combination of Putin’s first visit to Iturup and the missile drills has added fresh pressure to one of the longest-running territorial disputes in East Asia, with Moscow now visibly demonstrating strike capabilities near islands Japan still considers its own.
Previously, Russia sent four missile-armed warships near Japan, with the vessels passing about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from Hokkaido a day after Putin visited Iturup, one of the disputed Kuril Islands claimed by Japan.

articles.title: Russia’s Shopping Mall Strike on Zelensky’s Hometown Kills 15, Injures 130 as Rescue Continues
articles.body:
Russia struck the largest shopping mall in central Ukraine’s Kryvyi Rih with multiple drones on Friday afternoon, killing at least 15 and injuring at least 130, including 23 children.
Local media channels shared photos and footage of the attack, suggesting the Solnechnaya Galereya mall in the city was struck by multiple drones.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Videos circulating online show bloodied civilians being carried off from the scene of the attack.
Medics were seen attending to those injured by the attack.
Oleksandr Vikul, the head of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, confirmed the attack at 4:39 p.m. and said “many people are visually injured.”
Vikul later said the mall was repeatedly attacked by jet-powered Shahed drones “flying at extremely low altitudes” and cautioned about potential follow-up strikes.
Oleksandr Hanzha, the head of the region’s military administration, said at 5:11 p.m. that two were confirmed dead while 15 were confirmed injured before adding that casualty numbers are likely to increase.
Hanzha later said at 5:40 p.m. that 50 have been confirmed injured, while an update by the Prosecutor General’s Office said that number had risen to 52, including six children.
According to Hanzha at 6:18 p.m. the number of injured rose to 91, with 21 people seriously injured. The death toll rose to 6.
The latest update at 6:40 p.m. reported 96 people injured, including children, as Russian forces attacked four districts nearly 60 times using drones, artillery and an aerial bomb.
Zelensky Informs UN Secretary-General Guterres About Russian Strikes
The Zelenodolsk and Hrushivka communities in the Kryvyi Rih district also came under attack. In Nikopol district, three people were injured. A 56-year-old woman was hospitalized in moderate condition, while men aged 32 and 52 will receive outpatient treatment.
In the Synelnykove district, a 48-year-old man was taken to hospital in moderate condition. A 51-year-old woman received outpatient treatment.
As of 7:55 p.m. Hanzha reported that the attack had killed at least 14 people and injured 121, including 22 children. Twenty-nine victims, including five children, are in serious condition.
The death toll rose to 15, while the number of injured increased to 130, including 23 children. “The number of casualties continues to rise,” Hanzha said in his report at 9:38 p.m. local time.
Zelensky condemns the strike, calls it terrorism
Kryvyi Rih is the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelensky, which has been one of the many cities targeted by Russian strikes during Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zelensky condemned the strike in his Telegram statement.
“The Russians carried out an utterly cynical and vile strike on an ordinary shopping center,” Zelensky said, adding that “such strikes are acts of terrorism,” and calling for partners to respond accordingly – “with real pressure on the aggressor.”
At 8:40 p.m. local time, Zelensky issued a second statement, confirming that authorities are still establishing whereabouts about people who may have been inside the shopping center when the attack happened.
“An absolute Russian atrocity” he said. “They’re just monsters. We will definitely respond.”
Separately, Zelensky spoke by with UN Secretary-General António Guterres about Russia’s continued attacks, civilian casualties and broader threats to global food security.
On Aug. 16, a Russian attack on ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine’s largest foreign-invested steelmaker, killed two workers and forced a partial shutdown of production.
One of the deadliest strikes on the city took place in April 2025, when a children’s playground was hit, killing at least 18 and injuring over two dozens.

articles.title: Settlers kill a Palestinian teen in a West Bank clash, and other Middle East developments
articles.body:
Settlers kill a Palestinian teen in a West Bank clash, and other Middle East developments
A Palestinian teenager was killed by Israeli settlers Friday after a rock-throwing incident in the occupied West Bank.
Also, Turkey announced it is asking for an international warrant for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for his role in stopping several boats trying to break a naval blockade of Gaza in May, and an Israeli human rights watchdog is warning that settler violence has expanded from rural to urban areas in the West Bank.
Here’s a look at the latest developments in the Iran war and the wider Middle East on Friday. Full coverage can be found here.
Palestinian teen killed by Israeli settlers after rock-throwing incident
A 17-year-old Palestinian was killed and another man wounded by Israeli settler gunfire after rocks were thrown Friday in Sa’ir, north of Hebron in the occupied West Bank, the Palestinian Health Ministry said.
The ministry identified the teenager as Karim Sanad Raja Shalaldeh. The teenager’s father told The Associated Press at the hospital that Israeli settlers had killed his son.
The Israeli military said soldiers were dispatched to Sa’ir after Palestinians threw rocks at Israeli civilians who were in the area without prior authorization. Some Israelis were injured and a security official opened fire.
Separately, the Palestinian General Authority for Civil Affairs informed the Health Ministry that 58-year-old Fathi Khazem was fatally shot by Israeli forces early Friday in Jenin.
An Israeli army official speaking on condition of anonymity in line with military rules said Khazem attempted to stab an Israeli soldier during an overnight operation. No Israeli soldiers were injured.
The Israeli official said Khazem was the father of Raed Khazem, who shot and killed three people in Tel Aviv in April 2022.
Violence has escalated in the West Bank where at least 87 Palestinians have been killed in almost 1,500 attacks by Israeli settlers and soldiers this year, according to Palestinian officials. Three Israelis have been killed by Palestinians in 2026.
— By Koral Saeed in Herzliya, Israel.
Turkey seeks international warrant for Netanyahu over May blockade
Turkey is seeking an international warrant for Netanyahu’s arrest over Israel’s interception of an international flotilla that attempted to break a naval blockade of Gaza.
The Interpol red notice sought against Netanyahu and one other Israeli national was tied to an Istanbul court case trying 35 defendants in absentia for alleged “genocide,” other crimes against humanity, torture, unlawful detention and hijacking, Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said in a statement posted on X.
The charges stem from the Israeli navy’s interception in May of several vessels in international waters off Cyprus days after the flotilla departed from the Turkish port of Marmaris. Some detained activists reported mistreatment.
Turkey is among the most vocal critics of Israel’s government.
Netanyahu responded on social media, calling Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan an antisemitic dictator who has “massacred Kurds, harbors Hamas terrorists, occupies half of Cyprus, and jails record numbers of journalists and politicians who oppose him.”
“Erdogan’s pathetic attempt to intimidate the leaders and soldiers of Israel, the only true democracy in the Middle East, will go nowhere,” Netanyahu said Friday.
Rights group says Israeli settler violence heads to established Palestinian cities
An Israeli group that collects information about potential human rights violations against Palestinians says reported incidents of Israeli settler violence have moved from the rural West Bank toward larger, more populated Palestinian cities and towns.
The establishment of new settlements and outposts throughout the West Bank has emboldened extremist settlers, who are now encroaching on larger communities that previously were far from the front lines of settler violence, Yesh Din said in its report released Friday titled “The Next Frontier.”
The uptick in violence corresponds with the Israeli government’s approval of new settlements and the expansion of outposts that it doesn’t authorize but often leaves in place, according to the report.
“As outposts advance deeper into Palestinian territory, violence, harassment and terror follow,” Yesh Din wrote.
Some 3 million Palestinians live under Israeli military rule in the West Bank alongside roughly 560,000 Israeli settlers.
Economic woes return to Lebanon
Lebanon’s economy is projected to contract 6.4% this year because the latest Israel-Hezbollah war reversed the economic recovery of the previous year, the World Bank said Friday.
The destruction from the war that started in March and related sharp drop in tourism reversed a 4.2% growth seen in 2025 in Lebanon’s economy, the organization said.
The World Bank also predicts a sharp increase in inflation driven by supply disruptions, higher shipping costs, and rising oil prices, which will further reduce purchasing power.
Lebanon’s economy has been in crisis since a 2019 banking collapse.
11 countries call Israeli airstrikes in Syria an extreme escalation
The foreign ministers of 11 countries are calling Israel’s airstrikes on a Syrian air base an extreme escalation.
The ministers of Turkey, Algeria, Indonesia, Jordan, Lebanon, Malaysia, Mauritania, Pakistan, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, Somalia and the Palestinian territories warned that attacks on Syria undermine its reconstruction efforts as well as its attempts to restore security, according to a joint statement released by the Turkish Foreign Ministry.
The Israeli strikes hit the Abu Duhur base early Tuesday, causing damage but no casualties. Netanyahu’s office said Israel targeted the base because Syria was about to breach an agreed “status quo in security matters” by allowing Turkish troops to deploy there.

articles.title: 107 out of 135 Russian drones neutralized over Ukraine
articles.body:
107 out of 135 Russian drones neutralized over Ukraine
Kyiv • UNN
On the night of August 21, Russia launched 135 drones at Ukraine. Air defense destroyed or suppressed 107 of them; 27 strikes were recorded at 16 locations.
Russia launched 135 drones at Ukraine overnight, of which 107 were shot down or suppressed, the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force said on Friday, UNN reports.
Details
According to the Ukrainian Armed Forces Air Force, during the night of August 21 (from 18:00 on August 20), the enemy attacked with 135 Shahed-type attack UAVs (including jet-powered ones), Gerbera drones, and Parody-type decoy drones from the following directions: Kursk, Millerovo, Oryol, Primorsko-Akhtarsk – Russia, Donetsk – temporarily occupied territory, the temporarily occupied territory of the Autonomous Republic of Crimea.
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile forces, electronic warfare and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of Ukraine’s Defense Forces.
According to preliminary data, as of 08:00, air defense forces had shot down/suppressed 107 enemy Shahed-type UAVs, Gerbera drones, and drones of other types in the north, south, and east of the country. Hits by 27 attack UAVs at 16 locations were recorded, as well as the fall of downed drones (debris) at 3
The attack is ongoing; several enemy UAVs are in the airspace.

articles.title: US op to smuggle Gulf oil unlikely to alleviate underlying risks
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
US operation to smuggle oil from Gulf unlikely to alleviate ‘underlying risks’, analysts say
Despite reports that the United States is attempting to move oil out of the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz in an effort to circumvent restrictions imposed during the US-Israel war with Iran, analysts have told The New Arab that any such operation is unlikely to reduce the fundamental risks facing energy shipments from the region.
Washington has reportedly been conducting a secret operation for several weeks to move up to 10 million barrels of oil per day, roughly half of pre-war export levels, out of the Gulf, according to an Axios report published on Wednesday.
Citing two US officials, the report said that between 15 and 20 tankers a day had been transiting to and from the strait through a southern channel along Oman’s coast.
However, Neil Quilliam, an associate fellow with Chatham House’s Middle East and North Africa Programme specialising in energy policy and geopolitics, said the reported operation was not a sustainable solution to the disruption in the Gulf.
"The operation itself does not surprise me, but I see it as a short-term workaround that allows Trump to claim greater control over the Strait," Quilliam told The New Arab. "The underlying risk has not changed."
He said the operation "was not sustainable and already comes with significant risk", pointing to a June incident in which a US Apache helicopter was reportedly downed by an Iranian drone while supporting earlier efforts to move oil through the Gulf.
The episode triggered a fresh round of clashes between US and Iranian forces, reflecting a pattern of recurrent escalation since the Memorandum of Understanding that ended the full-scale war in June.
"While Iran’s surveillance and coastal monitoring capabilities have been degraded by US military action, it retains the ability to launch drones and other strikes against vessels, which we have seen in recent weeks," Quilliam said.
Without US facilitation, support vessels and broader logistical backing, commercial operators would be unlikely to undertake such transits independently, Quilliam added.
"As a result, this remains a costly and high-risk enterprise that is likely to become a prime target for Iran," he said.
Difficult to verify
The report, which also said the US operation was being coordinated with Gulf states, is difficult to independently verify, according to the analysts who spoke to The New Arab.
Hamish Kinnear, principal Middle East and North Africa analyst at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, said verification was complicated by tankers switching off their transponders while moving through the strait.
"There is a delay to the satellite imagery and ship chartering data that can be used to reconcile reported volumes against actual volumes," Kinnear told The New Arab.
Quilliam similarly said the lack of vessel-tracking data made firm assessments of the scale of the operation difficult.
"Given that many of the tankers traverse the straits with their transponders off, it is very difficult to provide accurate figures for the numbers of vessels, and therefore the volumes of crude, that have exited this way," he said.
Pressure on prices
The Strait of Hormuz, through which around one-fifth of global oil consumption normally passes, has been a central point of contention in negotiations between Washington and Tehran. The near-total disruption to shipping has pushed global oil prices sharply higher, from around $60 per barrel before the war to a peak of roughly $118.
Although prices have since fluctuated, a barrel of oil was trading at around $93 on Friday, placing renewed pressure on the Trump administration, which has repeatedly pledged to bring down costs for US consumers.
Kinnear said market pricing suggested traders had already accounted for at least some successful "dark" transits through the waterway.
"For now, the industry consensus is the oil price, which is creeping up despite these new claims," he said. "The fact that benchmark prices are still below USD100 per barrel in part reflects the baked-in price impact of successful dark transits."
If US claims that traffic through the strait has increased prove accurate, Kinnear said this could strengthen Washington’s hand in negotiations with Tehran.
"That doesn’t necessarily make a deal more likely, as Tehran may seek to escalate in other ways to re-establish its negotiating position — by once again targeting energy infrastructure in the Persian Gulf, for example," he added.
Quilliam said the operation should not be viewed solely as an attempt by Washington to influence oil prices. Gulf governments also had a clear interest in maintaining exports through the strait, he said.
"The US has always had an interest in ensuring oil prices sit within a reasonable range, and the price at the pump is, of course, a critical concern domestically, given the upcoming midterm elections," Quilliam said.
"However, an operation like this would obviously be coordinated with Gulf allies, who have their own important reasons to want oil to continue moving out of the strait. So, I would not characterise this as a US attempt to manipulate the market, but rather a response to pressure on oil prices, the result of which benefits both Trump domestically and Gulf allies’ budgets."

articles.title: Russia Launches Multiple Ballistic Missiles at Kyiv, Explosions Heard Across Capital
articles.body:
Explosions were heard across Kyiv late Friday, Aug. 21, as Russia launched several ballistic missiles toward the Ukrainian capital, according to Ukraine’s Air Force.
The Air Force first warned of a ballistic missile threat from the northeast shortly before 10 p.m. local time. Minutes later, it reported a missile moving through the Chernihiv region and then heading toward Kyiv.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Several ballistic missiles toward Kyiv!” the Air Force reported at 9:59 p.m., followed a minute later by another warning of additional ballistic missiles targeting the capital.
Kyiv Post journalist reported that explosions were heard in Kyiv during the air raid alert.
The threat was not limited to ballistic missiles. Shortly afterward, the Air Force reported Russian Banderol loitering munitions moving toward Brovary and Kyiv.
There were no immediate official reports of casualties or damage from the latest attack.
The strike comes just days before Ukraine marks its 35th Independence Day on Monday, Aug. 24.
Earlier Friday, Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) urged people to remain particularly vigilant in the run-up to and during Independence Day, warning of possible Russian provocations and terrorist attacks.
The latest ballistic attack also comes a day after one of the deadliest Russian assaults on the capital this year. According to Ukrainian authorities, 16 people were killed and 42 injured in Kyiv during the Aug. 20 attack, which struck residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure.

articles.title: Yemeni drones strike Aramco oil facilities, Najran airport
articles.body:
Yemeni drones strike Aramco oil facilities, Najran airport
TEHRAN — Yemeni Armed Forces launched back-to-back drone strikes on August 20, targeting a sensitive military installation at Najran Airport and a major Aramco oil facility in southern Saudi Arabia.
Armed Forces spokesman Brigadier General Yahya Saree said both operations achieved their objectives, framing the action as a direct response to persistent Saudi drone incursions over Saada province.
A naval blockade on Saudi shipping
The Najran strikes mark the latest enforcement move under a strategic doctrine outlined by Saree on August 19.
Sanaa has established three non-negotiable equations to counter foreign aggression: imposing an equal maritime siege, striking enemy troop concentrations anywhere they assemble, and actively defending Yemeni sovereignty against airspace breaches.
The naval campaign has already crippled Saudi maritime logistics. Between July 20 and August 19, Yemeni naval forces targeted eight Saudi oil tankers across the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the Arabian Sea.
Another 48 Saudi oil vessels were intercepted and turned back, including 34 in the Arabian Sea and Indian Ocean.
This aggressive enforcement has halted nearly 85 percent of the kingdom’s oil exports passing through the Bab al-Mandab Strait toward Asian markets.
To reduce exposure, commercial vessels now regularly broadcast “non-Saudi cargo” flags, while international insurance companies require complete data on cargo origin and crew nationalities before granting clearance.
Illustrating the dominance and the ultimatum
On the battlefield, Yemeni units continue to inflict heavy losses on Saudi-backed mercenary units.
A 10-minute combat compilation published by Yemen’s War Media on August 21 illustrates this growing tactical dominance.
The video documents Rujum multi-rotor hexacopters dropping precision mortar rounds vertically onto Presidential Leadership Council (PLC) positions in Marib and along the western coast.
In one strike, a dropped munition hits a Saudi M1A2S Abrams main battle tank, triggering a massive secondary explosion that destroys the heavy armor.
Another sequence records a lethal double-tap strike on PLC technicals, where a second mortar bomb detonates as mercenary troops rush to assist initial casualties.
The strikes killed dozens of Saudi-backed mercenaries, destroyed heavy bulldozers, and incinerated weapons caches.
Offshore, Yemeni units sank two Saudi military landing ships transporting arms near Mokha port and destroyed over ten armed gunboats operated by Saudi-backed elements.
In an attempt to cover up these losses, Saudi-backed mercenaries claimed on Friday to have targeted Yemeni construction equipment in western Yemen. However, these claims fail to alter the strategic balance on the ground.
Sanaa’s military command has warned Riyadh that any further escalation will draw a swift, comprehensive response.
Saree declared that Riyadh has no choice but to permanently lift its blockade, end the aggression, pay delayed public salaries, and pull out all occupying forces.
The spokesman also renewed his appeal to Yemenis stationed in Saudi-backed camps, urging them to abandon enemy ranks and return home before further retaliatory operations take place.

articles.title: FSB arrests foreign national over Ukrainian drone plot (VIDEO)
articles.body:
FSB arrests foreign national over Ukrainian drone plot (VIDEO)
Russian security officers have detained a foreign national suspected of surveilling critical infrastructure sites on behalf of Ukrainian intelligence, the Federal Security Service (FSB) announced on Friday.
The suspect was taken into custody this month in Murmansk Region near the border, as he sought to illegally cross into Norway, the agency said in a statement. The detained man is believed to have a longstanding relationship with Kiev’s special services, having voluntarily contacted them back in 2023 for the first time, according to FSB.
The man’s Ukrainian handlers had ordered him to travel to Moscow and conduct reconnaissance at a key train hub “to identify freight trains transporting petroleum products, as well as administrative buildings in the city center,” the FSB said. He was involved in an “attempt to launch an FPV drone” to gather the intelligence, it added.
The Kiev regime has intensified attempts to stage terrorist attacks in Russia to compensate for the mounting pressure it has been experiencing on the frontline, as well as its inability to inflict “meaningful damage on critical infrastructure sites in Moscow Region,” the agency warned. The planned attacks involve short-range kamikaze drones that were supposed to be launched from an immediate vicinity of targeted sites by planted agents and local collaborators recruited online, including victims of fraudulent Ukrainian call centers, the FSB said. Involvement in such activities incurs heavy penalties under Russian law, up to life behind bars, the agency stressed.
Last month, the FSB said it had thwarted a major Ukrainian FPV drone plot, which involved smuggling 24 AI-guided drones into the country and using them to target a key defense industry enterprise and military airfields. The failed operation had been prepared by Kiev’s intelligence with the direct involvement of Western handlers, the agency said at the time.
The disassembled drones had been flown into Russia using fixed-wing UAVs and balloons, which were collected by the suspects and transferred deeper into the country for assembly and preparations for the attack. However, the whole operation had been closely monitored by Russian secret services from the very beginning, and the perpetrators and their accomplices ended up in custody.

articles.title: NATO Military Committee to Return to Ukraine After Eight Years
articles.body:
Ukraine expects the NATO Military Committee to visit the country in October, marking its first such visit in eight years, Ukrainian Armed Forces (AFU) Commander-in-Chief Mykhailo Drapatyi said on Friday, Aug. 21.
Drapatyi made the announcement after his first meeting with NATO Military Committee Chair Adm. Giuseppe Cavo Dragone, whom he thanked for his support for Ukraine at the Alliance’s highest military level.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We are expecting the NATO Military Committee to visit Ukraine in October. The last such visit took place eight years ago,” Drapatyi said in a Facebook post.
Drapatyi said Dragone had visited Ukraine three times and had seen the situation on the ground firsthand.
The Ukrainian commander briefed Dragone on the situation at the front and discussed Ukraine’s military priorities, including long-range strikes, flexible infantry tactics and the use of robotics on the battlefield.
Air defense remains Ukraine’s priority
Drapatyi said air defense was also a key focus of the discussion, describing the protection of Ukrainian airspace as his priority.
“Protecting the sky is my priority,” he said.
He also emphasized that Ukraine is not only receiving military support from NATO allies but is sharing battlefield experience gained during Russia’s full-scale war.
“We are not only receiving support. We are passing on combat experience that no one else has today, and it works for the security of the entire Alliance,” Drapatyi said.
Australia Hits Russian Man With ‘Foreign Interference’ Charges Over Plot to Infiltrate Ukrainian Military
The NATO Military Committee is the Alliance’s senior military authority and advises NATO’s political leadership on military matters.
Drapatyi said Ukraine and its allies were working toward a common goal and thanked NATO members for their support.

articles.title: British spy plane deploys to Norway for Arctic Stone
articles.body:
An RAF Rivet Joint has deployed to Ørland in Norway for a week-long exercise with the Royal Norwegian Air Force, including training intended to improve interoperability with Norwegian F-35A fighters.
An RAF Rivet Joint intelligence-gathering aircraft has deployed to Ørland in Norway for Exercise Arctic Stone, where British personnel are training alongside the Royal Norwegian Air Force and working with Norwegian F-35A fighters, the UK Defence Journal understands.
According to an RAF news update, the activity is intended to strengthen interoperability between Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A fleet while contributing to NATO’s situational awareness on its northern flank.
Operated by 51 Squadron, the RAF’s Rivet Joint specialises in gathering intelligence from signals across the electromagnetic spectrum. Sensors aboard the aircraft allow its crew to intercept and analyse signals while airborne, providing strategic and tactical intelligence that can contribute to a wider picture of military activity and the surrounding security environment. Ground-based specialists from No. 54 Signals Unit also process and exploit the information gathered by the aircraft.
The RAF described the aircraft’s role by stating: “The aircraft specialises in monitoring signals across the electromagnetic spectrum, giving it the ability to deliver real-time strategic and tactical intelligence in a way few other assets can match.” It added that the combination of airborne crews and ground specialists provides commanders with improved situational awareness “day and night, whatever the operational conditions.”
Exercise Arctic Stone is using that capability in two connected roles. RAF personnel are training directly with their Norwegian counterparts, including activities designed to improve cooperation between the Rivet Joint and Norway’s F-35A force, while the intelligence gathered during the deployment is intended to give commanders a clearer assessment of the operating environment.
The RAF said the exercise would allow both air forces to improve their ability to work together within NATO operations.
Norway’s location makes it particularly relevant to NATO operations in the High North, where the Alliance maintains air, maritime and surveillance activity across an area extending towards the Norwegian and Barents Seas. The RAF said the deployment reflected what it described as the region’s “growing strategic importance” and its increasing relevance to NATO’s northern defences and wider European security.
The service said: “As the security picture in the region continues to evolve, the presence of RAF assets working alongside key allies and partners in the area is becoming an ever more important part of how NATO maintains stability on its northern flank.”
Rivet Joint’s role differs from that of conventional airborne surveillance aircraft because its principal focus is the detection and analysis of electromagnetic emissions rather than visual reconnaissance alone. The RAF argues that modern intelligence operations increasingly require information from multiple sources to be combined, particularly as military communications, sensors and other systems become more digitally connected.
The deployment also provides an opportunity to test how intelligence collected by the aircraft can support other platforms operating in the same battlespace. Integration with Norwegian F-35As is intended to improve the exchange and use of information between different aircraft types, while giving personnel experience of operating within a multinational NATO environment.

articles.title: Iran’s top generals warn of ‘devastating’ response to any threat
articles.body:
Iran’s top generals warn of ‘devastating’ response to any threat
TEHRAN —Iran’s top military commanders have warned that the country is prepared to respond with “crushing, deterrent and devastating” force to any threat or miscalculation by its adversaries, as Tehran continues to emphasize the growing self-reliance of its defense industry.
Major General Ali Abdollahi, Chief of Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces, issued the warning in a message to Caretaker Defense Minister Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza ahead of Iran’s Defense Industry Day on Aug. 22.
Abdollahi described Iran’s defense industry as a manifestation of the country’s indigenous military capabilities, saying its development had strengthened Tehran’s ability to deter threats despite 'unjust sanctions and hostile policies by major powers.'
He paid tribute to defense ministry specialists and personnel who, he said, had played a central role in developing Iran’s military capabilities, including those killed while working on the country’s defense programs.
The commander said the defense industry had become a critical component of Iran’s national power and a key pillar of its security and national standing.
According to Abdollahi, the Defense Ministry’s advances in recent years have extended beyond the production of military hardware, representing a 'deterrent defense industrial revolution.'
He said the transformation encompassed weapons design, technology management, defense economics, knowledge-based supply chains and a more integrated production system aimed at meeting the demands of modern warfare.
Abdollahi attributed Iran’s defense capabilities to a long-standing policy of self-reliance and scientific development, saying the country’s emphasis on domestic technological capacity had enabled it to develop a broad range of defensive and offensive capabilities.
He also linked Iran’s military advances to 'the country’s experience during successive conflicts,' saying the capabilities developed over decades had been demonstrated both in the region and beyond.
The top commander paid tribute to members of Iran’s defense industry who had been killed and said the armed forces maintained a comprehensive state of readiness across multiple domains, including land, maritime, air, air defense, space and cyberspace.
He warned that Iran would respond to any conventional or emerging threat, as well as a 'miscalculation' by its adversaries.
“Any miscalculation or threat will be met with revolutionary, crushing, regret-inducing and devastating responses,” Abdollahi said.
The remarks reflect Tehran’s continued emphasis on military preparedness and indigenous defense production as key elements of its deterrence strategy amid heightened tensions with the United States and Israel.
The caretaker defense minister, Brigadier General Majid Ebn al-Reza, in a separate message on the occasion of Iran’s Defense Industry Day on Friday, emphasized that Iran has never initiated aggression against any country and will not allow any military attack against it.
Ebn al-Reza stressed that the country’s defense capabilities are aimed at preventing war and aggression, rather than waging war, while reaffirming Tehran’s determination to defend its territory, independence and security.
“Iran’s defense power today is not for warmongering, but rather for preventing war and aggression. We have never been, and will never be, the initiators of aggression against any country,” the general stated.
“We are not people who engage in military aggression, but we will never allow military aggression against our territory, independence and security,” he underlined.

articles.title: Russia occupied Anton’s home when he was 10. At 18, he volunteered to fight against Ukraine
articles.body:
Now held in a POW camp in western Ukraine, Anton does not consider himself a traitor. He calls Putin “my President” and said he joined Russia’s army to defend “my land,” the BBC reported.
The BBC interviews show what more than a decade of Russian rule has produced in occupied Donbas. Moscow has replaced Ukrainian schools, media, and public institutions while presenting the occupied regions as permanent parts of Russia. It also recruits residents or forces them to fight against Ukraine.
The BBC said prisoners could refuse and were interviewed without guards or cameras.
Almost all its Ukrainian-born interviewees from territories occupied since 2014 said they had enlisted willingly. Anton said he was not a traitor and called Vladimir Putin “my President.”
His friends also volunteered. Messages announcing their deaths followed: “Dead, dead, dead.”
Forced conscription of Ukrainians in occupied territory
One prisoner from Donetsk Oblast told the BBC he had been forced to fight. He wanted only to return to his wife and children.
The BBC cited an official intelligence-based estimate that Russia forcibly conscripted more than 50,000 Ukrainians in occupied areas. It noted that other estimates were higher.
Ukrainian veteran Pavlo Pshenychnyi told Hromadske that occupation authorities used planted drug evidence to push him into Russia’s army. They threatened him with up to 12 years in prison.
Article 51 of the Fourth Geneva Convention prohibits occupying powers from compelling protected residents to serve in their armed forces.
Anton and the Russification of occupied Ukrainian territory
Russia took control of Anton’s home while he was still in primary school. By adulthood, he called himself Russian and dismissed his Ukrainian surname as irrelevant.
Putin’s 2025 policy decree set a 95% target for “all-Russian civic identity” by 2036 and ordered the integration of occupied Ukrainian regions into Russian education, culture, and media.
Kherson-based outlet MOST reported that Russia will introduce compulsory textbooks on 1 September, presenting four occupied Ukrainian regions as historically Russian.
Ukraine’s Center for Countering Disinformation reported in 2025 that more than 100 teenagers from occupied Luhansk attended a Russian military camp. They received firearms, drill, and guard-duty training.
The center described the camp as part of a wider effort to spread Russian war propaganda and hostility toward Ukraine.
Petro Yatsenko of Ukraine’s POW Coordination Headquarters told the BBC that these prisoners were strongly pro-Russian. He said their national identity was “very blurred.”
Ukraine still considers them Ukrainian and treats Russia’s control of their home regions as temporary, the BBC noted.

articles.title: UK-German strike programme includes hypersonic weapon
articles.body:
The UK and Germany are jointly developing deep-strike options including a stealthy cruise missile and a hypersonic glide vehicle, with both countries working towards outline entry into service during the 2030s.
The UK and Germany are working on both stealthy cruise missile and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions under their joint Deep Precision Strike programme, with outline in-service dates extending into the 2030s, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Defence Minister Luke Pollard provided further detail on the programme in a written parliamentary answer to Conservative MP Stuart Anderson, who asked what the UK’s partnership with Germany on deep precision strike weapons entails.
Pollard confirmed that a Memorandum of Understanding signed by the two countries in March 2026 has allowed British and German teams to begin aligning their military requirements and jointly examining technical solutions with industry.
He said: “The UK and Germany signed a Memorandum of Understanding in March 2026 which has enabled joint activities, including with industry, to align military requirements and invest in technical solutions under the Deep Precision Strike programme.”
The programme is examining two distinct missile approaches. Pollard confirmed: “The programme includes Stealthy Cruise and Hypersonic Glide Vehicle missile solutions.”
A stealthy cruise missile would broadly pursue survivability through reduced detectability and a powered flight profile, while a hypersonic glide vehicle represents a different technical approach, travelling at hypersonic speed following launch and manoeuvring towards its target. The parliamentary answer does not provide performance figures, ranges or details of the propulsion and launch arrangements envisaged for either solution, of course.
Pollard said the two governments had reached what he described as “positive alignment” on some of the principal requirements for the programme. He said: “There is positive alignment between the UK and Germany on key programme parameters, including operational concepts and outline target in service dates into the 2030s.”
The wording indicates that the programme remains at a relatively early technical and requirements stage, with the two countries working towards common operational concepts before later development and procurement decisions. British and German teams are currently overseeing technical work already placed with industry while preparing the next stage of contracting.
Pollard said: “Joint UK and Germany teams are now focused on delivering the currently contracted technical work with industry as well as shaping follow on contracts, underpinned in the UK by the funding outlined under the Defence Investment Plan.”
The Deep Precision Strike effort forms part of growing UK-German defence cooperation and is intended to address future requirements for weapons capable of striking targets at considerable distance. The latest answer is significant in explicitly identifying both stealthy cruise and hypersonic glide vehicle solutions as components of the work, while also placing the anticipated service timeframe in the 2030s.
The current phase is focused on technical work with industry, alignment of military requirements and the preparation of follow-on contracts as Britain and Germany determine how the programme will progress towards development and eventual fielding.

articles.title: She joined Ukraine’s army in 2019. Seven years later, she is still feeding the front
articles.body:
Mariia's working day starts at 4:30 a.m. A cook with the reconnaissance battalion of Ukraine's 40th Artillery Brigade, she has cooked for as many as 860 soldiers at once—borsch at military scale, and the steady work of keeping a brigade fed—Army Inform writes in a profile of her service.
Mariia's seven years in uniform put a human scale on a war that began in 2014: one working life spent feeding soldiers.
Mariia's path to that kitchen began long before the full-scale invasion. She wanted to enlist in 2014, when Russia's war in the Donbas started, and joined the army in 2019, she told Army Inform. Her first posting took her to Popasna, in the east, where she served for eight months. Russia's full-scale invasion, in February 2022, caught her unit in Kharkiv Oblast.
One moment from the first weeks of the invasion has stayed with her, she told Army Inform: in March 2022, an elderly couple who assumed the soldiers had nothing gave them what little they had themselves—ten eggs and four cigarettes. She has kept cooking in the years since.

articles.title: Russian 'double-tap' strike on shopping center in Ukraine kills 14, wounds 120
articles.body:
At least 14 people were killed and more than 120 wounded on Friday when two Russian drones struck a shopping center in the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih, authorities said.
Twenty-two children were among the wounded in the daytime attack on President Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown, regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha said on the Telegram messaging app.
"There are 29 people in serious condition, including five children," he said.
He posted a photo of black smoke billowing from a large industrial building.
'Absolutely cynical, despicable,' says Zelensky
Zelensky called the attack "absolutely cynical and despicable," saying that a second Russian drone hit the shopping center half an hour after the first in a deliberate attempt to target emergency services.
"Attacks like these are nothing less than terrorist acts," Zelensky said on Telegram, urging the world to hold Russia to account.
Russia is escalating its air war on Ukraine as fighting on the battlefield grinds toward the 4-1/2 year mark. On Thursday, 17 people were killed in a Russian ballistic missile attack on the Ukrainian capital Kyiv.
Ukraine has also stepped up its own attacks on Russia, targeting oil facilities and logistics infrastructure to try to undermine Moscow's ability to wage war.

articles.title: Royal Navy ends four-month command of NATO task group
articles.body:
Commodore Maryla Ingham has handed command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor after four months spanning Baltic Sentry, Arctic operations, major anti-submarine exercises and a deployment across the Atlantic.
The Royal Navy has completed four months in command of Standing NATO Maritime Group One, handing leadership of the alliance task group to France after operations stretching from the Baltic and High North to the eastern seaboard of the United States, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Commodore Maryla Ingham formally handed command to French Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor in Reykjavik, Iceland, bringing to an end a tenure that began in April and included Baltic Sentry, Arctic Sentry, Exercise Dynamic Mongoose and the US-led FLEETEX 250. According to a Royal Navy news update, the task group also supported protection of critical national infrastructure, anti-submarine warfare, boarding operations, gunnery, casualty evacuation and multinational integration across several maritime theatres.
The handover follows an interview with UK Defence Journal last month in which Ingham described the pace and breadth of the deployment while speaking from her flagship at sea in the middle of a gunnery shoot. She said the group had moved almost immediately into Baltic Sentry after taking command, spending around a month on the operation before heading north for Dynamic Mongoose 26 off Norway, a major anti-submarine exercise involving three live submarines, five maritime patrol aircraft and a multinational surface force.
Ingham told UK Defence Journal: “We started off in April. We went straight into enhanced vigilance activity, Baltic Sentry, which is to protect critical underwater infrastructure, and we were there for about a month.” She continued: “Then we went up off Norway, and we were the lead for Exercise Dynamic Mongoose 26, which was a major ASW exercise, multinational, three live submarines, five MPAs. Goodness, I can’t even remember how many ships we had.”
From there, the group crossed the Atlantic for FLEETEX 250, a US Second Fleet-led exercise which at one point expanded to ten ships, before taking part in the International Naval Review marking the 250th anniversary of the United States Navy in New York. The Royal Navy said the wider exercise involved 30 warships operating off Virginia and North Carolina. Ingham subsequently described the group’s integration into the Commander Task Force Atlantic activation as particularly important because it demonstrated multinational command and control across the surface, air and underwater domains.
She told UK Defence Journal that the activity was “all about demonstrating command and control of multinational forces on the sea, in the air, and underwater, and that’s the first time that’s been practised.” After returning across the Atlantic, the group called at Glasgow before heading back to sea for gunnery and operations in the High North ahead of the eventual handover in Iceland.
One of the most tangible operational changes during Ingham’s command came through Baltic Sentry, where NATO has increased its focus on protecting subsea cables, pipelines and other critical infrastructure. Ingham said the operation had reduced NATO’s reaction time to incidents involving critical underwater infrastructure from around 17 hours to approximately one hour. She also described a Baltic operating picture in which almost all activity could now be observed or tracked by the alliance.
“It’s also reduced our reaction time to critical underwater incidents from around 17 hours to an hour,” she said. “And it’s really enhanced our situational awareness.” She added: “I’m really confident that there is very little that happens in the Baltic without us being aware of it.”
The group encountered Russian naval forces during the deployment, although Ingham characterised those interactions as routine and professional rather than confrontational. “Did we have interactions with the Russian Navy? Yes, we did. But they were all safe and professional,” she said. “At the end of the day, a lot of those areas are international waters, and we all patrol them together, because that’s the nature of the sea.”
She repeatedly spoke on the protection of seabed infrastructure as one of the group’s central missions, arguing that the Baltic operation had improved not just the quantity of forces available but the way they were coordinated. British, French, Spanish and Turkish ships were among those contributing to Baltic Sentry, alongside aircraft and other NATO capabilities. Ingham said the alliance now had considerably more maritime assets available for such tasks than Russia and was using them in a more structured way.
Another distinctive feature of the deployment was the way the British command staff operated from allied warships. Ingham and her Royal Navy battle staff initially commanded from the German frigate FGS Sachsen before transferring to the Canadian frigate HMCS Ville de Québec, the first time a Royal Navy-led task group had commanded operations successively from ships belonging to two different allied navies. The Royal Navy said this reflected the level of trust and integration within the group.
Ingham made the same point more practically during her interview with UK Defence Journal, describing NATO naval interoperability as something embedded in everyday procedures rather than simply an aspiration. “Out of the 32 nations in NATO, over 25 of them are maritime nations, and we all operate using the same tactics, techniques and procedures,” she said. “So it’s actually really, really seamless to be able to operate in another ship, and we’ve proven that.”
She used replenishment at sea as one example. NATO ships use common fittings and procedures, allowing vessels from different nations to refuel from one another without lengthy adaptation. “Any NATO ship can fuel off any NATO tanker,” Ingham said. “Everybody knows what to expect. Everybody knows how to do it. Everybody practises it. And so when you need to fuel, you’re literally in, fuel, gone.”
The Royal Navy also contributed a Wildcat helicopter from 815 Naval Air Squadron while the staff was embarked in FGS Sachsen, adding surveillance, reconnaissance and force-protection capability. Ships from France, Germany, Belgium, Denmark, the Netherlands, Portugal, Turkey, Spain, Norway, Canada and the United States served with the group at different points during the deployment.
Ingham said, as quoted in the Royal Navy update: “Leading Standing NATO Maritime Group One has been a great privilege. I am incredibly proud of my Battle Staff and the ships from across the Alliance that have served alongside us, demonstrating NATO’s unwavering commitment to collective defence and deterrence.”
She added: “Throughout my tenure, we have shown that our strength at sea comes not from any one Nation, but from the unity, trust and professionalism that bind us together as Allies. In an increasingly complex security environment, that solidarity remains our greatest strategic advantage.”
That reflected the argument she made to UK Defence Journal when asked what the standing maritime group ultimately exists to achieve. “The first one is deterrence, and we mustn’t ever forget that this is a deterrent alliance,” she said, before pointing to Britain’s dependence on maritime trade and undersea communications. She cited 95% of UK imports arriving by sea, around half of its food and 97% of internet data travelling through subsea cables.
For Ingham, the deployment also demonstrated the less visible value of a standing multinational force. “We’re specialist mariners. We are professional, calm, getting on with our jobs. We are not looking for trouble,” she said. “We’re a defensive alliance here to defend over a billion people.”
The handover in Reykjavik brings Ingham’s fifth command at sea to an end and her first commanding a multinational battle staff. Her own description of command remained notably simple despite the scale of the task group: “Execute the mission. Two, keep the ship safe. Three, look after your people.”
Rear Admiral Nicolas Molitor now assumes responsibility for SNMG1 as the standing force continues NATO’s maritime deterrence and defence mission across northern European and Atlantic waters.

articles.title: Russia attacks Ukraine-Moldova border checkpoint for second night in a row
articles.body:
Russia attacks Ukraine-Moldova border checkpoint for second night in a row
Russia struck Ukraine’s Odesa region with drones overnight on August 21, hitting the Tabaky international checkpoint on the border with Moldova, Ukraine’s State Border Guard Service reported.
The attack damaged the checkpoint’s buildings and structures, forcing it to close. Traffic is now being redirected to other border crossings.
It’s the second attack on a border checkpoint in the past 24 hours. The day before, amid a massive strike on Kyiv, Russian forces also struck a border checkpoint on the border with Moldova in the Odesa region, among other targets, Volodymyr Zelensky said. Foreign Ministry head Andrii Sybiha added that these are “not isolated incidents,” saying Russia “is increasingly testing the resolve of NATO and its partners by violating the sovereignty of neighboring countries.”
Moldova’s Defense Ministry reported that a drone entered the country’s airspace overnight on August 20, amid the strikes on Ukraine. Preliminary data indicate it was a Shahed-136, the Russian modification known as Geran-2.
At Meduza, we are committed to transparency about our use of artificial intelligence in the newsroom. The story you’re reading was written by one of our living, breathing journalists and translated from Russian using an AI model configured to follow our strict editorial standards. This translation process is the result of extensive testing and refinements to ensure our English-language coverage is timely and accurate. A Meduza editor reviews every draft before publication.
