articles.title: Russian groups keep trying—and failing—to reach Lyman, gateway to Donbas’ fortress belt, officer says
articles.body:
Logistical problems are stopping Russian small infantry groups from reaching Lyman, a 53rd Brigade officer told Army TV on 21 August, ArmyInform reported.
Russia is trying to capture Lyman and use it as a launchpad for an advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk. Its forces have repeatedly tried to push into the city. They have reached its eastern edge but have not secured a foothold inside, according to Ukraine’s Joint Forces.
Junior Lieutenant Volodymyr Hirniak, a communications officer with Ukraine’s 53rd Separate Mechanized Brigade, said the situation in the unit’s sector remained tense but had “not changed too radically.”
Russian forces continued to use drones, including fiber-optic models, Hirniak said. On the ground, they were sending small infantry groups to slip through Ukrainian lines and create confusion inside the brigade’s defensive positions.
The tactic was neither new nor confined to the 53rd Brigade’s sector, he added. Russia’s immediate aim was to reach Lyman and “open a gate” for further advances.
However, logistical problems were preventing the groups from achieving that aim, according to Hirniak. Ukrainian troops later detected and neutralized the infiltrating teams, he said.
ArmyInform did not report how many groups had attempted to advance, where within the brigade’s sector the incidents occurred, or over what period. Hirniak’s account could not be independently verified.
Why Russia keeps pushing toward Lyman
Lyman is a frontline city in northern Donetsk Oblast that blocks Russia’s northern route toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, part of Ukraine’s fortified Donbas “fortress belt.” Russia occupied the city for about four months in 2022 before Ukrainian forces liberated it on 1 October.
Joint Forces spokesman Viktor Trehubov said on 4 August that Russia needed to capture Lyman and establish a base there before advancing south toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Russia has pressed towards Lyman for more than a year. In July 2025, another Ukrainian officer said Russian gains near the city remained slow and costly despite repeated attempts to exploit gaps in Ukrainian lines.

articles.title: Over 11,000 Zanoza FPV drones delivered to special military op zone — manufacturer
articles.body:
MOSCOW, August 21. TASS/. More than 11,000 Zanoza FPV drones of various models have been delivered to Russia’s special military operation zone in Ukraine since 2022, the manufacturer, Zanoza Drones, told TASS.
"The 10-inch Zanoza-10 FPV drone, developed by Urals specialists, is being successfully deployed across all key sectors of the battle contact line, where it has proven its effectiveness despite the enemy’s intense electronic warfare. To date, total deliveries exceed 11,000 drones in various configurations: of these, more than 10,000 are standard radio-controlled versions and over 1,000 are specialized fiber-optic-controlled drones. "We are not resting on our laurels: active work is underway to increase the range of the fiber-optic versions, while paying special attention to maintaining the reliability of the communication channel and reducing the risk of signal loss at maximum ranges," the company stated.
The company specified that it continues to improve the drones based on combat experience and feedback from Russian military personnel. "Based on feedback from the front, we carried out a comprehensive upgrade of the Zanoza-10 hardware component, significantly enhancing protection against external and onboard interference, which guarantees the stability and clarity of the radio signal under the harshest combat conditions," the manufacturer noted.
The Zanoza series drones are designed to carry a warhead of up to 3.5 kg over a distance of up to 40 km. "The drone’s confirmed strike range under real-world conditions reaches 42 km. The drone is effective not only as a means of engaging armored targets, vehicles, and fortifications. It can be used for reconnaissance, as well as for delivering necessary supplies to the combat zone. The fiber-optic version of the drone is completely immune to electronic jamming and is equipped with 15-, 20-, and 25-km cables," the company emphasized.

articles.title: US Army Corps of Engineers chartered plane crashes near Alaska radar site, killing all 8 aboard
articles.body:
Plane crashed on second attempt to land in heavy fog in Alaska, killing all 8 aboard, officials say
JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — A plane that crashed at a remote military site in western Alaska, killing all eight people on board, was making its second runway approach in heavy fog when it lost contact, authorities said Friday.
The Cessna’s two pilots could not see the gravel airstrip and were flying solely by instruments when the plane crashed about midday Thursday, Clint Johnson, the National Transportation Safety Board’s Alaska region chief, told a virtual news conference.
Regulations required that they abort their first landing attempt because of the lack of visibility, he said, and the plane crashed on its second attempt, about one-third of a mile (0.5 kilometers) from the runway. The runway is surrounded by mountainous terrain on three sides, and the Federal Aviation Administration recommends pilots use GPS and other instruments when they land there.
On board were the pilots, two employees of the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and four contractors. Two of the contractors were employees of Calista Brice, a collection of companies that perform construction, engineering, logistics and other work in remote areas. Calista Brice is a subsidiary of Calista Corp., an Alaska Native regional corporation.
The military has not said what work they were performing at the Cape Newenham Long Range Radar Site, about 450 miles (725 kilometers) west of Anchorage on Alaska’s southwest coast.
NTSB investigators were traveling to the scene Friday.
The radar site was built in the 1950s as part of a network designed to provide early warning of a missile attack by the Soviet Union. Today, it monitors the skies off the coast in the direction of Russia, North Korea and China.
Those on board were “dedicated professionals carrying out a vital mission in a demanding environment,” U.S. Air Force Lt. Gen. Robert Davis, commander of Alaskan Command, the Alaskan North American Aerospace Defense Command Region and Eleventh Air Force, said in a statement Thursday.
“This is a devastating loss for our military family and the communities we serve,” Davis said.
Johnson said search teams found the fragmented wreckage after the twin-engine Cessna 441, also known as a Cessna Conquest, lost contact. Its final flight path was captured by radar at the site, he said.
Weather conditions were changing Thursday as heavy fog rolled through the area. An automated observation system not far from the airport reported a low cloud ceiling, fog and visibility of about 10 miles (16 kilometers) in the minutes before the crash, but the next update about 15 minutes after it showed visibility of less than one-quarter mile (0.40 kilometers), according to Carrie Haisley, the meteorologist in charge of the National Weather Service’s Alaska sector operations center.
Mike O’Donnell, who oversaw airport safety programs and accident investigations for much of his 17 years at FAA, said it sounded as if weather conditions were bad enough that the pilots should have diverted and landed somewhere else.
The airstrip is at a private military site managed by the Pacific Air Forces Regional Support Center. It’s part of a network of remote radar sites that tracks aircraft operating in Alaska’s airspace and along its borders, a statement from Alaskan Command said.
The outpost at Cape Newenham closed in 1983 after a new radar was installed, and now the site is visited only occasionally by civilian contractors who perform maintenance on the system.
The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers said the two employees who died were part of a “project delivery team en route to a project site in support of the U.S. Air Force.” The statement did not provide additional details about the work.
Johnson said the flight was operated by Security Aviation based in Anchorage. The charter company did not immediately respond to emails seeking comment.
___
Associated Press writer Kathy McCormack in Concord, New Hampshire, contributed to this report. Funk reported from Omaha, Nebraska.

articles.title: More than 170 combat engagements took place and 6,700 drones were launched — General Staff on the situation at the front
articles.body:
More than 170 combat engagements took place and 6,700 drones were launched — General Staff on the situation at the front
Kyiv • UNN
Russian forces carried out 75 airstrikes, launched 6,751 drones, and dropped 219 guided aerial bombs. They attacked most actively in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions.
Overall, since the beginning of this day, 172 combat engagements have taken place at the front. The enemy launched 6,700 drones and dropped 219 guided aerial bombs, and is actively operating in the Pokrovsk and Kostiantynivka directions, UNN reports, citing the General Staff’s update.
The aggressor carried out 75 airstrikes using 219 guided aerial bombs, deployed 6,751 kamikaze drones for the attacks, and carried out 1,939 shellings of the positions of our troops and populated areas
In the North Slobozhanskyi and Kursk directions, four combat engagements have taken place since the beginning of the day; the enemy carried out 54 shellings of the positions of our troops and populated areas.
During the day, in the South Slobozhanskyi direction, the enemy stormed the positions of our units 11 times toward the settlements of Izbytske, Radkivka, Kovalivka, Okhrimivka, and Mytrofanivka. Two of these assault actions are ongoing.
In the Kupiansk direction, the enemy conducted no offensive operations.
Four attempts by the invaders to advance were repelled in the Lyman direction toward the settlements of Lyman, Shyikivka, Cherneshchyna, and Novoselivka. One of these attacks is ongoing.
In the Sloviansk direction, the Defense Forces halted eight attempts by the invaders to advance in the areas of the settlements of Kryva Luka, Pyskunivka, and Mykolaivka. The battle continues.
In the Kramatorsk direction, the Russian invaders carried out four offensive actions toward Yurkivka and Nykonorivka and in the area of Nykyforivka.
In the Kostiantynivka direction, the Defense Forces repelled 20 enemy assaults in the areas of the settlements of Kostiantynivka, Ivanopillia, Illinivka, Novoselivka, Novomykolaivka, Shakhove, Sofiivka, Vilne, and toward the settlement of Dolha Balka. One combat engagement is ongoing.
The enemy carried out 23 attacks in the Pokrovsk direction. The occupiers attempted to advance in the areas of the settlements of Bilytske, Udachne, Muravka, Novopidhorodne, and toward the settlements of Hannivka, Novyi Donbas, Svitle, Shevchenko, Vasylivka, and Serhiivka. Two combat engagements are still ongoing.
According to preliminary estimates, 35 occupiers were eliminated here today and 14 wounded; one tank, six vehicles, three artillery systems, one fuel and lubricants depot, one ammunition depot, and 27 shelters for enemy personnel were destroyed. Two vehicles, five guns, and 98 shelters for enemy personnel were damaged. A total of 416 unmanned aerial vehicles of various types were destroyed or suppressed.
In the Oleksandrivka direction, the enemy carried out three attacks in the areas of Novyi Zaporizhzhia, Maliivka, and Yalta.
In the Hulyaipole direction, the Defense Forces repelled three enemy attacks toward the settlement of Tsvitkove.
In the Orikhiv direction, our defenders halted two attempts by the enemy to advance in the areas of Plavni and Mali Shcherbaky. One of them is still ongoing.
In the Prydniprovske direction, the enemy conducted no offensive operations.
There were no significant changes in the situation in the other directions, the General Staff concluded.

articles.title: Kayhan: The time has come for America to leave West Asia
articles.body:
Kayhan: The time has come for America to leave West Asia
Kayhan, in an article, points to the desperation of the United States in its war with Iran. Six months have passed since the US and Israel launched their war against Iran, but Iran fought not only the United States but also NATO members, regional states, and Israel, and forced them all to their knees through steadfast resistance.
Experts argue that Iran fought two nuclear powers without fear, and in the midst of this conflict a new deterrent capability emerged for Iran. By closing the Strait of Hormuz — and causing severe economic shock to the US and the global economy — Iran demonstrated both the ability and the will to shut the strait. Iran’s extensive missile and drone attacks on at least 20 US bases in eight regional countries, combined with Washington’s inability to protect these bases or ensure the security of their host nations, have led many analysts, including some inside the United States, to conclude that the time has come to shut down these bases and withdraw US forces from West Asia.
Iran: Avoiding extremist interpretations of the Caspian Convention
The Iran newspaper analyzes the legal status of the Caspian Sea, Iran’s position within this body of water, and the signing of the Caspian Convention. Iran’s power and interests in the Caspian Sea do not stem solely from legal frameworks or international treaties. Rather, Iran’s true value lies in its geographic position — a position that can become geopolitical power only through infrastructure development, strengthened transport corridors, active participation in Central Asia, Caucasus, and Eurasian routes, and an energetic diplomatic strategy. Both the “50 percent share for Iran view and, conversely, the 9 percent share” view are forms of extremism that ignore the mechanisms outlined in the convention. Therefore, the issue must be examined precisely and based on legal and security considerations, without falling into either extreme. Ultimately, Iran must consider three elements simultaneously — law, power, and timing — and understand their interdependence to make optimal use of existing opportunities and secure its national interests.
************Ettelaat: Trump claims he has launched an economic war against Iran
 
 Ettelaat reviews Trump’s latest claim. Trump — having failed on the military front and now under pressure from global and domestic public opinion — has adopted a hostile anti‑Iranian stance and declared the start of an economic war. Trump’s contradictory behavior shows he is trying to construct a narrative of victory for himself after an unjustified attack on Iran. This approach has deepened Tehran’s distrust and reinforced Washington’s repeated pattern of avoiding commitments in signed agreements. Washington’s efforts to portray Iran as weakened economically or militarily, followed by attempts to create hope that Iran might accept an unequal agreement, are described as a miscalculation — one that Iranian officials have repeatedly rejected.
Javan: Iran’s symmetric response in Hormuz and Bab al‑Mandab
Javan discusses Iran’s coordination with its regional allies and a strategic defeat for the United States. Iran and its partners, with a precise understanding of the new battlefield, delivered a symmetric — and even superior — response. Iran, in strategic coordination with the Houthis, first sought to bring the Strait of Hormuz fully under its control. Then, it contributed to further restricting and nearly closing Bab al‑Mandab. As a result, two critical chokepoints of global energy and trade were simultaneously placed under pressure. This action increased economic and political costs for the US and its allies. By targeting the same type of strategic assets that the US had focused on — production, supply, and transport chains — Iran delivered a proportionate and deterrent response. What has unfolded in recent weeks is not a series of isolated incidents but a coherent and predictable pattern of conflict in which both sides are operating within a single battlefield: the battlefield of strategic supply chains.
Shargh: Disruption in Iran–UAE trade and economic relations
Shargh analyzes the suspension of the UAE’s trade exchanges with Iran. The flames of war in the Persian Gulf have engulfed two major trading partners. After the conflict, the UAE has run into the hard barrier of the Strait of Hormuz in exporting its oil and is experiencing a downturn in its tourism industry. Meanwhile, Iran is facing strained relations with one of its largest commercial partners. The war has driven the two neighboring trade partners apart to the point that Iran has barred Emirati oil tankers from passing through the Strait of Hormuz, and the UAE has explicitly announced that all trade and financial transactions with Iran are suspended until further notice. The political and economic interests of neighboring states are deeply intertwined, and neither side can easily deny this reality. Therefore, both countries must reconsider their relationship and create conditions for peace and reconciliation.

articles.title: Stars and Stripes editor says he has been fired for insubordination after doing interview
articles.body:
Pentagon dismisses Stars and Stripes leadership after editor, reporter oppose military interference
The Pentagon on Friday fired the editor-in-chief of Stars and Stripes and a top reporter for insubordination after they spoke publicly against any interference by the Defense Department in the military news outlet that has a long history of editorial independence. It was the latest move by an administration that has grown increasingly aggressive toward the news media.
The newspaper’s publisher, who announced his impending retirement days ago, was also dismissed.
Erik Slavin, editor-in-chief of the military newspaper that is partly funded by the Pentagon, told The Associated Press he was dismissed for insubordination after an interview he gave that objected to potential censorship by the U.S. military. He received a notice of separation, as did publisher Max Lederer — who had just announced his upcoming retirement — and Middle East reporter Lara Korte, Slavin said.
The moves come at a time when the Trump administration, in its second term, has been progressively combative toward the media — including sharply curtailing Pentagon access for the press corps that covers the Defense Department. Trump or other parts of the executive branch have also, in policy and in the courts, grappled with The Wall Street Journal,The Associated Press and The New York Times — in addition to using the FCC to target broadcast networks.
Slavin said he was being fired “for stating in a CBS interview that hypothetical censorship of news for service members would constitute a red line.” Korte participated in the same interview.
“I stand by the principle that Stars and Stripes must remain editorially independent, as required by law and by the department’s own policies,” Slavin said.
Media leaders are troubled
National Press Club President Mark Schoeff Jr. called the firing of Slavin “another brazen attempt by the Pentagon to dictate coverage of the military” and said it should be immediately reversed.
“Firing a newspaper editor after he publicly defended his newsroom’s editorial independence is deeply troubling, and it should concern every journalist and every member of the U.S. military who depends on independent reporting,” Schoeff said.
Neither Lederer nor Korte immediately responded to emailed requests for comment. Korte said on X: “Today, I was informed that the Department of Defense is firing me for insubordination after I told a CBS reporter that I work for Stars and Stripes — not the Pentagon, not the administration, and not any policy maker.”
Earlier this week, longtime publisher Lederer announced his retirement effective at the end of September. He made his announcement a few weeks after the Pentagon installed a new deputy publisher, an active duty service member, under him at the newspaper without his prior knowledge. Three Democratic senators on Thursday wrote to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, asking why the new deputy — Navy Capt. William Urban — had been installed.
The retirement of Lederer, who had been at Stars and Stripes for three decades and publisher since 2007, comes as Hegseth’s Pentagon has moved to exert editorial control and eliminate what it asserts are “woke distractions.”
“Stars and Stripes will be custom tailored to our warfighters,” Sean Parnell, Hegseth’s spokesman, wrote in January on X. “It will focus on warfighting, weapons systems, fitness, lethality, survivability and ALL THINGS MILITARY. No more repurposed DC gossip columns; no more Associated Press reprints.”
In April, the Pentagon fired Jacqueline Smith, ombudsman for the newspaper, whose job had been to safeguard editorial independence.
Lederer, the second full-time civilian in the position, wrote in a staff memo this week that it had “become clear that my philosophy of leadership, and my understanding of the value and mission of Stars and Stripes, differ in fundamental ways from the direction the leadership of the Department of Defense has for the organization.”
Newly installed Pentagon leader outlines his plan
In a letter posted on Stars and Stripes, Urban wrote of his plans and said: “I understand that I am now part of a team, committed to editorially independent journalism that best serves our most important customer, which is our service members, their families, and our greater military community.”
“I am a media junkie who has served as a communication professional engaged in being a spokesman for some of the hardest Public Affairs assignments in the Navy and Department of War for more than 20 years,” he wrote.
It was unclear whether Urban, currently titled “military deputy to the publisher,” would now become head publisher. “I can’t comment on what my role will be in the future,” he told the AP.
In a telephone interview, Urban said Stars and Stripes has “a strong team of professional journalists that are focused on the mission of providing our military service members and their families the best possible product. That mission is going to continue. All of us in leadership will continue to advocate for … the best possible journalism going forward.”
He said he had no formal journalism experience but cited his years in public affairs and communications. He said he would be focused on expanding digital journalism at the paper, because the service members to which it caters are often young and are “digital natives.”
“I think we need to get better on the digital side,” he said, “to make sure that we are reaching as many service members as we possibly can and having the impact that we should be having.”
